title: From Fabrication Disorder to Quantum-Protocol Yield in Inverse-Designed Silicon Photonic Beam Splitters
abstract: Telecom-band silicon spin-photon qubits offer a promising platform for scalable quantum networks and distributed information processing, but their fixed emission wavelengths require compact, low-loss beam splitters with precise splitting and fabrication robustness. Conventional designs can face trade-offs between footprint, optical performance, and wavelength-specific operation. Here, we employ adjoint-based inverse design to optimize photonic geometries beyond conventional layouts, developing 1*2 Y-splitters and 2*2 directional couplers for the silicon T (1326 nm) and Al1 (1482.44 nm) spin-photon qubits. The devices achieve footprints of 2.9 and 26 um^2, respectively, with excess losses of 0.14-0.44 dB and back-reflection below 5*10^-4. We assess fabrication tolerance using 100-realization Monte Carlo simulations incorporating etch bias, line-edge roughness, thickness, and refractive-index variations. Mirror symmetry reduces the splitting-ratio spread of the Y-splitter by a factor of seven to nine relative to the directional coupler. We translate these variations into dual-rail fidelity, ideal splitting-ratio-limited Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility, and random-number min-entropy. All realizations satisfy a protocol-performance threshold of 0.95. At 0.99, the tolerated splitting-ratio deviation shrinks from 0.035 for visibility to 0.0035 for min-entropy, and the simulated yields are 68% (T) and 91% (Al1) for coupler visibility and 90% (T) and 66% (Al1) for Y-splitter min-entropy. The tolerance of the target protocol, rather than the device alone, therefore sets the fabrication requirement for silicon spin-photon beam splitters.
one_liner: Inverse-designed silicon beam splitters connect fabrication disorder directly to quantum-protocol performance and yield.
why_it_matters: The study shows that protocol-specific tolerances, especially min-entropy requirements, can dominate photonic fabrication specifications.
detailed_summary: Adjoint optimization produces compact 1×2 Y-splitters and 2×2 directional couplers for silicon T- and Al1-center spin-photon wavelengths, with 0.14–0.44 dB excess loss and back-reflection below 5×10^-4. Monte Carlo analysis over 100 fabrication realizations maps geometric and material disorder into dual-rail fidelity, Hong–Ou–Mandel visibility, and random-number min-entropy. Every realization exceeds a 0.95 protocol threshold, while yields at 0.99 vary strongly by device, wavelength, and protocol metric.
main_result: The devices achieve compact low-loss splitting while revealing protocol-dependent simulated yields and a seven- to ninefold symmetry benefit in splitting-ratio robustness.
application_angle: The workflow enables foundry tolerances to be specified from quantum-network or randomness-generation requirements rather than optical metrics alone.

title: Qubrio: High-Performance Quantum Compilation via Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer an adaptable alternative to traditional quantum compilation heuristics, which bottleneck progress by demanding costly manual redesigns whenever hardware evolves. However, naive single-pass LLM approaches fail under the unique challenges introduced by quantum compilation. We introduce Qubrio, a practical agentic framework that significantly reduces heuristic redesigns through a three-level decomposition. By (1) partitioning programs into sequential operation stages, (2) deploying specialized agents for placement, routing and optimization, and (3) using disaggregated feedback for precise error correction, our system reliably navigates complex physical constraints. Beyond serving as a direct compiler, our LLM framework also uncovers novel strategies that facilitate convoy-style shuttling, substantially enhancing hardware concurrency without sacrificing fidelity. We further integrate these strategies into the previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) compiler, recovering a significant fraction of the LLM's performance advantages. On realistic workloads, our compiler achieves significant improvements in hardware runtime and program fidelity over the SOTA baseline PowerMove, seamlessly adapting to new hardware capabilities. Qubrio features an open user interface for practical use, and its code is publicly available at https://github.com/crosaa/Qubrio.
one_liner: Qubrio uses collaborating LLM agents to place, route, and optimize quantum programs under evolving hardware constraints.
why_it_matters: It reduces reliance on manually redesigned compiler heuristics and discovers shuttling strategies that improve runtime and fidelity.
detailed_summary: Qubrio decomposes compilation into sequential program stages and assigns specialized agents to placement, routing, and optimization. Disaggregated feedback supports targeted correction of constraint violations, while the agents identify convoy-style shuttling that increases hardware concurrency. On realistic workloads, the framework improves runtime and program fidelity over PowerMove and transfers part of its advantage back into a conventional compiler.
main_result: Qubrio outperforms the PowerMove baseline in reported hardware runtime and program fidelity while adapting to new hardware capabilities.
application_angle: The framework could shorten the engineering cycle for compilers targeting rapidly changing quantum processor architectures.

title: Achievability of CSS codes performance limits over Pauli channels under separate ML decoding with bounded graphical complexity
abstract: Capacity-approaching quantum error correction faces a fundamental tension: the required parity-check matrices need to become increasingly dense, while practical decoding and syndrome extraction favor sparse, bounded-degree structures. Reconciling these competing requirements remains an important open problem in quantum code design. We construct Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) code ensembles that approach the CSS rate over memoryless Pauli channels under maximum-likelihood decoding while retaining sparse, bounded-degree graphical representations. The construction separates parity-check density from graphical complexity: although capacity-approaching components may require dense parity-check matrices, they are represented by sparse concatenated factor graphs. We first study a construction combining low-density parity-check (LDPC) and low-density generator-matrix (LDGM) component codes and numerically analyze the average weight distributions of the resulting codes. Motivated by these results, we introduce a second construction based on concatenated LDPC and LDGM codes and generalized irregular repeat-accumulate (GIRA) codes. We derive bounds on the average weight distribution of the resulting sum ensemble and use the Miller-Burshtein framework to prove simultaneous reliability of the two CSS decoding components. Consequently, the proposed ensemble achieves rates arbitrarily close to the CSS hashing bound under separate bit- and phase-error correction, while maintaining bounded graphical complexity, thus providing a foundation for future iterative decoders and indirect syndrome-extraction architectures.
one_liner: Sparse factor-graph CSS ensembles approach the hashing bound under separate maximum-likelihood decoding over Pauli channels.
why_it_matters: The construction reconciles capacity-approaching error correction with bounded graphical complexity suited to practical decoding architectures.
detailed_summary: The authors separate parity-check density from graph complexity by representing dense capacity-oriented components through sparse concatenated factor graphs. They develop LDPC–LDGM and LDPC–LDGM–GIRA constructions, analyze ensemble weight distributions, and apply the Miller–Burshtein framework. The resulting CSS ensemble approaches the CSS hashing bound with separate bit- and phase-error correction while retaining bounded graph degree.
main_result: The proposed ensembles achieve rates arbitrarily close to the CSS hashing bound under separate maximum-likelihood decoding with bounded graphical complexity.
application_angle: The construction provides a theoretical basis for scalable iterative decoders and indirect syndrome-extraction hardware.

title: MBUndo: Sound, Automatic, and Efficient Measurement-Based Uncomputation for Quantum Circuits
abstract: Quantum programs that use temporary values, known as \emph{ancilla} qubits, must explicitly \emph{uncompute} each ancilla back to zero to ensure that the program produces correct outputs. Conventional uncomputation uses unitary quantum gates, whereas leading quantum algorithms now leverage \emph{measurement-based uncomputation} (MBU), which replaces costly unitary $T$ gates with cheaper measurements and phase corrections. Current quantum programming frameworks can use measurement to uncompute specific gates such as Toffoli. No automatic transformation, however, accepts an arbitrary circuit whose ancillas are computed and uncomputed via the standard approach and converts the circuit to use MBU\@. Researchers instead apply MBU to individual circuit designs by hand, which limits algorithm development and compiler optimization. Such a transformation has not existed due to two fundamental unknowns: where MBU applies and which gates realize MBU for an arbitrary computation. To solve these, we first present a static analysis that identifies, for each ancilla qubit, each circuit position where measurement is sound --- subsuming basic assumptions that MBU only applies at the end of a circuit. Next, we present circuit transformations that soundly turn unitary uncomputation gates into efficient phase corrections after measurement --- generalizing rewrite rules from prior literature that are either limited to a single gate or not applicable to a general circuit. We present \textsf{MBUndo}, an integrated compiler pass that automatically converts circuits to measurement-based uncomputation. It requires no user annotations other than which qubits are ancillas, the same as needed by existing uncomputation synthesizers, and can enhance their output circuits. We evaluate \textsf{MBUndo} on 22 benchmarks to reveal \emph{T} gate reductions of ${>}36.5\%$ over uncomputation synthesizers.
one_liner: MBUndo automatically replaces general unitary ancilla cleanup with sound measurement-based uncomputation.
why_it_matters: Automating this transformation cuts expensive T gates without requiring programmers to redesign individual quantum circuits by hand.
detailed_summary: MBUndo statically identifies circuit positions where measuring each ancilla is sound, extending applicability beyond end-of-circuit cases. It then replaces unitary uncomputation with measurement and derived phase corrections for general computations. Across 22 benchmarks, the compiler pass reduces T-gate counts by more than 36.5% relative to uncomputation synthesizers.
main_result: The automatic compiler pass delivers greater than 36.5% T-gate reduction on 22 benchmarks while preserving circuit semantics.
application_angle: Lower T counts can reduce magic-state consumption, execution time, and resource overhead in fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Barycentric programming: Classical realization of programs for universal quantum processors
abstract: A programmable quantum processor implements a target unitary using information stored in a classical or quantum program register. For arbitrary unitaries in $\mathrm{SU}(d)$, quantum programs attain the optimal leading-order memory cost, whereas deterministic classical rounding requires twice as much memory for the same diamond-distance error. We show that this gap disappears when classical randomization is allowed. We introduce barycentric programming, which stores the label of a unitary randomly selected from a finite set, with probabilities chosen so that first-order approximation errors cancel in the averaged unitary channel. Consequently, the diamond-distance error scales quadratically with the discretization spacing. For any $ν$-parameter family of unitaries forming a compact, smooth manifold without boundary, this method achieves error $\varepsilon$ using only $(ν/2)\log_2(1/\varepsilon)+O(1)$ classical bits. We also prove a matching lower bound for arbitrary quantum programs, determining the optimal leading-order program size for general unitary families. Thus, classical randomization achieves the optimal scaling $(ν/2+o(1))\log_2(1/\varepsilon)$ without requiring coherent quantum memory.
one_liner: Randomized classical programs match the leading memory scaling of quantum programs for universal unitary processors.
why_it_matters: Barycentric error cancellation removes the apparent asymptotic memory advantage of coherent quantum program registers.
detailed_summary: Barycentric programming randomly selects a unitary from a finite set with probabilities chosen to cancel first-order approximation errors in the average channel. This makes diamond-distance error quadratic in discretization spacing. For a compact smooth ν-parameter unitary family, it uses (ν/2)log2(1/ε)+O(1) classical bits, matching a derived lower bound for arbitrary quantum programs.
main_result: Randomized classical programs attain the optimal leading scaling of (ν/2+o(1))log2(1/ε) bits without coherent quantum memory.
application_angle: Universal processors can achieve memory-optimal approximate programming using simpler classical storage and randomized control.

title: Performance analysis of cat and GKP breeding protocols with squeezed single-photon input
abstract: Homodyne breeding is a promising optical route for generating large cat states and Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill (GKP) grid states, using readily available squeezed-cat states as inputs. We analyze the performance of protocols, using squeezed single-photon seeds, $\hat{S}(r)\ket{1}$, as squeezed-cat resources and propagating them through the same cat-to-GKP breeding pipeline. For a symmetric tree with $N=2^{m_1}$ seeds, the heralded resource state reduces to a state with a polynomial-Gaussian wavefunction controlled by a single effective width, achieving near-unit fidelity with the desired cat resource state. Our analysis yields closed-form even-cat fidelities and an inverse-design rule for the seed squeezing. We apply these resources to GKP breeding, and find a large overlap with a practical GKP state. We also investigate the effects of practical imperfections, including finite homodyne acceptance windows and photon loss. This study shows that squeezed single-photon inputs provide a viable resource assignment for homodyne cat and GKP breeding, replacing the demanding requirement for high-resolution photon-number-resolving heralding with an on-demand single-photon source.
one_liner: Squeezed single photons provide a practical seed resource for homodyne breeding of optical cat and GKP states.
why_it_matters: The approach replaces demanding photon-number-resolving heralding with on-demand single photons and homodyne conditioning.
detailed_summary: A symmetric breeding tree with N=2^m1 squeezed-single-photon seeds yields a polynomial-Gaussian state governed by one effective width and closely approximating the desired cat resource. The analysis derives closed-form even-cat fidelities and an inverse rule for selecting seed squeezing, then propagates the resource through a cat-to-GKP pipeline. Finite homodyne windows and photon loss are also evaluated as practical imperfections.
main_result: Squeezed single-photon seeds achieve near-unit cat-resource fidelity and large overlap with a practical GKP state in the analyzed breeding protocol.
application_angle: The scheme offers a more accessible route to bosonic resource states for photonic fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Quantum teleportation using photon-added two-mode squeezed Fock states: A comparison with photon-subtracted counterparts
abstract: Quantum state engineering frequently employs non-Gaussian operations, particularly photon addition and subtraction, to tailor and improve the nonclassical characteristics of quantum states. We investigate how photon addition to a two-mode squeezed Fock state (TMSFS) influences its performance in the Braunstein-Kimble quantum teleportation protocol. We obtain the Wigner characteristic function of the photon-added TMSFS (PA-TMSFS) and evaluate the corresponding teleportation fidelities for both Gaussian and non-Gaussian input states. We further compare the teleportation performance of PA-TMSFS with that of its photon-subtracted counterpart by accessing their fidelity enhancements over the parent TMSFS and considering the probabilistic nature of both the operations. Our results demonstrate that photon subtraction provides superior teleportation performance compared with photon addition, with this advantage becoming more pronounced when the success probabilities of the corresponding non-Gaussian operations are considered. In particular, the symmetric $(1,1)$ photon subtraction yields the optimal trade-off between teleportation fidelity and success probability among the configurations investigated. These findings highlight that photon subtraction retains its advantage even when the underlying entangled resource is already non-Gaussian.
one_liner: Photon subtraction outperforms photon addition for teleportation with two-mode squeezed Fock-state resources.
why_it_matters: The analysis identifies symmetric single-photon subtraction as the best fidelity–success-probability trade-off for engineered continuous-variable teleportation resources.
detailed_summary: The study derives the Wigner characteristic function of photon-added two-mode squeezed Fock states and calculates Braunstein–Kimble teleportation fidelities for Gaussian and non-Gaussian inputs. It compares photon addition and subtraction both by conditional fidelity enhancement and by operation success probability. Symmetric (1,1) photon subtraction gives the strongest overall trade-off among the examined configurations.
main_result: Photon subtraction, especially symmetric (1,1) subtraction, provides higher practical teleportation performance than photon addition.
application_angle: The result guides probabilistic resource-state engineering for higher-fidelity continuous-variable quantum communication.

title: Single-port homodyne detection achieves optimal multiphase sensing in an $n$-port ring cavity
abstract: Estimating several phases simultaneously is more than estimating them one at a time: the optimal measurements for different parameters may not commute, and in a multiparameter problem the quantum Cramér-Rao bound is not automatically achievable. Ring cavities are a natural setting for this question, since a single coherent input can be made to interact repeatedly with every internal phase before it is read out. We study the simultaneous local estimation of the $n$ internal phases of a lossless $n$-port ring cavity probed by a fixed-energy multimode coherent state, optimizing over the full coherent-input space and over the operating point of the cavity. We identify a necessary and sufficient condition for the global optimum: the input energy should be distributed equally among the ports, and the internal phases and input phases satisfy a simple phase-matching condition for every port. The optimum is unique up to a common optical phase and minimizes both the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) cost and the sloppiness of the model. At this point the quantum Fisher information matrix is full rank and its spectrum is obtained in closed form, the Uhlmann curvature vanishes, and no incompatibility penalty has to be paid. The precision retains the coherent-state scaling and the dependence on the number of phases, but the cavity feedback reduces the prefactor relative to $n$ independent single-pass experiments. Finally, we show that this bound may be achieved in practice: the Fisher information of a balanced homodyne measurement at each output port, with local-oscillator phases locked to the prepared input phases is equal to the optimal quantum Fisher information. Our results establish the ring cavity as a platform for optimal multiphase sensing and provide the ultimate benchmark against which nonclassical probes may be evaluated for further precision enhancement.
one_liner: Balanced single-port homodyne readout attains the quantum limit for simultaneous phase sensing in an n-port ring cavity.
why_it_matters: It supplies an achievable quantum benchmark and explicit operating conditions for practical cavity-enhanced multiparameter sensors using coherent light.
detailed_summary: The authors optimize a fixed-energy multimode coherent probe and the operating point of a lossless n-port ring cavity for simultaneous estimation of all internal phases. Equal energy per port plus a portwise phase-matching condition yields a full-rank quantum Fisher information matrix, zero Uhlmann curvature, and no incompatibility penalty. Balanced homodyne detection at each output, with local oscillators phase-locked to the inputs, attains the optimal quantum Fisher information.
main_result: A practical balanced-homodyne measurement exactly reaches the globally optimal multiphase quantum Fisher information.
application_angle: The scheme enables cavity-enhanced multiparameter sensing with standard coherent sources and experimentally accessible homodyne receivers.

title: Electromagnetic Information Theory for Programmable Metasurfaces
abstract: Programmable metasurfaces enable fine-grained control of electromagnetic waves and are creating new opportunities for information extraction, information transfer and information processing. Yet, despite exciting experimental demonstrations, their fundamental capabilities remain poorly understood. In this Perspective, we argue that programmable metasurfaces, and programmable wave systems more generally, call for an electromagnetic information theory that addresses limits at two levels, in a unified manner across applications like communications, sensing and computing. First, for a given physical platform, such a theory should bound achievable information manipulations, such as sensing precision, information-transfer rates, and computational performance. Second, at a more fundamental level, it should determine what non-programmable and programmable physical resources bound these system-specific limits, and what minimum resources are required to attain a prescribed level of performance. We discuss emerging theoretical approaches to these questions, and their connection to experimentally realizable systems. We examine how device thickness, programmable degrees of freedom, nonlocality, coupling and multiple scattering constrain these limits. Establishing the envisioned framework could clarify the ultimate capabilities of programmable metasurfaces and guide the design of future wave-based information systems.
one_liner: This Perspective outlines an electromagnetic information theory for bounding programmable metasurface sensing, communication, and computing.
why_it_matters: A unified resource-based framework could translate physical constraints into actionable performance limits for programmable wave hardware.
detailed_summary: The Perspective proposes bounding both the information-processing capabilities of a given programmable wave platform and the physical resources required to reach prescribed performance. It connects sensing precision, transfer rates, and computation to thickness, programmable degrees of freedom, nonlocality, coupling, and multiple scattering. The paper surveys emerging theory and its relationship to experimentally realizable metasurface systems rather than reporting a new device demonstration.
main_result: The authors formulate a research program linking metasurface resources and physical constraints to fundamental information-performance bounds.
application_angle: Such bounds could guide hardware sizing and architecture choices for wave-based sensors, communication links, and analog processors.

title: Towards Optimal Routing Strategies for qLDPC codes on Silicon Spin Qubits
abstract: One of the major challenges of implementing high-rate quantum error correction codes, like qLDPC codes, is realizing the required long-range interactions. Spin qubit platforms can provide this connectivity by shuttling qubits next to each other whenever they need to interact. When doing this, the performance of the code depends on the shuttling strategy. We study memory experiments of the [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle (Gross) code on two shuttling grids for future spin qubit devices: a square grid and a square grid with diagonals. We compare three shuttling strategies, structured and random initial layouts, and a range of shuttling noise models spanning best- and worst-case scenarios. The best strategy minimizes the longest distance travelled rather than the total distance. The initial layout has only a weak effect, whereas adding diagonals to the grid reduces the logical error rate by up to two orders of magnitude which may have implications for future hardware design.
one_liner: Diagonal shuttling links can cut logical errors by up to two orders of magnitude for a qLDPC code on silicon spin-qubit grids.
why_it_matters: The work connects qubit-routing policy and grid connectivity directly to fault-tolerant memory performance, informing future spin-qubit layouts.
detailed_summary: The study simulates memory experiments for the [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle code on square shuttling grids with and without diagonal connections. Three routing strategies, structured and random initial layouts, and multiple shuttling-noise models are compared. Minimizing the maximum distance traveled performs better than minimizing total distance, while diagonal links reduce logical error rates by as much as two orders of magnitude.
main_result: Routing that minimizes the longest shuttle and hardware with diagonal paths deliver the best simulated logical-memory performance.
application_angle: The findings provide concrete routing and interconnect-design rules for implementing high-rate qLDPC protection in scalable spin-qubit processors.

title: Inducing cooperative dynamics in an inhomogeneous many-emitter ensemble with a pulse sequence
abstract: Driving a many-particle quantum system with an appropriately tuned external field can give rise to features in its nonequilibrium dynamics that are absent in the equilibrium counterpart. Cooperative dynamics in a dense ensemble of quantum emitters manifested through superradiance, a burst in the emission intensity as a function of time, is typically suppressed by spectral disparities among emitters in the ensemble. We demonstrate the enhancement of cooperative dynamics in a spectrally inhomogeneous ensemble of quantum emitters when it is driven by a periodic pulse sequence. Using both a semi-analytical mean-field solution and a digital quantum simulation, we examine the coherence of the pulse-driven ensemble and the intensity of the emitted radiation as a function of the spectral disparity in the ensemble, as a function of time, the number of atoms in the system, and as a function of the inter-pulse delay. We identify clear signatures of the enhanced cooperative dynamics for the pulse-driven inhomogeneous ensemble when dephasing in the dynamics of the ensemble is suppressed by a sufficient number of pulses during the individual emitter lifetime. These results demonstrate a post-fabrication tuning knob based on externally applied control fields for the dynamics of the many-emitter ensemble.
one_liner: Periodic control pulses restore superradiant cooperative dynamics in spectrally inhomogeneous emitter ensembles.
why_it_matters: The pulse sequence offers a post-fabrication method to counter ensemble dephasing without requiring tighter emitter-frequency uniformity.
detailed_summary: Using a semi-analytical mean-field model and digital quantum simulation, the authors study coherence and emitted intensity in pulse-driven, spectrally disordered emitter ensembles. They vary spectral disparity, emitter number, time, and inter-pulse delay to identify conditions for enhanced cooperative emission. Superradiant signatures recover when enough pulses suppress dephasing within the individual-emitter lifetime.
main_result: A sufficiently rapid periodic pulse sequence suppresses dephasing and enhances cooperative emission despite spectral disorder.
application_angle: External pulse control could tune fabricated emitter arrays for brighter collective light sources and improved light–matter interfaces.

title: Needle-beam generation from SPDC photons using inverse-designed flat optics
abstract: We experimentally demonstrate the generation of needle-like beams from spontaneous parametric downconversion (SPDC) light using a compact inverse-designed multilevel diffractive lens (MDL). The nonclassical nature of the SPDC source is independently verified through a three-detector heralded Hanbury Brown-Twiss measurement performed before the MDL, yielding a zero-delay second-order correlation value of approximately 0.14. Spatial measurements using an intensified charge-coupled device reveal that the MDL maintains a tightly confined focal distribution over an axial distance of approximately 11 mm under collinear SPDC illumination, substantially reducing diffraction-induced broadening compared with a conventional plano-convex lens of the same nominal focal length. Under non-collinear SPDC illumination, two distinct regions of extended axial confinement are observed, demonstrating the dependence of the engineered focal distribution on the incident spatial field. These results establish a compact flat-optical approach for engineering extended-focus SPDC photon fields, with potential applications in structured quantum photonics.
one_liner: An inverse-designed flat lens creates an approximately 11 mm needle-like focus from nonclassical SPDC light.
why_it_matters: The experiment brings compact extended-depth focusing to photon-pair sources while preserving a verified nonclassical input field.
detailed_summary: The experiment sends SPDC light through an inverse-designed multilevel diffractive lens and maps the resulting field with an intensified CCD. A heralded three-detector Hanbury Brown–Twiss test before the lens gives a zero-delay second-order correlation near 0.14. Under collinear illumination the focus remains tightly confined over about 11 mm, while non-collinear illumination produces two extended-confinement regions.
platform_or_system: SPDC source with multilevel diffractive flat lens
main_result: The flat optic produces an extended needle-like SPDC focus with substantially less axial broadening than a conventional lens.
application_angle: Compact control of photon-field depth of focus can support structured quantum illumination, imaging, and spatially engineered photon interactions.

title: Nonreciprocal generation of Bell states via cooperative dissipation in a qubit-magnon system
abstract: Directionally generating and controlling quantum states is critical in chiral quantum technologies. Here, we propose a scheme for the nonreciprocal generation of Bell states via cooperative dissipation in a qubit-magnon system, consisting of a superconducting transmon qubit and a yttrium iron garnet sphere subject to a bias magnetic field. The cooperative dissipation between them is induced by coupling both to a common transmission-line waveguide. Due to this cooperative dissipation, the system possesses a dark eigenstate within the single-excitation subspace. Under appropriate parameter conditions, the dark eigenstate reduces to a specific Bell state. With the assistance of a drive pulse, the system can be prepared in this Bell state (i.e., the dark eigenstate). In particular, we find that the dark eigenstate corresponds to different Bell states under positive ($+\mathbf{B}_0$) and negative ($-\mathbf{B}_0$) bias fields. Consequently, nonreciprocal Bell-state generation is achieved: $+\mathbf{B}_0$ yields one Bell state, while $-\mathbf{B}_0$ yields the other. Moreover, we define a fidelity-based nonreciprocal rate to quantify this nonreciprocity. Our work establishes cooperative dissipation as a versatile resource for nonreciprocal entangled-state generation, opening a promising route toward chiral quantum technologies.
one_liner: Cooperative waveguide dissipation enables magnetic-field-selectable Bell states in a transmon–magnon hybrid system.
why_it_matters: The scheme turns engineered loss into a directional entanglement resource for chiral quantum networks and hybrid quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: A superconducting transmon and a magnon mode in a YIG sphere couple to a shared transmission-line waveguide, producing cooperative dissipation and a dark state in the single-excitation manifold. Under suitable parameters, that dark state becomes a Bell state that can be populated with a drive pulse. Reversing the bias magnetic field switches between two Bell states, yielding fidelity-defined nonreciprocal state generation.
main_result: The proposal generates distinct Bell states for opposite bias-field directions through a cooperatively dissipative dark state.
application_angle: It offers a route to directional entanglement generation for chiral quantum interconnects and hybrid microwave quantum processors.

title: Brillouin comb line amplifiers for optical atomic clocks
abstract: Optical atomic clocks outperform the microwave clocks at the heart of current timing and navigation infrastructure by orders-of-magnitude, and recent progress in on-chip integration provides the opportunity to widely deploy them. Conventionally, a narrow linewidth laser interrogates the atomic transition, and an optical frequency comb divides its stabilised frequency (hundreds of terahertz) down to a microwave that is electronically countable. The laser(s) impose a significant size, weight, power and cost penalty, which is a current barrier to low-cost, scalable, fully on-chip optical clocks. Here, we position the frequency comb as the central engine of the clock by using Brillouin-amplified comb lines for atomic spectroscopy, which eliminates the need for stable clock lasers. Amplified comb lines reach an ultra-low frequency noise floor of $6\,\mathrm{Hz^2/Hz}$ at $30\,\mathrm{kHz}$ offset, an order-of-magnitude below a high-end commercial fibre laser. We realize a clock based on the $\mathrm{5S}_{1/2}\rightarrow\mathrm{5D}_{5/2}$ transition in $^{87}\mathrm{Rb}$ with competitive fractional frequency stability of $2\times10^{-13}$ at $τ= 1\,\mathrm{s}$, averaging to $9\times10^{-15}$ at $τ= 1000\,\mathrm{s}$. Lastly, we demonstrate a photonic chip-integrated Brillouin amplifier with a record 62.9 dB gain and up to 40 dB transferred noise suppression when pumped with a simple, low-cost diode laser. This opens a new route to compact optical clocks and enables use of atomic transitions lacking low-noise lasers by broadening a comb to the required wavelength and amplifying single lines.
one_liner: Brillouin-amplified frequency-comb lines replace dedicated clock lasers in a compact rubidium optical clock.
why_it_matters: Comb-centered interrogation could reduce the size, power, cost, and wavelength constraints that impede deployable optical clocks.
detailed_summary: Individual optical-comb lines are Brillouin-amplified to an ultra-low frequency-noise floor of 6 Hz²/Hz at a 30 kHz offset. Using the 87Rb 5S1/2→5D5/2 transition, the clock reaches fractional stability of 2×10^-13 at 1 s and 9×10^-15 at 1000 s. A chip-integrated amplifier provides 62.9 dB gain and up to 40 dB transferred-noise suppression with a low-cost diode pump.
main_result: The system demonstrates laser-free comb-line interrogation of an optical clock plus record 62.9 dB gain in an integrated Brillouin amplifier.
application_angle: The architecture supports smaller, lower-cost optical clocks and access to atomic transitions without suitable low-noise clock lasers.

title: Many-Body Correlations in Phase-Space Microscopes
abstract: The recently proposed "phase-space microscope" (PSM) extends quantum gas microscopes by allowing joint, single-shot measurements of position and momentum. We show that the $n$-body correlation functions constructed from such phase-space snapshots determine, in principle, all $n$-body observables of a many-body quantum state. This establishes phase-space imaging as a complete probe of strongly correlated matter, beyond what snapshots of position and momentum can provide---a limitation that goes back to a famous question posed by Pauli. Even without the full reconstruction of the density matrices, the PSM provides valuable insight into the quantum states. We demonstrate this power through several applications: witnessing entanglement hidden from both position and momentum, including between spatially separated collective degrees of freedom; resolving pairing structure across the BEC-BCS crossover, including the phase of the pair wavefunction and the reconstruction of its two-body Wigner function; probing inhomogeneous systems and preformed pairs without long-range order, relevant to the pseudogap phase; extracting the interaction energy in a magnetic field; and measurements of the local Chern marker. Furthermore, we discuss phase imprinting in the matter-wave Fourier plane as an alternative method for probing time-reversal-symmetry-broken phases such as chiral $p$-wave superconductors. Together, these results establish the PSM as a versatile new tool for exploring fundamental features of quantum many-body phases in strongly correlated quantum matter.
one_liner: Phase-space microscope correlations can reconstruct all n-body observables while exposing hidden entanglement and pairing structure.
why_it_matters: Joint single-shot position–momentum imaging could make strongly correlated phases accessible beyond conventional quantum-gas microscopy.
detailed_summary: The work shows that n-body correlations from joint position–momentum snapshots determine all n-body observables in principle. Proposed measurements reveal entanglement invisible in either marginal distribution and reconstruct pairing amplitude, phase, and two-body Wigner functions across the BEC–BCS crossover. The framework also accesses interaction energy, local Chern markers, pseudogap pairing, and time-reversal-broken phases.
main_result: The analysis establishes phase-space snapshots as an informationally complete probe of n-body observables and develops concrete many-body diagnostics.
application_angle: It provides an experimental toolbox for characterizing entanglement, topology, pairing, and inhomogeneous phases in quantum simulators.

title: Belief Propagation-Informed Tesseract Decoding of Quantum LDPC Codes
abstract: In quantum error correction, the decoder must estimate the errors from the measurement data accurately and fast enough to avoid a backlog. Search-based decoders such as Tesseract achieve high accuracy by finding a minimum-weight set of error events with an A* search, but their search effort grows rapidly with the physical error rate and the code size. To reduce this search effort while maintaining a logical error rate close to that of Tesseract, we propose a belief propagation (BP)-guided modification of the Tesseract decoder for quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Damped sum-product BP is applied to the triggered detectors before the Tesseract search. If the detectors triggered by the BP hard decision match the triggered detectors, this hard decision is accepted directly, and the Tesseract search is skipped. Otherwise, the BP marginal probability estimates, weighted by a trust coefficient, modify the search priority, while the path cost keeps the channel-prior weights so that the decoding objective is unchanged. The framework also supports BP-based initialization, in which selected BP decisions form the starting point of a residual search whose signed-cost objective allows incorrect initial decisions to be removed. A node-exploration limit bounds this residual search; if the limit is reached, the decoder falls back to the BP-guided search on the original triggered detector set. The method is evaluated on the [[72,12,6]], [[90,8,10]], and [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle codes under circuit-level noise. With BP-based initialization and a global trust coefficient, the number of Tesseract search nodes expanded is reduced by up to more than two orders of magnitude at low physical error rates, while the logical error rate remains close to that of Tesseract.
one_liner: Belief propagation cuts Tesseract quantum-LDPC decoding searches by over 100× while retaining near-baseline logical accuracy.
why_it_matters: Lower search cost helps real-time decoders keep pace with syndrome acquisition as fault-tolerant quantum hardware scales.
detailed_summary: Damped sum-product belief propagation either supplies an immediately accepted correction or reshapes Tesseract's A* search priorities without changing its channel-prior objective. A residual-search variant initializes from selected BP decisions, allows bad decisions to be removed, and falls back safely when a node limit is reached. Tests on three bivariate bicycle codes under circuit-level noise reduce expanded search nodes by more than two orders of magnitude at low error rates while keeping logical error rates close to Tesseract.
main_result: BP-based initialization and guidance reduce Tesseract node expansions by over two orders of magnitude with little logical-error degradation.
application_angle: The approach improves the latency and computational feasibility of decoding scalable fault-tolerant quantum processors.

title: Taming a macroscopic free mass through continuous quantum measurement
abstract: The free particle is the most elementary dynamical system in quantum mechanics. Despite remarkable progress in quantum control of increasingly massive solid-state mechanical oscillators, the analogous control of the free-particle counterpart has remained elusive. Dissipation and environmental noise have prevented such control in the inherently low-frequency domain of free-particle dynamics---a regime of growing importance for quantum sensing and tests of fundamental physics. Here we realize a suspended 1-milligram rotor operating in the free-particle regime with exceptional environmental isolation. Combining this isolation with a low-noise measurement architecture, we directly resolve thermal fluctuations in the motion associated with a damping rate of only 7~nHz. Through continuous quantum measurement of the rotor, we localize its otherwise unconfined motion, obtaining conditional states with entropic temperatures as low as 140~nK as a quantitative measure of control in the free-particle regime. This is two orders of magnitude below temperatures previously achieved in tabletop optomechanical experiments. We demonstrate immediate utilities of the new operating regime, setting new constraints on modifications of quantum mechanics and benchmarking inferred entanglement-to-decoherence rate ratios nearly two orders of magnitude beyond the state of the art for tests of gravity at the quantum-classical interface.
one_liner: Continuous quantum measurement localizes a 1 mg free rotor into conditional states with entropic temperatures down to 140 nK.
why_it_matters: Quantum control of a macroscopic free mass opens a low-frequency regime for precision sensing and tests at the quantum–gravity boundary.
detailed_summary: A suspended 1 mg rotor operates in the free-particle regime with sufficient isolation to resolve thermal motion associated with only 7 nHz damping. Continuous quantum measurement conditionally localizes its unconfined motion, producing states with entropic temperatures as low as 140 nK. The platform also tightens constraints on modified quantum mechanics and improves inferred entanglement-to-decoherence benchmarks for gravity tests by nearly two orders of magnitude.
main_result: The experiment achieves continuous-measurement control of a macroscopic free mass at a 140 nK conditional entropic temperature.
application_angle: The isolated low-frequency platform can enhance force sensing and enable stronger tests of collapse models and gravity-induced quantum effects.

title: Geometric Phase and Spinor Beam Dynamics of Paraxial Beams
abstract: We show that treating a paraxially propagating electric field as a spinor provides a natural way to include geometric phase in beam propagation models. Importantly, by exploiting differences in the way geometric phase and dynamical phase accrue during propagation, we show that spatial variations in the former can have surprising and rather remarkable consequences for beam dynamics. As an example, we design a beam with a centroid that is predicted to follow a curved path through free space, a prediction we subsequently validate in experiment. The model presented herein does not contradict existing propagation models, but rather shows how to leverage the extra degree of freedom afforded by the spinor angle to make new predictions.
one_liner: A spinor description uses spatially varying geometric phase to make a paraxial beam follow an experimentally verified curved free-space path.
why_it_matters: Geometric-phase engineering adds a new control degree of freedom for structured-light transport, routing, and optical information encoding.
detailed_summary: The authors formulate a paraxial electric field as a spinor so geometric and dynamical phases enter propagation distinctly. Spatial variation of the spinor angle is then designed to alter beam dynamics without contradicting standard paraxial propagation. A beam whose centroid follows a curved trajectory through free space is predicted and experimentally validated.
main_result: Spinor-angle engineering produces and experimentally confirms a beam with a curved centroid trajectory in free space.
application_angle: The method could support passive beam routing and geometric-phase channels in free-space photonics and optical communications.

title: Inline inter-core phase control in multi-core fiber with a commercial polarization controller
abstract: Inter-core phase control is a prerequisite for interferometry in multi-core fiber (MCF), but no compact inline element for this purpose is presently available, and existing approaches require fanout to single-mode fiber or free-space optics. We show that a commercial inline polarization controller, a low-loss and widely available component, can be operated as an inline inter-core phase shifter. Two-core interferometry on a jacketed four-core patchcord gives a reversible inter-core phase of $0.95 \pm 0.02$~rad from a single device, with an operating-point-independent lower bound of $0.38$~rad, driven through repeated load-unload cycles at a rate set by the actuator. A diametrically compressed disk model is used to predict the operating condition: with the input polarization aligned to a principal stress axis the device imparts a relative phase between cores without rotating the polarization state of either, which we verify by polarimetry on all four cores. The response is polarization dependent, falling to less than $0.58$~rad for the orthogonal input. The result is a practical, inline route to inter-core phase control and stabilization in all-MCF interferometers, requiring neither fanout to single-mode fiber nor free-space optics.
one_liner: A commercial inline polarization controller provides reversible inter-core phase tuning in jacketed multi-core fiber without fanout or free-space optics.
why_it_matters: The low-loss, readily available component offers a compact route to phase stabilization for multi-core-fiber interferometers and spatial-mode quantum links.
detailed_summary: The authors repurpose a commercial polarization controller as an inline phase shifter for multi-core fiber. In two-core interferometry on a jacketed four-core patchcord, one device produces a reversible phase shift of 0.95 ± 0.02 rad and an operating-point-independent lower bound of 0.38 rad. A stress-optic disk model and four-core polarimetry show that alignment to a principal stress axis changes relative core phase without rotating either core's polarization.
platform_or_system: Jacketed four-core fiber with inline polarization controller
main_result: The device achieved reversible inter-core phase tuning up to 0.95 ± 0.02 rad while preserving polarization at the aligned operating condition.
application_angle: It can simplify compact phase control and stabilization in all-fiber multi-core interferometers used for spatial-mode quantum communication.

title: Agentic Pipelines for Mapping Topological Codes to Quantum Hardware
abstract: Mapping a prescribed many-body Hamiltonian to a particular quantum hardware is generally an approximate process, resulting in both intended and unwanted quantum dynamics. We introduce an AI-agent-assisted workflow that uses Lean to establish whether an effective device Hamiltonian retains the intended low-energy subspace of the target many-body Hamiltonian. We demonstrate this approach with topological quantum error correction (QEC), providing, to our knowledge, the first Lean-verified pipeline connecting a code space to low-energy states of a device model. Starting from qubits and parity checks, the pipeline constructs the ideal Hamiltonian whose lowest energy states form the intended code space, and determines the excitation gap that protects that code space. It then tests if the device retains the required number of isolated low-energy states and quantifies how closely their subspace matches the intended code space. We compare three bounds on unwanted energy shifts obtained by: summing the interaction strengths, grouping the anticommuting Pauli interactions, and diagonalizing the Hamiltonian. Pauli grouping yields a bound that is tighter than the conventional sum and closer to the diagonalization result, avoiding overly conservative compensation requirements. The workflow also identifies the strongest unwanted interactions and the qubits they affect, providing specific targets for improving device couplings and controls. We demonstrate our framework using an eight-qubit toric-code array on a superconducting device, where the same driven device generates both the required four-qubit interactions as well as unwanted dynamics. An AI agent identifies viable device parameters within a prescribed leakage budget, and Lean verifies four isolated low-energy states close to the ideal code space. Our workflow supports predictive hardware engineering for analog implementations of QEC codes.
one_liner: An AI-assisted, Lean-verified pipeline maps topological-code spaces onto realistic superconducting-device Hamiltonians and diagnoses harmful couplings.
why_it_matters: It links formal verification to quantitative hardware design, enabling engineers to test whether imperfect analog devices retain a protected QEC code space.
detailed_summary: The workflow constructs a target stabilizer Hamiltonian, computes its protective gap, and checks whether a device Hamiltonian retains the required isolated low-energy subspace. Pauli grouping gives tighter unwanted-energy-shift bounds than summing interaction strengths while avoiding full diagonalization. For an eight-qubit superconducting toric-code array, an AI agent selects parameters within a leakage budget and Lean verifies four low-energy states close to the ideal code space.
main_result: The pipeline formally verified four isolated device eigenstates approximating the intended toric-code space and identified viable operating parameters and dominant unwanted interactions.
application_angle: The method supports predictive design and control optimization for analog quantum-error-correction hardware before costly device iterations.

title: Quartet state of the neutral nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond and optimized spin readout under near-infrared two-photon excitation
abstract: Photoionization of the excited nitrogen-vacancy center (NV-) in diamond leaves the neutral defect in a metastable quartet state of unknown energy. Using two-photon optically detected magnetic resonance with a tunable femtosecond laser, we resolve its onset in the spin contrast at 1.23 +/- 0.02 eV and, with the ground-state threshold from the same setup, place the quartet 0.54 +/- 0.04 eV above the neutral ground state. The threshold sets the optimum excitation for spin readout at 1060-1075 nm, in the near-infrared tissue window, with 26-37% higher shot-noise-limited sensitivity than at 1030-1040 nm.
one_liner: Two-photon ODMR locates the neutral NV center's metastable quartet and identifies a near-infrared excitation band with improved spin-readout sensitivity.
why_it_matters: The result resolves a key NV photoionization energy and improves readout in the biological tissue window, benefiting diamond sensing in optically challenging samples.
detailed_summary: Tunable femtosecond two-photon ODMR reveals the onset of the neutral NV quartet contribution to spin contrast at 1.23 ± 0.02 eV. Combining this threshold with the ground-state threshold measured in the same setup places the quartet 0.54 ± 0.04 eV above the neutral ground state. Excitation at 1060–1075 nm yields 26–37% higher shot-noise-limited sensitivity than operation at 1030–1040 nm.
platform_or_system: Diamond nitrogen-vacancy centers under femtosecond two-photon excitation
main_result: The quartet energy was determined and the optimal 1060–1075 nm readout band delivered up to 37% higher shot-noise-limited sensitivity.
application_angle: Near-infrared readout in the tissue window could improve NV-based magnetic sensing and bioimaging where penetration depth and background are limiting.

title: Aberration stabilized light bullets in normal dispersion injected Kerr resonators
abstract: We investigate three-dimensional light bullets (LBs) in an optically injected, vertically emitting Kerr-Gires-Tournois interferometer operating in the normal dispersion regime. In the uniform field limit, the dynamics is governed by a generalized Lugiato-Lefever equation with third-order dispersion, paraxial diffraction, and fourth-order diffraction, stemming from lens and mirror aberrations close to the self-imaging condition. Using direct numerical simulations, we show that without aberration only transversely drifting, tilted multi-peak localized states (LSs) are stable in two dimensions, whereas no stable LBs exist in three dimensions. However, a small negative spherical aberration stabilizes a rich multistable family of two-dimensional LSs, including straight and tilted multi-peak LSs, oscillating states, and complex bound states, which persist even for negative paraxial diffraction. We identify an Andronov-Hopf bifurcation followed by a homoclinic transition toward tilted states, accompanied by hysteresis. Finally, we demonstrate that stable straight and tilted LBs exist in three dimensions in the presence of aberration, the latter forming a continuous family parametrized by the transverse tilt direction.
one_liner: Small negative spherical aberration stabilizes three-dimensional light bullets in a normally dispersive, optically injected Kerr resonator.
why_it_matters: Aberration becomes a controllable stabilization mechanism for spatiotemporal localized states that are otherwise unstable in normal-dispersion resonators.
detailed_summary: Numerical simulations use a generalized Lugiato-Lefever model with third-order dispersion, paraxial diffraction, and aberration-induced fourth-order diffraction. Without aberration, stable three-dimensional light bullets are absent; a small negative spherical aberration produces multistable straight and tilted bullets. The study also finds oscillatory and bound two-dimensional states, plus an Andronov-Hopf bifurcation and homoclinic transition with hysteresis.
main_result: Negative spherical aberration stabilized families of straight and tilted three-dimensional light bullets in the normal-dispersion regime.
application_angle: Engineered cavity aberrations may enable robust spatiotemporal localization for nonlinear photonic processing, pulse formation, and structured-light sources.

title: Exceptional Points and Optimized Encoding in Qubit Stabilizer Codes
abstract: Continuous blind stabilizer measurements turn stabilizer codes into a Liouvillian spectral problem in which Hamiltonian terms compete with dissipative error channels. We show that this competition generically enables Liouvillian exceptional points, whose occurrence at weak error rates is constrained by the code distance. Exceptional points are detrimental in this regime of error correction as they maximize the decay rate of encoded coherences. We then optimize the encoding of the logical qubit using the eigenmodes of the Lindblad operator. This phase-optimized encoding cancels the linear short-time decay of logical qubit coherences. We apply this encoding to the [[5,1,3]] code and demonstrate that it outperforms naive encoding methods near the exceptional point, improves the fidelity of a logical $π$ rotation and remains effective in the presence of additional weak error channels.
one_liner: Liouvillian exceptional points accelerate logical-coherence loss, while eigenmode-optimized encoding suppresses linear short-time decay in stabilizer codes.
why_it_matters: The work identifies a dissipative failure mechanism in continuously monitored QEC and provides an encoding strategy that improves logical operations near it.
detailed_summary: Continuous blind stabilizer measurements are formulated as a Liouvillian spectral problem balancing Hamiltonian dynamics and dissipative errors. The authors show that exceptional points can maximize encoded-coherence decay, with their weak-error occurrence constrained by code distance. For the [[5,1,3]] code, a phase-optimized encoding based on Lindblad eigenmodes cancels linear short-time coherence decay and improves logical π-rotation fidelity near the exceptional point.
main_result: Eigenmode-optimized logical encoding outperformed naive encodings near a Liouvillian exceptional point and remained effective with additional weak error channels.
application_angle: The encoding can guide control and state preparation in continuously monitored quantum memories and error-corrected processors exposed to coherent and dissipative imperfections.

title: Optimised finite key for satellite up-link entangled quantum key distribution
abstract: Entanglement-based quantum key distribution from ground to satellite has been proposed as a scalable primitive for global quantum networks and will be demonstrated as part of the imminent QEYSSat mission. Both theoretical studies and experimental emulations have shown that a significant asymptotic key rate can be expected. In this work we investigate this scenario with a more rigorous security analysis taking into account the finite size effects that arise from short block lengths common in satellite transmission. Our findings suggest a slight alteration of the optimal source operation when informed by finite statistics as opposed to the asymptotic regime, notably that the pump power should be slightly lowered. We quantify the annual key rate based on a dynamically optimised source operation for the Heriot-Watt ground station and several satellite parameters. We find an improved annual key rate when accumulating all raw key material before extracting a secure key instead of doing so for each overpass. We ultimately show that QEYSSat will be able to generate a significant secure annual key with both strategies.
one_liner: Finite-key optimization predicts significant annual secure key generation for satellite uplink entanglement-based QKD, including the QEYSSat scenario.
why_it_matters: The analysis converts short satellite passes and finite statistics into actionable source settings and key-accumulation strategies for an imminent mission.
detailed_summary: The study applies finite-size security analysis to ground-to-satellite entanglement-based QKD with short transmission blocks. Finite statistics shift the optimal source operation toward slightly lower pump power than the asymptotic optimum. Dynamic optimization for the Heriot-Watt ground station predicts higher annual key yield when raw material from all passes is accumulated before privacy amplification, while both evaluated strategies produce significant secure annual key.
main_result: Finite-key source optimization and cross-pass data accumulation increased predicted annual secure-key yield and supported viable QEYSSat operation.
application_angle: The results provide mission-level guidance for pump-power control, block aggregation, and secure-key extraction in global satellite quantum networks.

title: Long-range entangled criticality from coherent errors
abstract: We find that coherent error can induce a phase transition from the clean surface code phase into an extended long-range entangled critical regime with diverging Markov length. To demonstrate this, we establish two general results of independent interest. The first relates topology and quantum information to mixed-state entanglement: we show that when a noise channel acting on a topological code preserves a higher-form symmetry and nonzero coherent information, the noisy state for generic logical input is long-range entangled. The second generalizes the local recovery construction based on finite Markov length to any locally parameterized family, thus encompassing local Lindbladian evolution, coherent errors followed by syndrome dephasing, and thermal states. We apply these results to the honeycomb surface code, in which we find an extended long-range entangled critical regime that is a quasi-long-ranged counterpart of 1-form strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking. As a byproduct of these studies, we relate the conditional mutual information to conductance in a Majorana network model.
one_liner: Coherent errors drive a honeycomb surface code into an extended critical regime with long-range mixed-state entanglement.
why_it_matters: The work reveals a qualitatively new failure regime for topological quantum memories and links recoverability to Markov length, symmetry, and coherent information.
detailed_summary: The authors show that symmetry-preserving noise with nonzero coherent information generically leaves topological-code states long-range entangled. They extend finite-Markov-length recovery constructions to locally parameterized state families, including Lindbladian evolution, coherent errors followed by syndrome dephasing, and thermal states. Applied to the honeycomb surface code, the theory predicts an extended quasi-long-range-entangled critical regime and connects conditional mutual information to conductance in a Majorana network.
main_result: Coherent errors induce an extended long-range-entangled critical phase with diverging Markov length in the honeycomb surface code.
application_angle: The results refine error-model assumptions and recovery criteria for designing and benchmarking fault-tolerant topological quantum hardware.

title: High-fidelity quantum gate learning via physics-informed neural networks
abstract: We propose a physics-informed neural network (PINN) approach for high-fidelity quantum gate learning in both one- and two-qubit systems. We train a PINN using the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, where smooth control fields with fixed boundary conditions are obtained by minimizing a loss function that considers model dynamics, gate error, physical constraints, regularization terms, and multiple initial conditions. Training considers pairs of mutually unbiased bases, while independent validation combines Haar-random input states with the average gate fidelity. Unitary simulations yield an average gate infidelity of $8.49\times10^{-8}$ for Hadamard and values between $3.39\times10^{-7}$ and $4.96\times10^{-6}$ for controlled-NOT under $XX$, $YY$, and $ZZ$ interactions. We examine how the learned control fields depend on the coupling, training configuration, and available local fields, including five exchange-type dipolar scenarios. We test the learned control fields under the Lindblad master equation with dephasing and amplitude damping, theoretically reproducing the expected first-order fidelity loss in the weak-dissipation regime. Finally, boundary-adapted Chebyshev expansions represent 139 learned controls with a minimum common count of $K_\ast=24$ coefficients per control for all eleven family-averaged mean squared errors to fall below $10^{-6}$. Separately, square-pulse and Strang propagation at $K=30$ preserve all 31 continuous polynomial references within infidelity $10^{-5}$ at $N=128$ and all larger tested resolutions, under both sampling rules. These results connect multi-state gate synthesis, control-resource characterization, and compact square-pulse playback.
one_liner: A physics-informed neural network learns smooth, compact controls for high-fidelity one- and two-qubit gates.
why_it_matters: It combines accurate gate synthesis, open-system robustness tests, and hardware-friendly pulse compression in one control-learning framework.
detailed_summary: The PINN embeds the time-dependent Schrödinger equation and optimizes gate error, physical constraints, regularization, and multiple input states. Simulations reach an average Hadamard infidelity of 8.49×10^-8 and CNOT infidelities of 3.39×10^-7 to 4.96×10^-6 for XX, YY, and ZZ couplings. Learned controls reproduce weak-dissipation fidelity loss under Lindblad dynamics and can be represented using 24 common Chebyshev coefficients per control at family-averaged mean-squared error below 10^-6.
main_result: The method generates high-fidelity gates across several interaction models while enabling compact polynomial representation and accurate square-pulse playback.
application_angle: Compact, boundary-constrained pulses could simplify calibration and deployment of learned controls on finite-bandwidth quantum processors.

title: Analog quantum simulation of paraparticle statistics
abstract: Bosonic and fermionic quantum statistics describe all known elementary and emergent particles in three dimensions, although many attempts have been made to discover other valid quantum statistical frameworks. One recent formulation proposes "$R$-paraparticles," indistinguishable particles with nonlocal internal degrees of freedom governed by generalized exchange rules [Wang and Hazzard, Nature 637, 314 (2025)]. Here, we emulate a species of paraparticle that exhibits a generalized Pauli exclusion principle using a superconducting qubit lattice. We confirm its unique quantum statistics by measuring a $180^\circ$ phase shift under paraparticle exchange, observing antibunching independent of internal degrees of freedom under two-particle interference at a beamsplitter, and finding a thermal occupation inconsistent with both Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac statistics. These results demonstrate that parastatistics are observable on quantum simulation platforms, further motivating their use to explore theorized new phases of matter.
one_liner: A superconducting-qubit lattice emulates paraparticles and directly measures exchange, interference, and thermal signatures beyond bosons and fermions.
why_it_matters: The experiment makes exotic particle statistics accessible to programmable quantum hardware and opens a route to simulating unconventional phases of matter.
detailed_summary: The experiment realizes an R-paraparticle species with a generalized Pauli exclusion principle on a superconducting-qubit lattice. A 180° exchange phase, internal-state-independent antibunching at a beamsplitter, and anomalous thermal occupation distinguish the particles from bosons and fermions. Together, these observables provide complementary validation of the engineered statistics.
main_result: The simulator observes three characteristic signatures of paraparticle statistics, including a 180° exchange phase and generalized antibunching.
application_angle: Programmable paraparticle emulation offers a laboratory platform for exploring proposed statistics and associated unconventional many-body phases.

title: Ray propagation of circularly polarized light in an inhomogeneous medium: the optical Magnus effect from Maxwell's equations
abstract: We derive the ray propagation of circularly polarized light in an inhomogeneous, isotropic and lossless medium, including the first correction to geometrical optics, the optical Magnus (spin Hall) effect. Starting from Maxwell's equations and the eikonal expansion to first order in $1/k_0$, we show that the polarization is parallel transported along the ray, identify the Berry connection and curvature of the helicity states, and obtain a ray action in which the Berry phase appears as a correction to the optical path length. This action leads to a Hamiltonian in which the refractive index is evaluated at a position shifted by the Berry connection, $\mathcal H_σ(\mathbf r,\mathbf p)=|\mathbf p|-n(\mathbf r+\mathbf A_σ(\mathbf p)/k_0) \simeq|\mathbf p|-n(\mathbf r)-k_0^{-1}\boldsymbol\nabla n\cdot\mathbf A_σ(\mathbf p)$. In terms of the physical position, the equations of motion contain the Berry curvature as an anomalous velocity. We give the equivalent non-canonical bracket form, the gauge transformation, and the equivalent time-parametrized formulation with the Hamiltonian $\hbarω=\hbar c|\mathbf k|/n$, and we state the approximations involved. The resulting ray equations are compared with analytic and numerical results. A planar interface, the helical ray in a cylindrical medium and the exact conservation of angular momentum provide checks. The formulation is set up for numerical propagation of rays in a medium with a spatially varying refractive index.
one_liner: A Maxwell-to-ray derivation incorporates Berry curvature and the optical Magnus effect into numerical propagation through graded-index media.
why_it_matters: The formulation provides a controlled way to model helicity-dependent ray shifts that standard geometrical optics omits.
detailed_summary: Starting from Maxwell's equations, the authors carry the eikonal expansion to first order in inverse wave number and show that polarization is parallel transported. The resulting action contains a Berry-phase correction, while the physical-position equations acquire a Berry-curvature anomalous velocity. Interface propagation, helical rays in a cylindrical medium, and angular-momentum conservation serve as analytic and numerical checks.
main_result: The work derives equivalent Hamiltonian and noncanonical ray equations that capture helicity-dependent optical Magnus shifts from Maxwell's equations.
application_angle: The equations can be integrated into polarization-aware ray tracers for graded-index components, interfaces, and spin-dependent photonic transport.

title: Pump quantization changes optimal measurements for quantum sensing
abstract: Standard analyses of quantum phase sensing often neglect the overhead of generating squeezed-light by treating the pump as an undepleted classical resource. Realistically, the pump is a quantum object that undergoes significant depletion and entangles with the produced squeezed light, raising the question of how the crossover from a classical to a quantum pump limits the quantum advantage in sensing. Contrary to prior analyses, we show that quantum advantage persists despite pump quantization, but depends critically on the nonlinear $(χ^{(2)})$ source dynamics. In particular, we demonstrate that Heisenberg scaling emerges in the regime of strong pump depletion, rather than maximum signal squeezing. At maximum squeezing, the quantum Fisher information (QFI) for interferometric sensing of an unknown phase scales as $N^{3/2}$, where $N$ is the pump photon number, surpassing the shot-noise limit but establishing that squeezing itself is insufficient to attain Heisenberg scaling of $N^2$. At maximal pump depletion, where the signal flux is maximized, the QFI scales as $N^2$. In this regime, standard photon counting is suboptimal, while a joint nonlinear measurement of the entire pump-signal system is shown to achieve Heisenberg scaling. Our work shows that pump quantization changes both the optimal operating point and the measurement strategies required to preserve a realistic quantum advantage in phase estimation and, more broadly, many-body quantum dynamics.
one_liner: Quantizing a depleted χ(2) pump shifts Heisenberg-limited phase sensing from maximum squeezing to maximum pump depletion.
why_it_matters: It identifies the realistic operating point and joint measurement needed to retain quantum-enhanced scaling when the pump is treated as a finite resource.
detailed_summary: The analysis treats the χ(2) pump and generated signal as a joint quantum system rather than assuming an undepleted classical pump. At maximum squeezing, the phase-estimation QFI scales as N^(3/2), whereas maximum pump depletion yields Heisenberg scaling, N^2. Photon counting is suboptimal in that regime, but a joint nonlinear pump-signal measurement can attain the predicted scaling.
main_result: Heisenberg-scaling QFI survives pump quantization at maximal depletion, provided a joint nonlinear measurement accesses the full pump-signal system.
application_angle: The findings guide source biasing and receiver design for practical squeezed-light interferometers with finite pump energy.

title: Contrast-Enhanced Nonlinear Imaging with Moiré Flatband Superlattices
abstract: Nonlinear metasurfaces offer a compact platform for infrared-to-visible conversion and imaging, yet resonant enhancement is often accompanied by restricted angular acceptance, limiting the range of transverse spatial frequencies that can interact efficiently with the nonlinear modes. Here, we address this challenge using a one-dimensional photonic moiré superlattice supporting multiple quasi-flat bands in the near-infrared. These moiré modes combine strong near-field enhancement with broad momentum-space accessibility, enabling efficient third-harmonic generation (THG) while maintaining stable excitation over a large angular range. Experimentally, we observe strong THG emission near $467~\mathrm{nm}$ under broadband excitation from $ 1180$ to $ 2000~\mathrm {nm} $. We further employ the nonlinear moiré superlattice for infrared imaging by converting an infrared target into visible through the THG process. By encoding image information into displacement-dependent THG signals and decoding their spatial variations, we experimentally resolve weak features and internal textures with improved contrast compared with THG imaging using nonlinear films or conventional nonlinear metasurfaces. These results establish photonic moiré superlattices as a versatile platform combining efficient frequency conversion, broad angular acceptance, and mode-sensitive spatial encoding for high-contrast, label-free nonlinear imaging with enhanced feature discrimination.
one_liner: Moiré flatband photonic superlattices combine broadband angular acceptance with enhanced third-harmonic infrared-to-visible imaging.
why_it_matters: The demonstrated platform overcomes the angular-bandwidth tradeoff of resonant nonlinear metasurfaces while improving contrast for weak image features.
detailed_summary: A one-dimensional photonic moiré superlattice supports multiple near-infrared quasi-flat bands with strong near fields and broad momentum-space accessibility. Experiments observe third-harmonic emission near 467 nm under excitation spanning 1180–2000 nm. Displacement-dependent THG encoding and spatial decoding reveal weak features and internal textures with higher contrast than nonlinear films or conventional nonlinear metasurfaces.
main_result: The device performs broad-angle infrared-to-visible THG conversion and experimentally enhances contrast in nonlinear images of structured targets.
application_angle: The platform could enable compact, label-free infrared imaging with visible detection and improved discrimination of low-contrast spatial features.

title: The Impact of Internal Electric Fields on Accurate Diamond Magnetometry
abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center spin ensembles are a promising platform for accurate vector magnetometry, as they offer measurements referenced to a spin Hamiltonian in an anisotropic crystal with native vector sensing capabilities. However, charged dopants within the diamond produce random internal electric fields (RIEFs) that shift NV spin-transition frequencies, and their impact on the accuracy of NV magnetometry has not been investigated. Here, we characterize RIEFs' effect on NV spin-transition spectra and propose an analytical fitting function to improve accuracy in their presence. We build a Monte Carlo RIEF model that reproduces the asymmetric lineshapes observed in experimental optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) spectra, and use it as a testbed to quantify RIEF-induced errors by simulating ODMR spectra including RIEFs and comparing reconstructed magnetic fields to the known model input. With standard analysis approaches, we observe systematic errors exceeding the g-factor uncertainty in fields below $\sim$ 5 mT, while the proposed fitting function reduces the error by nearly an order of magnitude. Our results demonstrate that RIEFs can play a significant role in the systematic error budget for NV magnetometry, and offer a path towards improved accuracy in NV quantum sensing.
one_liner: Random internal electric fields in diamond can bias NV magnetometry, while a tailored ODMR fit cuts the resulting error nearly tenfold.
why_it_matters: The work identifies a previously unquantified systematic and provides a practical route to more accurate low-field vector magnetometry.
detailed_summary: Charged dopants generate random internal electric fields that distort ensemble-NV ODMR spectra and produce asymmetric lineshapes. A Monte Carlo model reproduces the observed spectra and shows that standard analysis can exceed g-factor-limited uncertainty below about 5 mT. An analytical fitting function reduces the resulting magnetic-field error by nearly an order of magnitude.
main_result: A RIEF-aware ODMR fitting model reduces low-field magnetic reconstruction errors by nearly one order of magnitude.
application_angle: The method can improve the accuracy and uncertainty budgets of calibrated NV vector magnetometers without changing the sensor hardware.

title: Reconfigurable multi-tone mmWave/THz generation powered by high-efficiency Kerr parametric oscillation
abstract: Broadband and simultaneously accessible multi-tone millimeter-wave (mmWave) and terahertz (THz) signals are attractive for multi-band wireless communication and spectroscopy applications, yet their generation remains constrained by electronic bandwidth limitations and inefficient optical frequency conversion. Here, we demonstrate reconfigurable photonic generation of multi-tone mmWave/THz signals with comb spacings of 100, 200, 300, and 400 GHz, using a strongly asymmetric dual-ring silicon-nitride (SiN) microresonator and a broadband spiral plasmonic photomixer. A localized avoided-mode crossing (AMX) introduced by an auxiliary ring supports a fixed optical parametric oscillation (OPO) mode pair over an extended pump-detuning range, consistent with passive compensation of detuning-dependent phase mismatch. This enables a maximum pump-to-generated-line conversion efficiency of 67.3 % with 25.06 dB of pump depletion across different pump wavelength selections.
