Direct photomixing of these optical states produces simultaneous multi-frequency tones spanning 100 to 900 GHz without intermediate optical amplification. The generated carriers are further characterized through down-converted spectra, frequency-noise power spectral density (PSD), and Allan deviation measurements, yielding a \b{eta}-separation linewidth of 26 kHz at an observation time of 0.1 s. Optical modulation offers high radiated power levels exceeding 2 mW at 100 GHz at a duty cycle of 1 %, while mitigating thermal breakdown in the photomixer. High optical conversion efficiency, reconfigurable and selectable comb spacings, and broadband multi-tone generation on a chip-scale platform provide a compact route toward reconfigurable multi-band mmWave/THz sources for wireless communication, spectroscopy, and sensing.
one_liner: A dual-ring SiN microresonator generates selectable 100–400 GHz comb spacings and simultaneous photomixed tones extending to 900 GHz.
why_it_matters: High conversion efficiency and amplification-free photomixing offer a compact route to reconfigurable multi-band mmWave and THz sources.
detailed_summary: A strongly asymmetric dual-ring SiN resonator uses a localized avoided-mode crossing to stabilize a fixed optical-parametric-oscillation mode pair across pump detuning. The device reaches 67.3% pump-to-generated-line efficiency and 25.06 dB pump depletion. Broadband plasmonic photomixing produces simultaneous 100–900 GHz tones without intermediate optical amplification, with a reported 26 kHz beta-separation linewidth at 0.1 s.
platform_or_system: Dual-ring SiN microresonator with plasmonic photomixer
main_result: The chip-scale system delivers selectable 100–400 GHz comb spacings and simultaneous carriers up to 900 GHz at high optical conversion efficiency.
application_angle: It supports compact, frequency-agile sources for multi-band wireless links, spectroscopy, radar, and THz sensing.

title: Gaussian Quantum Integrated Sensing and Communication
abstract: We consider a quantum integrated sensing and communication problem over an optical link in which a low-power transmitter simultaneously communicates with a receiver and identifies the range of a defect producing a backscattered signal. We model the system as a lossy thermal-noise bosonic channel, in which the target, modeled as a beamsplitter, affects the timing of the backscattered signal through its location. Motivated by the envisioned deployment of entanglement-enabled quantum networks, we develop two protocols that allow the transmitter to leverage shared Gaussian entanglement, in the form of independent two-mode squeezed vacuum states or coupled three-mode squeezed vacuum states, to assist both sensing and communication. Since entanglement is known to enhance sensing, as demonstrated in quantum illumination, and to increase communication rates through entanglement-assisted communication, the transmitter faces a trade-off in allocating its entanglement resources between the two tasks. Our main results characterize these trade-offs under the proposed protocols in terms of achievable communication rate/sensing error-exponent regions, which outperform time-sharing schemes and demonstrate a quantum advantage.
one_liner: Gaussian entanglement enables one low-power optical link to communicate while locating a backscattering defect better than time sharing.
why_it_matters: The protocols quantify how shared continuous-variable entanglement can be divided between data transmission and ranging in future quantum networks.
detailed_summary: The study models simultaneous communication and defect ranging over a lossy, thermal-noise bosonic channel. Two protocols use either independent two-mode squeezed-vacuum states or coupled three-mode squeezed-vacuum states shared with the receiver. Their achievable communication-rate and sensing-error-exponent regions outperform corresponding time-sharing strategies and exhibit a quantum advantage.
main_result: Gaussian-entanglement protocols achieve joint communication–ranging trade-offs beyond time sharing under loss and thermal noise.
application_angle: The framework is relevant to low-power quantum networks that must carry data while monitoring links or locating reflective defects.

title: Runtime Compilation for Quantum Circuits with PQF-Enabled $R_z$ Synthesis
abstract: In Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing (FTQC) using surface codes, reducing $T$-count is critical for efficient computation due to the high cost of $T$-state distillation. Probabilistic Quantum Circuit with Fallback (PQF) synthesis significantly lowers $T$-counts compared to standard protocols like Gridsynth, but introduces high circuit dynamism through extra gates inserted at runtime. This dynamism invalidates static compile-time routing, as these new $T$ gates require dynamic lattice surgery routing to establish non-intersecting ancilla paths to $T$-state factories while minimizing total execution time. To address this, we introduce $\text{R}^2$-PQF, a Runtime Routing protocol for PQF-synthesized quantum circuits. $\text{R}^2$-PQF dynamically routes gates layer-by-layer, computing paths during the execution of the previous logical timestep. To satisfy the strict computational window of $\sim t_{lattice\_surgery} + t_{reaction}$ and non-intersectionality constraints, we implement a Wavefront Breadth-First Search (W-BFS) and synthesise it on a 500MHz FPGA and 2 GHz ASIC. For a clock cycle of 2GHz, we achieve a median logical time-step of $1.51 μs$ for a 300 qubit Ising Hamiltonian circuit, demonstrating that $\text{R}^2$-PQF successfully resolves the vast majority of paths (with rare exceptions) within the execution window and enables the $T$-count benefits of PQF without latency penalties. Compared to a baseline stalling-based solution (the only no-runtime-recomputation solution), $\text{R}^2$-PQF speeds up circuit execution by $1.34\times$ on average and up to $1.76 \times$.
one_liner: An FPGA/ASIC runtime router enables dynamic PQF-based Rz synthesis in surface-code circuits without erasing its T-count advantage.
why_it_matters: Fast classical control is essential for turning lower-T-count synthesis into an actual fault-tolerant execution-time benefit.
detailed_summary: R2-PQF routes dynamically inserted gates layer by layer while the preceding logical timestep executes, addressing the non-intersecting ancilla paths required by lattice surgery. Its wavefront breadth-first search is synthesized for a 500 MHz FPGA and a 2 GHz ASIC. For a 300-qubit Ising circuit, the 2 GHz design gives a median 1.51 microsecond logical timestep and accelerates execution by 1.34 times on average, reaching 1.76 times.
platform_or_system: Surface-code controller on FPGA and ASIC
main_result: The runtime router resolves nearly all dynamic PQF paths within the control window while outperforming stalling by up to 1.76 times.
application_angle: It provides a concrete classical-control architecture for exploiting low-T-count synthesis in practical fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Entanglement Allocation for Quantum Integrated Sensing and Communication
abstract: Jointly supporting communication and distributed sensing over a shared, limited pool of entanglement resources is an attractive prospect for future quantum networks. We develop a network-level quantum integrated sensing and communication (Q-ISAC) framework in which a quantum base station dynamically allocates elementary Bell pairs between communication users and distributed sensing. Sensing resources are adaptively partitioned among multiple GHZ probes with dynamically selected sizes and sensing-node assignments. We derive an effective quantum Fisher information model accounting for probabilistic fusion, transmission loss, and memory decoherence, and formulate a finite-horizon allocation problem subject to communication QoS, expected sensing-information, sensing-reliability, and hardware constraints. A hierarchical constrained proximal policy optimization (HC-PPO) framework combines learned discrete sensing allocation with analytical continuous communication allocation. Numerical results show that GHZ probing requires approximately $27$--30% fewer sensing qubits than separable probing under modest probe-size caps and 65-67% fewer at the highest considered target under the same sensing requirements. Adaptive multi-GHZ partitioning provides greater robustness than single-GHZ sensing, while adaptive communication--sensing sharing outperforms the evaluated fixed splits. The proposed HC-PPO framework satisfies the joint requirements in at least 99.9% of test instances across the considered sensing targets and fusion probabilities. Monte Carlo evaluation separately shows that realized terminal information reached its target in 96-98% of realizations, distinguishing expected-information satisfaction from realized sensing performance.
one_liner: A hierarchical allocator dynamically shares Bell pairs among communication users and loss-aware multi-GHZ distributed sensing probes.
why_it_matters: The framework connects entanglement allocation, hardware constraints, communication QoS, and realistic sensing reliability at network scale.
detailed_summary: The network model includes probabilistic fusion, channel loss, memory decoherence, communication QoS, and finite hardware resources. A hierarchical constrained PPO policy selects discrete sensing configurations while continuous communication allocation is solved analytically. Simulations report 27–30% fewer sensing qubits than separable probing under modest GHZ-size caps, up to 65–67% fewer at the highest target, and joint constraint satisfaction in at least 99.9% of test instances.
platform_or_system: Bell-pair quantum network with distributed GHZ sensors
main_result: Adaptive multi-GHZ allocation reduces sensing-qubit demand and robustly meets joint sensing and communication constraints in simulation.
application_angle: The approach could guide real-time entanglement scheduling in quantum networks serving both distributed sensors and communication clients.

title: Accurate representation of the continuum orbital in a Gaussian basis set: application to Auger decay rates
abstract: Many processes in chemistry and physics, such as autoionization, photoionization, or electron-impact collisions, involve unbound electrons. Despite their importance, theoretical methods for modeling continuum electrons remain significantly less developed than those for purely bound electronic states. Here we present a novel approach for treating continuum electrons within Gaussian-based quantum chemistry. The method represents continuum orbital in a discrete basis of standard Gaussian-type orbitals (GTOs), where the continuum wave function is obtained by solving the Lippmann-Schwinger equation with proper boundary conditions using an analytical representation of the Green's function in an auxiliary GTO basis set. The resulting continuum orbital is multicentered and multichannel, providing a rigorous description of scattering states. As an initial application of the new methodology, we compute Auger decay rates for several atomic and molecular systems, including Ne, H$_2$O, CO$_2$, and Ar. We demonstrate a consistent improvement of the results with increasing the quality of the continuum representation. We show also that higher-order electron-correlation effects in the bound domain are essential for an accurate treatment of satellite transitions. The present formalism therefore provides a systematically improvable Gaussian-based framework for continuum-electron problems that is fully compatible with standard quantum chemistry methods.
one_liner: A Gaussian-basis Lippmann–Schwinger method represents multicenter continuum electrons and systematically improves calculated Auger rates.
why_it_matters: Compatibility with standard quantum-chemistry machinery could make accurate continuum-state calculations more accessible and extensible.
detailed_summary: The method solves the Lippmann–Schwinger equation with proper scattering boundary conditions using an analytical Green's function represented in an auxiliary Gaussian basis. It produces multicenter, multichannel continuum orbitals compatible with conventional Gaussian quantum-chemistry methods. Calculations for Ne, H2O, CO2, and Ar show systematic improvement with continuum-basis quality and reveal the importance of higher-order bound-state correlation for satellite transitions.
main_result: The framework yields systematically improvable continuum orbitals and Auger decay rates for atomic and molecular systems.
application_angle: It can support predictive modeling of ionization, autoionization, radiation damage, and electron-driven processes in molecules and materials.

title: An example of universal braiding in Links--Gould topological quantum computation
abstract: We construct a universal quantum computational encoding via braiding in Links--Gould fusion spaces associated to $U_q^H(\mathfrak{sl}(2|1))$ where $q$ is on the unit circle and is not a root of unity. The construction uses only neglectons and is realized in the morphism spaces $\mathrm{Hom}_{U_q^H}(V(0,α),V(0,-\frac{1}{2})^{\otimes 2N}\otimes V(0,α)).$ Under explicit positivity and arithmetic constraints these spaces admit a $2^N$-dimensional computational subspace with a positive definite Hermitian form. We prove single-qubit density in $\mathrm{U}(2,1)$ and approximate arbitrary unitary operators on $N$-qubit computational subspaces with arbitrarily small leakage. The calculations use explicit inclusions, projections, and Hermitian pairings without requiring $F$-matrices.
one_liner: Links–Gould fusion spaces support a universal qubit encoding whose braid operations approximate arbitrary unitaries with arbitrarily small leakage.
why_it_matters: It establishes a new mathematical route to universal topological quantum computation, although no physical implementation is demonstrated.
detailed_summary: The work encodes an N-qubit computational subspace in morphism spaces associated with UqH(sl(2|1)), using only neglectons and q on the unit circle away from roots of unity. Under explicit positivity and arithmetic constraints, the subspace has dimension 2^N and a positive-definite Hermitian form. The authors prove single-qubit density and show that braids approximate arbitrary N-qubit unitaries with arbitrarily small leakage, using explicit inclusions, projections, and pairings rather than F-matrices.
main_result: Braiding is proved universal on the encoded qubits, with arbitrary unitary operations approximable at arbitrarily low leakage.
application_angle: The construction expands the theoretical design space for intrinsically fault-tolerant topological quantum processors, pending identification of a realizable host system.

title: Asymptotic electromagnetic transition conditions for thin layers: the arithmetic-mean field and susceptibility hybridization
abstract: Effective transition conditions that replace a thin polarizable layer by a zero-thickness sheet are commonly applied in electromagnetic models of two-dimensional (2D) materials and metasurfaces. These conditions usually take the arithmetic mean of the fields on either side as the polarizing field at the boundary, and characterize the layer by the $0^\mathrm{th}$ moment of its susceptibility, but both choices are typically imposed rather than derived. We derive transition conditions for a finite-thickness, in-plane homogeneous, in-plane isotropic layer with a general nonlocal susceptibility, using a single-scale asymptotic expansion in $η= l\max(k_0,q)$, where $l$ is the layer thickness, $k_0$ the free-space wavenumber and $q$ the in-plane wavenumber. The sheet limit must be taken after resumming the out-of-plane depolarizing field, as this ensures that the resulting sheet susceptibility is independent of the material thickness. The arithmetic mean then emerges as the leading-order polarizing field for general susceptibility profiles. Asymmetries in the layer profile modify the effective susceptibility appearing in the transition conditions, rather than altering the arithmetic-mean field prescription. If the spatial profile is not even in both out-of-plane coordinates, in-plane and out-of-plane response hybridize, turning the diagonal volumetric susceptibility into a $q$-dependent effective tensor surface susceptibility with off-diagonal components. Mirror symmetry alone does not remove this hybridization. Comparison with exact solutions for local and separable layers shows that the derived conditions remain accurate to $O(η)$ across propagating and evanescent excitations, whereas the standard sheet conditions fail once hybridization becomes appreciable.
one_liner: An asymptotic sheet model derives arithmetic-mean boundary fields and captures susceptibility hybridization in asymmetric ultrathin layers.
why_it_matters: The corrected transition conditions improve electromagnetic modeling of 2D materials and metasurfaces under propagating and evanescent excitation.
detailed_summary: A single-scale expansion in η=l max(k0,q) replaces a finite polarizable layer with effective zero-thickness transition conditions. Resumming the out-of-plane depolarizing field yields a thickness-independent sheet susceptibility and derives the arithmetic-mean polarizing field at leading order. Asymmetric susceptibility profiles generate q-dependent off-diagonal surface response, and comparisons with exact local and separable models show O(η) accuracy for propagating and evanescent fields.
main_result: The derived sheet conditions retain O(η) accuracy while standard conditions fail when in-plane and out-of-plane susceptibility hybridization becomes significant.
application_angle: The model can improve simulation and inverse design of asymmetric nanophotonic sheets, metasurfaces, and integrated optical interfaces.

title: On the Hardness of Approximate Quantum Circuit Membership and Optimization
abstract: Quantum circuit optimization is an indispensable component of the quantum software stack, used to reduce noise, maximize performance, alleviate costs of quantum error correction, or target specific hardware. A related problem is approximate membership: for a fixed set of unitaries $S$, decide whether a given circuit $C$ is within distance $\varepsilon$ of a unitary in $S$ under some metric $m$. Membership is a special case of optimization, where $S$ is a set of unitaries implementable at no cost (e.g., with noise-minimal circuits, or without magic states). Janzing, Wocjan, and Beth (Int. J. Quantum Inf., 2005) showed that, for the operator metric, the case $S=\{I\}$ (approximate identity) is QMA-complete when $C$ is promised to be either close to the identity or far from it. We generalize this setting in three directions: (i) promise-free inputs, (ii) besides $S=\{I\}$, sets $S$ containing only Clifford unitaries, or only generalized permutation matrices (i.e., no superposition), and (iii) the trace-based, spectral, and operator metrics. We show that, in all cases, approximate membership is PP-hard for wide ranges of $\varepsilon$, provided $C$'s gate-set can implement Clifford+T, as the gate-sets of standard hardware do. If $S=\{I\}$, or if $S$ contains only generalized permutation matrices, $I\in S$, and $m$ is a trace-based distance, PP-hardness holds for all non-trivial $\varepsilon$. If $S=\{I\}$ and $m$ is a trace-based distance, PP-hardness holds even for circuits over classical-reversible gate-sets. Our results indicate that approximate membership is harder over promise-free inputs than the QMA-complete promise version, and that this hardness persists across quantum resources (any gates, non-Clifford, superposition) and distance metrics. They directly imply PP-hardness of circuit optimization when minimizing total, non-Clifford, or superposition gate depth or count.
one_liner: Promise-free approximate circuit membership is PP-hard across several target unitary sets, metrics, and hardware-standard Clifford+T gate sets.
why_it_matters: The result exposes fundamental limits on exact optimization of circuit depth, gate count, non-Clifford resources, and superposition operations.
detailed_summary: The paper studies whether a circuit lies within ε of identity, Clifford, or generalized-permutation unitary sets under trace-based, spectral, and operator metrics. For broad ε ranges, the promise-free problem is PP-hard when the circuit gate set implements Clifford+T; several identity and generalized-permutation cases remain hard for every nontrivial ε. These reductions also establish PP-hardness for minimizing total, non-Clifford, or superposition gate count and depth.
main_result: Approximate membership and associated circuit-optimization objectives are shown to be PP-hard across multiple resource sets and distance metrics.
application_angle: The bounds clarify why globally optimal hardware-aware compilation may be intractable and motivate heuristic or restricted optimization methods.

title: Reducing the arithmetic cost of quantum derivative pricing with language-model circuit design
abstract: Quantum amplitude estimation can estimate expected discounted payoffs with quadratically fewer oracle calls than Monte Carlo, but each call requires coherent computation. We use language-model-assisted circuit design to reduce reversible payoff arithmetic for a three-asset worst-of autocallable and a target accrual redemption forward (TARF). The constructions retain compact integer representations of market paths alongside contract history, reconstructing quantities temporarily for contract decisions and payoff-angle evaluation. Relative to matched internal references, the factor-sum autocallable and windowed TARF circuits reduce the product of Toffoli count and peak logical qubits $(N_{Tof} Q_{max})$ by factors of 2.39 and 4.84, respectively. At a second autocallable setting, fresh search recovers a 1.35-fold saving after the tested fixed adaptation loses its advantage. For the factor-sum circuit, we prove exact coherent execution of its integer specification for every input, incoming accumulator and measurement record, with clean workspace and phase cancellation. A separate lattice calculation gives a numerical angle-tolerance-violation probability of 6.248e-8 and evaluates pricing bias under the declared loading law, with bounded omission but no certified numerical enclosure. The results connect compact representations to lower-cost payoff arithmetic and separately assessed logical and financial correctness. Their resource scope excludes loading, payoff rotation and estimation.
one_liner: Language-model-assisted reversible designs reduce the Toffoli-count–qubit product for two derivative-pricing payoff circuits by up to 4.84×.
why_it_matters: Lower reversible-arithmetic cost could make amplitude-estimation workflows for structured financial products less demanding on fault-tolerant hardware.
detailed_summary: The authors design reversible payoff arithmetic for a three-asset worst-of autocallable and a TARF using compact integer path representations and temporary reconstruction. Against matched internal references, the factor-sum autocallable and windowed TARF reduce NTofQmax by factors of 2.39 and 4.84, while a separate search finds a 1.35× saving at another setting. Exact coherent execution is proved for the factor-sum integer specification, but resource estimates exclude data loading, payoff rotation, and amplitude estimation.
main_result: The proposed circuits cut the combined Toffoli-count and peak-logical-qubit cost by 2.39× and 4.84× for the two primary benchmarks.
application_angle: Compact payoff arithmetic reduces a major oracle cost in prospective quantum amplitude-estimation engines for complex derivative pricing.

title: Motional Decoherence of the internal state of an atom by vacuum and thermal fluctuations of a quantum field: Necessity of a fully relativistic treatment
abstract: We consider a massive object, such as a neutral atom or an Unruh-DeWitt detector, moving at constant speed in a quantum field and investigate how motion affects the quantum coherence of its internal degrees of freedom, manifesting as quantum dispersion in the absence of a quantum field, and decoherence in its presence. Our investigation aims to serve two purposes: One is to obtain the correct results for these effects, which are essential for the design of quantum information processing schemes where the quantum coherence of an atom's internal degrees of freedom is of major concern. The other is to expose the fallacies in commonplace approaches, which start with a non-relativistic calculation and then add on relativistic ``corrections". We first show a fully relativistic calculation of the internal dynamics based on covariance principles, and then one which ignores these principles, often justified by the atom's slow motion. By a direct comparison of results from these two approaches, we identify {significant discrepancies} in a non-relativistic treatment, even at low atomic speeds. The proper procedure, and a much safer one in terms of accuracy, is recommended here: first derive the dynamics and the necessary regularizations within a fully covariant relativistic framework. Only after the exact, internally consistent equations of motion are established should low-velocity limits be extracted from them. Only in this way can all the relativistic effects which matter: time dilation, aberration, non-inertial mass shifts, be systematically preserved, and accurate results obtained.
one_liner: A covariant treatment finds that nonrelativistic models can misestimate motion-induced internal-state dispersion and field-driven decoherence even at low speeds.
why_it_matters: Reliable coherence budgets for moving atomic qubits and detectors may require relativistic dynamics before taking any low-velocity approximation.
detailed_summary: The study compares fully covariant internal-state dynamics of a uniformly moving massive detector with a calculation that begins nonrelativistically. The covariant formulation incorporates time dilation, aberration, regularization, and motion-dependent mass shifts before a low-velocity limit is taken. Direct comparison indicates significant discrepancies in predicted dispersion and decoherence even when the object's speed is small.
main_result: The analysis shows that low-speed nonrelativistic treatments can omit consequential relativistic contributions to internal-state coherence dynamics.
application_angle: The framework can support more accurate coherence and noise estimates for moving atomic qubits, clocks, interferometers, and quantum sensors.

title: Long-lived quantum memories with rare-earth ions doped in crystals
abstract: Quantum memory is a core enabling device for large-scale quantum networks, serving as the fundamental building block for quantum repeaters and transportable quantum memories. Among various physical platforms, rare-earth-ion-doped crystals stand out as one of the most promising solid-state candidates for long-lived photonic quantum memories, owing to their exceptionally long spin coherence time and their compatibility with integration. In this review, we first introduce the physical mechanisms underlying long-lived spin coherence in rare-earth systems, with particular emphasis on the zero-first-order-Zeeman transition and dynamical decoupling techniques. We then review the experimental progress in this field, highlighting three distinct lifetimes--the spin coherence time, the light storage time, and the quantum storage time--and covering experiments that have achieved hour-scale spin coherence, minute- to hour-scale light storage, and minute-scale single-photon-level quantum storage. Finally, we discuss the remaining challenges that hinder the realization of practical long-lived quantum memories, explore potential strategies to overcome these obstacles, and outline the prospects for their future applications in quantum networks.
one_liner: This review surveys rare-earth crystal memories reaching hour-scale spin coherence, long-duration light storage, and minute-scale quantum storage.
why_it_matters: Rare-earth crystals combine exceptionally long coherence with solid-state integration, making them strong candidates for repeater-based quantum networks.
detailed_summary: The review explains long-lived coherence in rare-earth-ion-doped crystals, emphasizing zero-first-order-Zeeman transitions and dynamical decoupling. It distinguishes spin coherence time, classical light-storage time, and single-photon-level quantum-storage time rather than treating them as interchangeable metrics. Surveyed experiments include hour-scale spin coherence, minute-to-hour light storage, and minute-scale quantum storage, followed by integration and performance challenges.
main_result: The review documents hour-scale spin coherence and minute-scale single-photon-level quantum storage while identifying the barriers to practical memories.
application_angle: Long-lived, integrable memories could enable quantum repeaters, asynchronous photonic networking, and transportable quantum-state storage.

title: Wavefront engineering with atomic Huygens' surfaces made simple
abstract: Atomic arrays provide a cooperative platform for light-mediated interactions in nonlocal metasurfaces which can operate in the quantum regime without nanofabricated optical elements or intrinsic material absorption. We present a minimal atomic implementation to harness wavefront engineering and create a near-ideal intrinsic atomic Huygens' surface. A simple bilayer square lattice with a two-atom unit cell, not limited to small lattice spacings, provides near-unity reflectionless transmission and a full $2π$ phase control of transmitted light without the localized site-dependent level shifts of previous proposals. This simplification is achieved through nonlocal radiative excitations that provide the familiar electric-dipole response with even radiation parity as well as an odd-parity radiation channel whose leading multipolar interpretation combines magnetic-dipole and electric-quadrupole contributions in atoms exhibiting only electric dipole transitions. This eliminates the need to simultaneously excite pure electric-dipole and magnetic-dipole responses with exactly matched radiation. We derive a two-mode model for this response and show that it accurately captures full coupled-dipole simulations near the optimal lattice spacings. Because of the wide applicability of coupled-dipole models, the relevance of our microscopic analysis extends beyond atomic physics to nanostructured metasurfaces. Moreover, the same platform also connects directly to established subradiance-protected single-photon storage protocols, suggesting a route toward combining wavefront engineering, storage, and retrieval in a simple atomic bilayer.
one_liner: A simple atomic bilayer realizes near-unity reflectionless transmission with full 2π phase control for wavefront engineering.
why_it_matters: It simplifies quantum-compatible metasurfaces and could unite programmable wavefront control with subradiance-protected single-photon storage.
detailed_summary: The authors propose a square-lattice atomic bilayer with a two-atom unit cell as an intrinsic Huygens surface. Nonlocal radiative excitations supply even- and odd-parity channels, producing near-unity reflectionless transmission and full 2π phase coverage without site-dependent level shifts. A two-mode model agrees with coupled-dipole simulations near optimal lattice spacings.
main_result: The bilayer provides near-unity reflectionless transmission and complete 2π control of the transmitted optical phase.
application_angle: The architecture could support reconfigurable quantum wavefront shaping combined with single-photon storage and retrieval.

title: Decoy-state quantum key distribution with a leaky Mach-Zehnder receiver
abstract: We prove the security of phase-encoded decoy-state BB84 quantum key distribution for a Mach-Zehnder receiver with imbalanced beam splitters and two threshold detectors that leak fine-grained information about the detection patterns. For this, we derive a lower bound on Bob's single-photon contributions and combine it with the decoy-state method and a recent phase-error framework for leaky receivers. The leakage-induced correction to the phase-error rate is independent of channel loss, providing a loss-tolerant treatment of receiver leakage even in the presence of beam-splitter imbalance. Our results provide a practical route toward loss-tolerant security proofs for imperfect QKD receivers in the presence of receiver leakage.
one_liner: A security proof makes decoy-state BB84 loss-tolerant despite beam-splitter imbalance and fine-grained detector leakage.
why_it_matters: It closes a practical receiver-side security gap without allowing leakage penalties to grow with transmission distance.
detailed_summary: The work treats phase-encoded decoy-state BB84 using an imbalanced Mach-Zehnder receiver and two threshold detectors that leak detailed detection-pattern information. It derives a lower bound on Bob's single-photon contributions and combines it with a leaky-receiver phase-error framework. The resulting leakage correction is independent of channel loss.
main_result: The authors establish loss-tolerant security bounds for decoy-state BB84 with both beam-splitter imbalance and receiver leakage.
application_angle: The proof supports secure deployment of QKD using realistic interferometric receivers with imperfect components and information leakage.

title: Wigner-Function Fingerprints of Collective Excitations in Mirror-Terminated Waveguide QED
abstract: We investigate the emission profiles of singly excited collective states and propose a matched-mode witnessing protocol in a mirror-terminated waveguide quantum electrodynamics system. The amplitudes and relative phases of the initial collective excitation are encoded in the temporal mode of the emitted single-photon wavepacket, providing a route to state verification through the common waveguide output. We identify the emission mode associated with a chosen target state and employ an auxiliary virtual-cavity representation to evaluate the quantum state of this selected output mode. For a matched initial state, the selected mode contains the emitted single photon, whose Wigner function exhibits a pronounced non-classical negative dip, serving as a distinct fingerprint of the target many-body state. With the reference mode held fixed, different initial configurations yield different photon occupations and phase-space distributions, demonstrating the state selectivity of the protocol. These results connect collective-state verification with temporal-mode analysis of the emitted radiation, offering access to collective coherence with reduced reliance on qubit-resolved correlation measurements.
one_liner: Temporal-mode Wigner fingerprints reveal collective single-excitation states through one common waveguide output.
why_it_matters: The method accesses collective coherence without demanding qubit-resolved correlation measurements across the emitter array.
detailed_summary: In a mirror-terminated waveguide-QED system, the amplitudes and phases of a collective excitation are mapped onto an emitted single-photon temporal mode. A virtual-cavity construction extracts the quantum state of a mode matched to a chosen target. Matching produces a pronounced negative Wigner dip, while other collective states yield distinguishable occupations and phase-space distributions.
main_result: A matched output mode produces a state-selective, nonclassical Wigner-function fingerprint of the initial collective excitation.
application_angle: The protocol offers a reduced-measurement route to verifying collective states in waveguide-coupled quantum networks.

title: Spectral Quantum Memory for Implicit Neural Representations
abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) model signals as continuous functions from coordinates to values, but their performance depends strongly on how spectral capacity is allocated. Yet most Quantum INR (QINR) architectures treat spectral components as independent outputs of separate quantum blocks. We introduce the Spectral Quantum Memory Model (SQMM), a memory coupled quantum INR in which sequential hybrid data reuploading layers (bands) communicate through a shared coherent quantum memory register. Each band reads the memory, computes on its own coordinate upload, and writes part of its state back, so later bands can build on the computation of earlier ones. When memory read and write layers are input independent, we prove that the memory state forms an operator valued Fourier series whose support is contained in the Minkowski sum of the initial memory spectrum and the local band spectra. Downstream bands then condition their Fourier coefficients on the spectral content stored by earlier bands, and the memory coupling creates no new primitive frequencies. This theory motivates a spectral memory alignment loss that encourages memory to encode the spectrum expressed by the deployed prefix of the model. Across audio and image reconstruction benchmarks, SQMM improves over compact QINR and INR baselines.
one_liner: A coherent quantum memory links sequential spectral bands in compact implicit neural representations.
why_it_matters: The architecture improves audio and image reconstruction while clarifying how coherent memory redistributes spectral information across quantum blocks.
detailed_summary: SQMM couples sequential hybrid data-reuploading bands through a shared coherent quantum memory register. The authors prove that the memory state forms an operator-valued Fourier series whose support lies within the Minkowski sum of the initial memory and local band spectra. A spectral-alignment loss then improves reconstruction over compact quantum and classical INR baselines on audio and image tasks.
main_result: Shared coherent memory enables sequential spectral conditioning and improves compact INR reconstruction benchmarks without creating new primitive frequencies.
application_angle: The design provides a resource-conscious quantum-circuit architecture for continuous signal, audio, and image representation.

title: Adaptive Self-Optimization of Polarization Efficiency for Low-Power NV Center Thermometers Based on PAS-Q
abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond have attracted considerable attention for micro- and nanoscale thermometry owing to their high precision and spatial resolution. However, achieving sufficient electron spin polarization and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) typically requires high-power or long-duration laser excitation, which introduces heating and degrades measurement accuracy and stability. To address this trade-off, a reinforcement learning (RL)-based approach is proposed to optimize spin polarization under low-heating constraints. First, a physical model integrating five-level optical pumping rates and NV spin polarization dynamics is established. A temperature-rise constraint model is then developed based on pulsed optically detected magnetic resonance (P-ODMR) measurements under varying laser powers and pulse widths in an external magnetic field. Subsequently, a Progressive Action-Space Q-learning (PAS-Q) algorithm is employed to explore the parameter space and identify optimal laser power and pulse-width combinations. The agent is trained through numerical simulations and the resulting strategy is implemented in a hardware system. Experimental results demonstrate a 44% reduction in laser-induced heating, a 33% increase in spin polarization rate based on T1 relaxation analysis, and a 71% reduction in optimization time compared with traditional methods. This approach enables efficient spin polarization with reduced laser heating and improved optimization efficiency, and may be extended to other heat-sensitive quantum spin sensors, including silicon-vacancy centers in diamond and divacancy defects in silicon carbide.
one_liner: Reinforcement learning tunes NV optical pumping to reduce heating while increasing spin polarization efficiency.
why_it_matters: Adaptive low-power control directly addresses laser heating, a major accuracy and stability limit in microscale NV thermometry.
detailed_summary: The study combines a five-level NV optical-pumping model with a temperature-rise constraint derived from pulsed ODMR measurements. Progressive Action-Space Q-learning searches laser power and pulse width in simulation before deployment on hardware. Experiments report 44% less laser heating, a 33% higher polarization rate from T1 analysis, and 71% shorter optimization time than traditional methods.
main_result: Hardware tests achieved 44% lower heating, 33% faster spin polarization, and 71% less optimization time.
application_angle: The controller can improve thermometry in heat-sensitive samples and may transfer to SiV and silicon-carbide defect sensors.

title: Cooperative Suppression of Two-Particle Excitation by Kerr Nonlinearity and Cavity Loss ion a Driven Holstein-Tavis-Cumming System
abstract: We apply the numerically accurate multiple Davydov Ansatz (multi-$\rm D_2$) method to investigate the nonequilibrium dynamics of an open molecular cavity system using an extended driven-dissipative Holstein-Tavis-Cummings model incorporating Kerr nonlinearity. Our results reveal that the synergy between Kerr nonlinearity and exciton-phonon coupling induces an anharmonic level structure, imposing a stringent energy penalty that isolates the one-excitation manifold. This establishes a robust single-excitation-dominated regime that dynamically manifests photon blockade, characterized by suppression of the pure two-photon state and isolation of the one-excitation manifold. While strong coherent driving induces power broadening that overcomes the nonlinear barrier and opens multiphoton channels, cavity dissipation counteracts this process by acting as a highly selective manifold filter. By preferentially depleting fragile multi-photon states while sheltering single excitations within dissipation-free dark states, the cavity mode decay rate actively cooperates with Kerr nonlinearity to restore and reinforce the photon blockade effect. These findings elucidate the intricate interplay among nonlinearity, driving, and dissipation, offering a theoretical blueprint for engineering robust single-photon sources in open molecular cavity platforms.
one_liner: Kerr nonlinearity and cavity loss cooperatively stabilize photon blockade in a driven molecular cavity model.
why_it_matters: The analysis identifies dissipation as a selective resource for preserving single-excitation behavior under strong driving.
detailed_summary: Multi-D2 simulations study an open Holstein-Tavis-Cummings model containing coherent drive, exciton-phonon coupling, Kerr nonlinearity, and cavity decay. Kerr and vibronic interactions create an anharmonic spectrum that penalizes two-particle occupation, although strong driving opens multiphoton channels. Cavity loss preferentially removes fragile multiphoton states while single excitations persist in dark states.
main_result: Selective cavity decay cooperates with Kerr anharmonicity to restore and reinforce single-excitation-dominated photon blockade.
application_angle: The mechanism provides a theoretical design route toward robust single-photon sources based on open molecular cavities.

title: Breakdown of Linearized Dispersion in Waveguide QED
abstract: Exploring interactions between quantum emitters and guided photons, waveguide quantum electrodynamics (wQED) offers a versatile platform for quantum simulation and quantum interconnect. To simplify the quantized light-matter interactions, a linearized dispersion approximation (LDA) was widely used in wQED under the conditions of weak coupling and narrow photonic bandwidth. However, a growing number of strong-coupling wQED experiments have called the validity of LDA into question. Here, by investigating giant atoms coupled to a semi-infinite waveguide, we propose a principle to judge the validity of LDA. We find that the decoherence of the atoms exhibits rich dynamical behaviors determined by different numbers of bound states in and out of the continuum (BICs and BOCs) formed in the energy spectrum of the total atom-photon system. Based on this, we show that despite the LDA can partially preserve some of BICs, it completely erases BOCs. This causes the dominant role of LDA in the atomic dynamics to break down. Providing a physical insight into the validity of LDA, our results lay a firm foundation for exploring fundamental physics and its application frontier in strong-coupling wQED platforms.
one_liner: A bound-state criterion reveals when linearized photon dispersion fails for giant atoms in strong-coupling waveguide QED.
why_it_matters: The result identifies physics erased by a standard approximation, improving the reliability of strong-coupling waveguide-QED models and device designs.
detailed_summary: The authors analyze giant atoms coupled to a semi-infinite waveguide and relate decoherence dynamics to bound states inside and outside the photon continuum. The linearized-dispersion approximation can retain some bound states in the continuum but eliminates bound states outside the continuum. Consequently, it can miss the dominant atomic dynamics even under conditions where it is commonly applied.
platform_or_system: Giant atoms in a semi-infinite waveguide
main_result: A spectral bound-state criterion shows that linearized dispersion completely removes out-of-continuum bound states and can therefore fail in strong-coupling dynamics.
application_angle: The criterion can guide accurate modeling of quantum interconnects, emitters, and simulators operating beyond weak coupling and narrow bandwidths.

title: Quantum Simulation of Electronic Structure using Quantum Density Functional Theory on a Programmable Integrated Photonic Circuit
abstract: Quantum simulations of molecular electronic structure hold the potential for computational advantage but are inherently limited by the linear scaling of qubit requirements with respect to system size. Quantum Density Functional Theory (Q-DFT) addresses this constraint by reformulating the interacting many-body problem in terms of a non-interacting Kohn--Sham reference system. Here, we present and experimentally validate a Q-DFT algorithm that requires only $\mathcal{O}(\log_2(N))$ qubits to simulate a system of $N$ orbitals, thereby reducing resource overhead. More precisely, we solve the Kohn--Sham problem for the lithium hydride (LiH) molecule using the ensemble extension of the variational quantum eigensolver paradigm that minimizes the energy of the system in the subspace spanned by the ground and first excited states. To execute this task, we encode the problem with qubits on a quantum photonic platform, utilizing an architecture that combines a deterministic quantum dot single-photon source with a programmable integrated photonic circuit. By evaluating the molecular ground- and first excited-state properties, this work establishes a pathway for simulating larger molecular systems, demonstrating the viability of integrating qubit-efficient algorithms with advanced reconfigurable photonic hardware for near-term quantum chemistry applications.
one_liner: A quantum-dot source and programmable photonic chip implement a logarithmic-qubit Q-DFT calculation of LiH states.
why_it_matters: It experimentally combines qubit-efficient electronic-structure algorithms with reconfigurable photonic hardware for near-term quantum chemistry.
detailed_summary: The experiment solves the Kohn–Sham problem for lithium hydride using an ensemble variational eigensolver spanning its ground and first excited states. The formulation requires O(log2 N) qubits for N orbitals rather than a linearly growing register. Qubits are encoded in photons generated by a deterministic quantum-dot source and processed by a programmable integrated photonic circuit.
platform_or_system: Quantum-dot single-photon source with programmable photonic circuit
main_result: The photonic processor experimentally evaluates LiH ground- and first-excited-state properties using a logarithmic-qubit Q-DFT encoding.
application_angle: The approach could reduce hardware requirements for molecular simulations and help photonic processors address larger quantum-chemistry problems.

title: Bayesian optimization enhanced magnetic field gradient detection based on spin-orbit coupled Bose-Einstein condensates
abstract: Magnetic field detection is of great significance in modern fields such as medical diagnostics, geological exploration, inertial navigation, and space physics. We have previously investigated the expansion dynamics of a spin-orbit-coupled Bose-Einstein condensate. Building on these results, here we propose a scheme for magnetic-field-gradient detection by establishing a quantitative relationship between the condensate's rotational deflection angle and the magnetic-field gradient. In this work, we present the parameter dependence of this scheme and perform a systematic optimization. We introduce a Bayesian optimization algorithm to automatically and efficiently search for the optimal combination of key parameters, thereby significantly enhancing the sensitivity of the magnetic field gradient measurement. The results show that the optimized gradiometer improves the sensitivity by a factor of five. This work not only provides a new approach for magnetic field gradient measurement but also serves as a reference for machine learning-empowered quantum precision measurement.
one_liner: Bayesian optimization improves a spin-orbit-coupled BEC magnetic-gradient sensor's simulated sensitivity by fivefold.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates how automated parameter optimization can materially improve an atom-based gradiometer without changing its basic sensing mechanism.
detailed_summary: The proposed sensor infers a magnetic-field gradient from the rotational deflection angle of an expanding spin-orbit-coupled Bose–Einstein condensate. The authors map the relevant parameter dependencies and use Bayesian optimization to search efficiently for a favorable operating point. Their calculations report a factor-of-five sensitivity improvement after optimization.
main_result: Bayesian optimization identifies parameters that improve the proposed magnetic-field-gradient sensitivity by a factor of five.
application_angle: The scheme offers a machine-learning-assisted route toward atom-based gradient sensing for navigation, geophysics, medicine, and space measurements.

title: Temporal stretching of single-photon pulses by intra-cavity frequency conversion
abstract: Spectral bandwidth and frequency mismatch between quantum light emitters and quantum components is a common problem in the realization of hybrid quantum information networks. Here we propose a simultaneous solution to both of these problems by using a free-space cavity with an embedded nonlinear crystal that, through frequency conversion, facilitates perfect coupling into a cavity mode. The slow leakage of the cavity effectively stretches the photon pulse, resulting in a much longer photon pulse at a different wavelength. We show that the amount of stretching is strictly limited by the finesse and length of the cavity. Including realistic internal losses in the cavity, we show that it is possible to stretch a photon by at least two orders of magnitude with high efficiency. The proposed setup can thus constitute a valuable addition to the toolbox of quantum information technologies.
one_liner: Intra-cavity frequency conversion can shift and stretch single-photon pulses by over 100× while retaining high efficiency.
why_it_matters: One device could simultaneously reconcile wavelength and bandwidth mismatches between otherwise incompatible quantum-network components.
detailed_summary: The proposal embeds a nonlinear crystal in a free-space cavity so frequency conversion couples an incident photon perfectly into a cavity mode. Slow cavity leakage then emits the converted photon as a substantially longer pulse at a new wavelength. Modeling with realistic internal loss predicts at least two orders of magnitude of stretching at high efficiency, with the limit set by cavity finesse and length.
main_result: Realistic modeling predicts efficient wavelength conversion accompanied by at least a 100-fold increase in single-photon pulse duration.
application_angle: The converter could interface quantum emitters, memories, detectors, and communication channels with mismatched wavelengths or spectral bandwidths.

title: Observation of pseudospin-locked chiral edge transport in gyromagnetic photonic crystals
abstract: Photonic pseudospins enable selective excitation and routing of light, but perturbations that mix opposite pseudospins can induce backscattering in helical edge channels. Here, we experimentally demonstrate pseudospin-locked chiral edge transport in gyromagnetic photonic crystals, combining pseudospin selectivity with nonreciprocal unidirectional propagation. By jointly engineering lattice deformation and magnetic bias, we control dipolar-quadrupolar band inversions and construct interfaces supporting pseudospin-selective chiral channels. Microwave near-field and transmission measurements reveal a single chiral edge branch that is selectively excited by only one source handedness and exhibits pronounced nonreciprocal transport. Extending this mechanism to multidomain structures, we combine two pseudospin channels into a common waveguide, separate them into distinct outputs, and route them through intersecting interfaces. These configurations realize a nonreciprocal photonic pseudospin multiplexer and demultiplexer, together with a waveguide crossing exhibiting average measured crosstalk of -14.1 and -15.8 dB for its two input channels. Our results present an experimental route to integrating pseudospin-selective channel control with chiral edge transport, providing a foundation for nonreciprocal photonic networks that use pseudospin to organize and route multiple wave channels.
one_liner: A gyromagnetic photonic crystal routes pseudospin-selective microwave edge modes unidirectionally through multiplexers and crossings.
why_it_matters: The experiment combines pseudospin channel selection with nonreciprocal transport, enabling more robust and organized routing in photonic networks.
detailed_summary: Lattice deformation and magnetic bias are jointly engineered to control dipolar–quadrupolar band inversions and form pseudospin-selective chiral interfaces. Near-field and transmission measurements show a single edge branch excited by only one source handedness and propagating nonreciprocally. Multidomain devices implement pseudospin multiplexing, demultiplexing, and an interface crossing with average crosstalk of −14.1 and −15.8 dB for the two inputs.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates pseudospin-locked chiral transport plus nonreciprocal multiplexing, demultiplexing, and low-crosstalk waveguide crossing.
application_angle: The architecture supports compact nonreciprocal microwave-photonic networks that route several channels by pseudospin while suppressing unwanted propagation paths.

title: Rotating two-dimensional Bose--Einstein condensates in power-law traps: collapse, Thomas--Fermi scaling, and the inverse-square endpoint
abstract: In two dimensions, the kinetic and contact energies scale identically under dilation, a trap $V=r^s/s$ as $λ^{-s}$. We follow this balance through the power-law family $-2\le s\le4$, $s\neq0$, for both signs of the coupling $g$, with rotation, using scaling bounds, radial solutions, Bogoliubov spectra, and two-dimensional imaginary-time states. Attraction collapses the cloud at the Townes coupling $g_{*}$ in every trap, with width $\ell\proptoδ^{1/(s+2)}$, $δ=1-|g|/g_{*}$; repulsion spreads it to a Thomas--Fermi (TF) radius $\propto g^{1/(s+2)}$. A rotating collapse leaves the axis once the rotation frequency $Ω$ exceeds its dipole frequency, which softens only for $s>2$; in a quartic trap this happens at $δ\simeq0.32\,Ω^6$, within $3\%$ of the Bogoliubov threshold; it then collapses on the minimum ring of the rotating-frame potential, which also empties a repulsive TF cloud at $Ω=(3g/π)^{1/6}$. For repulsive vortex states the TF energy error splits exactly into a density-gradient and a flow part of comparable or larger size. At $s=-2$ only the cutoff sets a length: the energy is exactly covariant with it, the condensate falls to the center for both signs, and repulsion leaves a halo of density $\propto1/(gr^2)$ whose extent grows exponentially with $g$. Near collapse, split-step imaginary time has a first-order stationary bias invisible to residual tests.
one_liner: A unified analysis maps collapse, rotation thresholds, Thomas–Fermi scaling, and inverse-square behavior in trapped 2D condensates.
why_it_matters: The results clarify stability limits and numerical pitfalls relevant to preparing and modeling rotating two-dimensional quantum gases.
detailed_summary: The study combines scaling bounds, radial solutions, Bogoliubov spectra, and two-dimensional imaginary-time calculations across power-law traps with attractive or repulsive interactions. Attraction collapses at the Townes coupling, while repulsive clouds follow Thomas–Fermi radius scaling; rotation can displace collapse onto a ring above a dipole-mode threshold. At the inverse-square endpoint the cutoff fixes the only length scale, and the authors also identify a first-order stationary bias in split-step imaginary-time simulations near collapse.
platform_or_system: Rotating 2D Bose–Einstein condensates in power-law traps
main_result: The work derives collapse and spreading laws, rotation-induced instability thresholds, inverse-square scaling, and a hidden numerical bias near collapse.
application_angle: These stability maps and diagnostics can inform trap design, vortex-state preparation, and trustworthy simulations of rotating quantum-gas experiments.

title: Autonomous cooling of Kerr-cat qubits to minutes-long bit-flip times
abstract: Quantum error correction becomes more hardware efficient when physical noise is strongly biased towards one error channel. Cat qubits realize such a bias by encoding information in two opposite coherent states of a superconducting oscillator, so that bit flips are exponentially suppressed with photon number while phase-flip rates increase only linearly. In Kerr-cat qubits, a driven double-well potential confines these states and enables fast coherent control, but excitations can induce interwell switching, limiting bit-flip times to milliseconds. Here we show that the nonlinear interaction generating the confinement can also cool these excitations. When an intra-well transition becomes resonant with a lossy readout mode, excitations are transferred out of the qubit and dissipated, as established by spectroscopy and relaxation measurements. We observe the predicted exponential scaling of Kerr-cat bit-flip times with photon number, reaching 450 s, over five orders of magnitude beyond previous demonstrations. Phase-flip rates remain consistent with intrinsic photon loss at operating points with seconds-long bit-flip times. We further demonstrate fast Z gates without measurable degradation of bit-flip protection and single-shot readout with a bit-flip probability below $10^{-6}$ per measurement. Autonomous cooling thus brings minutes-long bit-flip protection to Kerr-cat qubits while retaining fast coherent control, without additional cooling drives or circuit elements.
one_liner: Autonomous cooling extends Kerr-cat qubit bit-flip times to 450 s while preserving fast gates and high-fidelity readout.
why_it_matters: The result delivers a five-order-of-magnitude gain in bit-flip protection without extra cooling drives or circuit elements.
detailed_summary: A lossy readout mode is tuned into resonance with an intra-well transition, transferring and dissipating excitations that otherwise trigger interwell switching. Spectroscopy and relaxation measurements confirm the cooling mechanism, while bit-flip lifetime scales exponentially with photon number and reaches 450 s. Fast Z gates retain the protection, and single-shot readout produces less than 10^-6 bit-flip probability per measurement.
main_result: The experiment achieves a 450 s bit-flip time, fast protected Z gates, and single-shot readout with below 10^-6 induced bit-flip probability.
application_angle: Minutes-long passive bit-flip protection could substantially reduce the hardware overhead of fault-tolerant quantum processors using noise-biased qubits.

title: Quantum sensing of a weak drive signal in cascaded quantum van der Pol oscillators
abstract: We have constructed a quantum sensing system composed of two quantum van der Pol (vdP) oscillators. Coherent and dissipative couplings are combined to establish a generic nonreciprocal coupling between the two vdP subsystems. A weak driving signal to be measured is applied to an oscillator (probe system) and then transferred via non-reciprocal coupling to another oscillator (measurement system) that is easier to measure. This allows for the acquisition of information about the driving strength of the signal being measured. For the classic cascaded dual vdP oscillators, complete non-reciprocal coupling yields a much higher susceptibility than a single classical vdP oscillator alone. For the quantum vdP system, the sensitivity generally does not diverge at the zero driving force point. When only dissipative coupling and two-particle loss are present, the system will have a dark mode at the zero driving force point, which enables the measurement precision to ultimately reach the Heisenberg limit in the time domain. Enhancing incoherent driving can effectively resist dissipation and thereby improve measurement precision. Moreover, in the strong incoherent driving regime, the improvement factor of non-reciprocal coupling over reciprocal coupling in terms of measurement precision tends to infinity as the two-particle loss rate of the measurement system approaches zero.
one_liner: Cascaded quantum van der Pol oscillators use nonreciprocal coupling and a dark mode to enhance weak-drive sensing.
why_it_matters: The architecture separates the probe from the readout subsystem and theoretically permits time-domain precision at the Heisenberg limit.
detailed_summary: A weak drive applied to a probe oscillator is transferred nonreciprocally to a second oscillator designed for easier measurement. With dissipative coupling and two-particle loss, a zero-drive dark mode enables Heisenberg-limited time scaling in the predicted estimation precision. Strong incoherent driving can counter dissipation and amplify the precision advantage over reciprocal coupling.
platform_or_system: Cascaded quantum van der Pol oscillators
main_result: The analysis identifies regimes where nonreciprocal coupling strongly improves weak-drive estimation and a dark mode enables Heisenberg-limited temporal precision.
application_angle: The scheme offers a route to remotely interrogating weak signals through a separate, experimentally accessible readout oscillator.

title: Band structure of two-dimensional graphene and of one-dimensional nanoribbons via variational quantum algorithms: from energies to wavefunction quality
abstract: Simulating quantum many-body systems classically encounters exponential bottlenecks, which quantum devices circumvent by natively encoding wavefunctions. In the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era, however, hardware noise constrains simulation accuracy. As a stepping stone toward strongly correlated materials, we compute the band structure of 2D monolayer graphene and 1D nanoribbons (zigzag and armchair) using a single variational workflow in the $p_z$ tight-binding approximation. Non-interacting ground states also provide essential initial reference states for subspace and warm-started variational methods to solve interacting spectra. By mapping the Bloch Hamiltonian to Pauli operators, we extract the ground band via the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) and excited subbands via Variational Quantum Deflation (VQD), validating our approach from ideal simulations to execution on physical IBM Quantum processors. In ideal simulations, the workflow reproduces exact diagonalization results with high precision, whereas hardware noise introduces energy deviations of a few hundredths of the hopping parameter. While qubit counts scale logarithmically with ribbon width, fixed-depth ansatz accuracy degrades with Hilbert space dimension. Crucially, deepening the ansatz improves ideal simulation accuracy by over three orders of magnitude but worsens energy estimates under noise, proving that practical circuit depth is bounded by hardware noise rather than expressivity. Finally, we complement energy evaluations with a wavefunction-level diagnostic measuring subspace containment. This diagnostic captures degenerate manifolds and exposes optimization failure modes disguised by energy agreement alone. Operating directly on NISQ hardware, this validated workflow establishes a controlled baseline for studying topological and strongly correlated phases in realistic materials.
one_liner: A VQE–VQD workflow computes graphene and nanoribbon bands on IBM hardware while diagnosing energy and wavefunction errors.
why_it_matters: Hardware tests expose the practical tradeoff between ansatz expressivity and noise, while subspace diagnostics reveal failures hidden by accurate energies.
detailed_summary: Bloch tight-binding Hamiltonians for monolayer graphene and zigzag or armchair nanoribbons are mapped to Pauli operators, with VQE extracting ground bands and VQD obtaining excited subbands. Ideal calculations closely reproduce exact diagonalization, whereas IBM processor runs show errors of a few hundredths of the hopping parameter. Increasing circuit depth improves ideal accuracy by over three orders of magnitude but degrades noisy results; a subspace-containment metric additionally detects degeneracy and optimization failures.
main_result: The study validates a unified band-structure workflow on physical quantum hardware and shows that noise, rather than ansatz expressivity, bounds useful circuit depth.
application_angle: The workflow provides a hardware-tested baseline for future quantum simulations of topological and correlated electronic materials.

title: Recoverability of Gravitational Entanglement under Decoherence
abstract: Decoherence can make gravitationally generated entanglement arbitrarily small, or even vanishing, without necessarily rendering the effective matter dynamics separable. We ask whether this hidden non-separability can be revealed using strictly local quantum error correction. For Newtonian gravity supplemented by physically relevant localization noise, including environmental noise, and noise from collapse models such as GRW, CSL, and Diósi--Penrose, we analyze when the underlying entangling resource is locally recoverable. For GRW- and CSL-type noise, we analytically establish that strictly local quantum error correction can make the ratio of the effective gravitational interaction strength to the residual decoherence rate arbitrarily large for any parametrization of the collapse model, even in regimes where the unencoded entanglement signal approaches zero. By contrast, the Diósi--Penrose model does not exhibit the same enhancement under bipartite protocol considered here, revealing a qualitative difference. These results show that the loss of detectable entanglement is not equivalent to the loss of a recoverable non-separable resource, and open a route toward practical recovery protocols.
one_liner: Local quantum error correction can recover hidden gravitational non-separability suppressed by several forms of localization noise.
why_it_matters: It distinguishes loss of directly observable entanglement from loss of the underlying recoverable quantum interaction resource.
detailed_summary: The work studies Newtonian gravitational interactions under environmental localization and GRW, CSL, and Diósi–Penrose collapse noise. For GRW- and CSL-type models, strictly local error correction can make the effective interaction-to-residual-decoherence ratio arbitrarily large, even when unencoded entanglement vanishes. The same bipartite enhancement is absent for the Diósi–Penrose model, providing a qualitative discriminator between noise mechanisms.
main_result: The analysis proves arbitrarily strong local-QEC recovery of the gravitational interaction relative to GRW or CSL decoherence, but not for Diósi–Penrose noise.
application_angle: Local encoding could improve proposed tests of gravity-mediated entanglement and help distinguish environmental decoherence from collapse-model predictions.

title: QECert: Formal Foundations for Quantum Error-Correction Theory in Lean
abstract: Quantum error correction provides the mathematical basis for protecting quantum information against noise. Existing formalizations have established foundations for stabilizer codes and code verification. However, a systematic formal treatment of the asymptotic constructions and fundamental limitations that underpin scalable quantum error correction is still needed. We present QECert, a Lean library providing reusable formal foundations for these theoretical questions. It connects quantum error-correction criteria, stabilizer and Calderbank-Shor-Steane codes, and algebraic and homological constructions within a common framework. Asymptotically good quantum low density parity check codes provide the principal case study. We formalize constructions and asymptotic parameter theorems spanning hypergraph products, balanced products, lifted products, and quantum Tanner codes. Further developments cover Bravyi-Poulin-Terhal bounds and related locality restrictions, constant overhead magic state distillation, and energy barriers and storage errors for quantum memories. QECert establishes a reusable formal foundation for studying the capabilities, resource requirements, and fundamental limitations of quantum error correction, supporting systematic verification and further development of its theory.
one_liner: QECert formalizes scalable quantum-error-correction constructions, bounds, and memory theory in the Lean proof assistant.
why_it_matters: Machine-checked foundations can prevent subtle proof errors and support trustworthy comparison of scalable QEC architectures and resource claims.
detailed_summary: QECert unifies quantum error-correction criteria, stabilizer and CSS codes, and algebraic and homological constructions in a reusable Lean library. Its formalized asymptotic results cover hypergraph, balanced, and lifted products as well as quantum Tanner codes. The library also treats locality bounds, constant-overhead magic-state distillation, energy barriers, and storage errors in quantum memories.
main_result: The library provides machine-checked foundations spanning major qLDPC constructions, asymptotic parameter theorems, locality limits, and quantum-memory results.
application_angle: QECert can support auditable design and resource analysis for fault-tolerant quantum computers, although it is a theory tool rather than a hardware demonstration.

title: Operational Thresholds for Long-Range Entanglement in Quantum Networks
abstract: Quantum networks distribute entanglement between distant nodes by combining many short entangled links using local quantum operations. These operations only succeed probabilistically, yet existing percolation-based theories of entanglement transmission treat them as perfect. We approach the problem through statistical physics, using a stochastic generalization of concurrence percolation to determine how reliable local operations must be for long-range entanglement to remain possible. On hierarchical $(U,V)$-flower networks, which permit full analytical control across network scales, we derive an exact renormalization recursion for the probability that an end-to-end entangled connection survives. For the $(2,2)$-flower this yields a closed-form operational phase boundary, $η_p = 2 - \frac{32}{27}η_s$, where $η_s$ and $η_p$ are the success probabilities of the series (entanglement swapping) and parallel (purification) operations, respectively. At this boundary the survival probability jumps discontinuously from $0$ to $S_\infty = 3/(4η_s)$. Numerically propagating the full distribution of end-to-end concurrence yields a second threshold in the initial link quality, which varies continuously with operational reliability. Above both thresholds the large-network state is binary: the connection either fails outright or approaches a perfect Bell pair. Our results thus reveal a two-threshold structure for long-range entanglement, in which operational reliability and initial link quality can compensate one another. Operational success rates therefore emerge alongside initial link quality as a primary design constraint for scalable quantum networks.
one_liner: Quantum-network percolation develops two thresholds set by local-operation reliability and initial entangled-link quality.
why_it_matters: It elevates probabilistic swapping and purification success rates to first-class engineering constraints for scalable entanglement distribution.
detailed_summary: A stochastic concurrence-percolation model incorporates imperfect entanglement swapping and purification on hierarchical flower networks. For the (2,2)-flower, the authors derive the exact operational boundary η_p = 2 - (32/27)η_s and a discontinuous survival-probability jump. Numerical propagation of concurrence distributions reveals a second threshold in link quality, above which large networks either fail or approach a perfect Bell pair.
main_result: The work derives an exact operational phase boundary and identifies a compensating two-threshold structure in operation success and elementary-link quality.
application_angle: The thresholds provide quantitative targets for swapping, purification, and source fidelity when engineering long-distance quantum-network links.

title: Comment on "Supervised Learning with Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings" (arXiv:2610.26833)
abstract: We discuss the relationship between quantum Hamiltonian embeddings (arXiv:2610.26833) and prior developments in Quantum Cognition Machine Learning (QCML), including QCML's earlier implementation on IBM quantum hardware. We consider the novelty claims and the computational role of encoding an entire dataset in a single ground state.
one_liner: A comment links quantum Hamiltonian embeddings to earlier quantum cognition machine learning and questions their novelty and dataset encoding claims.
why_it_matters: It clarifies prior art and the computational significance of encoding a full dataset into one ground state, but presents no new sensing experiment.
detailed_summary: The comment compares quantum Hamiltonian embeddings with earlier Quantum Cognition Machine Learning work, including a prior implementation on IBM quantum hardware. It examines claimed novelty and asks what computational benefit follows from encoding an entire dataset into a single ground state. The paper is primarily a conceptual and priority critique rather than an experimental sensing result.
platform_or_system: IBM quantum processors and Hamiltonian embeddings
main_result: The authors identify substantial connections to prior QCML work and challenge the novelty and computational interpretation of the proposed embedding method.
application_angle: The analysis helps researchers judge whether Hamiltonian-embedding classifiers offer actionable advantages for hardware-based quantum learning or sensing workflows.

title: Photon-Counting Readout via Electro-Optic Microwave-to-Optical Transduction for Axion Haloscopes
abstract: Axion dark matter searches require highly sensitive detection schemes with high scan rate to efficiently explore the parameter space. Building upon the conventional Sikivie haloscope, where axions convert into microwave photons inside a magnetic-field-immersed resonant cavity, we present a photon-counting scheme based on an electro-optic microwave-to-optical transducer. Through a comprehensive theoretical model under realistic experimental constraints, we find that the optimal operating regime employs an overcoupled microwave cavity, trading peak transduction efficiency for reduced transducer noise. Furthermore, combining parameters already demonstrated in existing devices, in a device with optimized extrinsic coupling rates, would yield a scan-rate enhancement of 5-10 relative to quantum-limited homodyne detection. Improvements in quality factors, coupling rates, and thermal management push this enhancement beyond 50. While our quantitative model is benchmarked at 9 GHz, the scheme adapts well to haloscopes across the 5-12 GHz range, where shrinking cavity volumes severely degrade the achievable scan rate. These results demonstrate the potential of electro-optical photon detection as a high-speed detection technique for axion dark matter searches.
one_liner: Electro-optic microwave-to-optical photon counting could accelerate 5–12 GHz axion haloscope scans beyond quantum-limited homodyne readout.
why_it_matters: A realistic transducer model predicts 5–10× scan-rate gains with demonstrated device parameters and over 50× with improved components and thermal control.
detailed_summary: The paper models an electro-optic transducer that converts haloscope microwave photons into optical photons for counting-based detection. Under realistic constraints, an overcoupled microwave cavity lowers transducer noise at the cost of peak conversion efficiency. At 9 GHz, parameters already demonstrated in separate devices yield a predicted 5–10× scan-rate enhancement over quantum-limited homodyne detection; improved quality factors, coupling, and thermal management raise the gain beyond 50×.
main_result: The model predicts 5–10× faster axion scans using demonstrated component parameters and more than 50× with optimized hardware.
application_angle: The approach could restore search speed in compact 5–12 GHz haloscopes, where shrinking cavity volume otherwise sharply reduces sensitivity and scan rate.

title: DynaMite: Dynamic Measurement Scheduling To Accelerate Fault-Tolerant Quantum Programs
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computers run millions of logical cycles to perform quantum error correction (QEC). As logical operations span entire logical cycles, the logical cycle time (LCT) dictates program runtime. Qubit measurements, critical to extract parity information for QEC, are the slowest operations and account for 43-86% of LCT. Measurement latencies impact fidelity: fast measurements lower our ability to correctly classify quantum states, whereas slow measurements increase the likelihood of decoherence. Hardware providers thus calibrate measurement latencies that maximize readout fidelity per qubit and use them to schedule all measurements during program execution. However, calibrated latencies are sub-optimal for logical performance because logical cycles span multiple QEC rounds, during which data qubits are not measured. This increases LCT and logical error rates (LERs) due to decoherence at the logical level. We propose DynaMite, a lightweight real-time measurement latency selection policy built on two key insights. First, logical cycles must use a measurement latency that is fast enough to reduce both LCT and LER for the QEC code, instead of the calibrated latency that only maximizes readout fidelity.
