Second, not all logical cycles are equal; many do not fully utilize the error budget of the QEC code, i.e., the number of failed parity checks it can tolerate without compromising LER. These cycles could use even faster measurements but do not, because latencies are chosen statically, whereas error information is only available at runtime. DynaMite exploits the fact that a logical cycle comprises multiple QEC rounds and selects the fastest latency for an upcoming round based on the error budget left and rounds remaining. Our evaluations show that DynaMite reduces LCT by 1.69x on average and up to 2.29x, and reduces LER to 0.46x on average and up to 0.13x of baseline.
one_liner: DynaMite dynamically shortens qubit measurements during QEC, reducing logical-cycle time while also lowering logical error rates.
why_it_matters: The policy targets the dominant 43–86% measurement share of logical-cycle time and reports 1.69× average acceleration with logical errors cut to 0.46× baseline.
detailed_summary: DynaMite selects measurement latency for each upcoming QEC round using the remaining error budget and number of rounds left in the logical cycle. This replaces static per-qubit latencies optimized only for physical readout fidelity with choices that jointly account for decoherence, cycle duration, and logical failure. Evaluation reports a 1.69× average and 2.29× maximum reduction in logical-cycle time, while logical error rates fall to 0.46× on average and 0.13× at best relative to baseline.
main_result: Dynamic latency selection achieves up to 2.29× shorter logical cycles and reduces logical error rates to as little as 0.13× the static-scheduling baseline.
application_angle: The lightweight runtime policy could improve throughput and reliability in fault-tolerant processors without requiring a new error-correcting code or major hardware redesign.

title: Quantum Advantage has Few Complexity Implications
abstract: We consider the complexity implications of proofs of quantumness and (quantum verifier) oblivious state preparation. We show that both of these objects can coexist with the easiness of nondeterministic computation. That is, we give evidence that proofs of quantumness can exist when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{NP}$ and that (quantum verifier) oblivious state preparation can exist when $\mathsf{BQP} = \mathsf{QCMA}$. In particular, we give a classical oracle relative to which (1) $\mathsf{P}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{NP}^\mathcal{O}$ (2) $\mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{PSPACE}^\mathcal{O}$ (3) Proofs of quantumness exist. In particular, there exists a language in $\mathsf{IP}^\mathcal{O} \subseteq \mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O}$ which is hard on average against $\mathsf{P}^\mathcal{O}/poly$. We give a unitary oracle such that (1) $\mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{QCMA}^\mathcal{O}$ (2) Quantum verifier oblivious state preparation exists. These oracle separations directly imply a number of related consequences. For example, our first result implies that proofs of quantumness cannot be used to construct classical or quantum cryptography with a relativizing proof. Our second result implies that quantum computation/classical communication oblivious transfer cannot be used to construct post-quantum one-way functions with a relativizing proof.
one_liner: Oracle separations show that proofs of quantumness and oblivious state preparation need not imply commonly expected complexity or cryptographic separations.
why_it_matters: The results delimit what quantum-verification primitives can establish through relativizing arguments, constraining security claims in quantum communication protocols.
detailed_summary: The authors construct a classical oracle where P equals NP, BQP equals PSPACE, and proofs of quantumness still exist. They also give a unitary oracle where BQP equals QCMA while quantum-verifier oblivious state preparation remains possible. These separations show that the primitives alone do not yield several classical or post-quantum cryptographic consequences through relativizing proofs.
platform_or_system: Oracle models of quantum verification and cryptography
main_result: Proofs of quantumness and quantum-verifier oblivious state preparation are shown compatible with collapsed nondeterministic complexity classes in appropriate oracle worlds.
application_angle: The work identifies proof barriers for deriving cryptographic security from quantum communication and verification primitives, guiding protocol designers toward non-relativizing assumptions or techniques.

title: Effect of high odrer dispersion on soliton interaction in coupled Kerr cavities
abstract: We investigate the interaction of dissipative Kerr solitons in two nearly identical coherently driven, coupled microresonators in the presence of third-order dispersion (TOD). Using an asymptotic reduction of the coupled Lugiato--Lefever equations, we derive effective interaction equations governing the soliton separation and collective drift for weak intercavity coupling. TOD breaks the parity symmetry of the soliton profile and qualitatively modifies the effective interaction, leading to asymmetric interaction forces and multiple stable and unstable soliton clusters. The existence and stability of these clusters are controlled by the relative phase of the driving fields and the group-velocity mismatch between the resonators. In particular, an appropriate value of the group-velocity mismatch can give rise to multiple stable bound states, whereas deviations from this value trigger successive saddle-node bifurcations, ultimately leading to periodic soliton collisions. The analytical predictions are confirmed by numerical simulations of the full coupled system.
one_liner: Third-order dispersion creates asymmetric forces, tunable bound states, and periodic collisions between dissipative solitons in coupled Kerr microresonators.
why_it_matters: The derived interaction laws expose phase and velocity-mismatch controls for stabilizing or switching multi-soliton states in coupled photonic resonators.
detailed_summary: An asymptotic reduction of coupled Lugiato–Lefever equations yields effective equations for soliton separation and collective drift under weak intercavity coupling. Third-order dispersion breaks parity symmetry, producing asymmetric forces and multiple stable and unstable clusters controlled by drive-phase difference and group-velocity mismatch. Moving away from the optimal mismatch induces successive saddle-node bifurcations and eventually periodic soliton collisions, consistent with full-system simulations.
main_result: The analysis predicts and numerically confirms dispersion-induced asymmetric interactions, multiple tunable bound states, and bifurcation-driven periodic soliton collisions.
application_angle: Controllable soliton binding and collision dynamics could support configurable microcomb states, optical timing functions, and integrated nonlinear-photonic signal processing.

title: Interpretable Quantum Photonic Generative Models
abstract: We propose a physical generative model for learning correlated multivariate data based on homodyne detection of photonic continuous-variable (CV) circuits. We use an $N$-mode photonic circuit in which two-mode squeezing provides correlations, local phase shifts tune the strength and sign of these correlations, and an adjustable interferometer redistributes them across modes. We train the circuit by matching its Pearson correlation matrix to the one obtained from data. We apply affine post-processing to adjust the marginals independently while keeping the relations intact. We test the model on the multivariate distribution of standardized log returns of financial assets, showing that the photonic model can represent rich correlation structures. We reproduce empirical correlations with residuals below $10^{-4}$ for five variables and recover the correct correlation signs for $94\% \pm 1\%$ of 190 correlation pairs at twenty variables, with $86\%$ of the residuals below $0.1$. As a separate technical contribution, we develop an approach for simulating Kerr gates with small nonlinearity via a Hubbard-Stratonovich expansion, making them suitable for CV-based simulators. Our results establish CV photonic circuits as a platform for interpretable generative learning, suitable for representing and fast sampling of distributions across different application domains.
one_liner: An interpretable continuous-variable photonic circuit learns multivariate correlations through squeezing, phase control, interferometry, and homodyne sampling.
why_it_matters: The model reproduces five-variable correlations below 10⁻⁴ residual and retains 94% of correlation signs across 190 pairs at 20 variables.
detailed_summary: The proposed N-mode continuous-variable circuit uses two-mode squeezing to generate correlations, local phase shifts to control their signs and strengths, and an interferometer to redistribute them. Training matches the circuit's Pearson correlation matrix to data, while affine post-processing adjusts marginal distributions independently. Tests on standardized financial log returns achieve residuals below 10⁻⁴ for five variables and recover 94% ± 1% of 190 correlation signs at 20 variables; the paper also introduces a Hubbard–Stratonovich method for simulating weak Kerr gates.
main_result: The photonic model accurately learns small multivariate correlation matrices and scales to 20 variables while preserving most pairwise correlation signs.
application_angle: Its interpretable optical controls and rapid sampling offer a hardware-oriented route to multivariate generative modeling in finance and other correlation-rich domains.

title: Dynamically modulated light-matter interactions for ancilla-tolerant bosonic control
abstract: Strong light-matter interactions are central to state-of-the-art quantum technologies, spanning platforms as diverse as Rydberg atoms, trapped ions, and superconducting circuits. In superconducting circuits, the strong dispersive coupling between microwave photons (light) and ancillary qubits (matter) has enabled universal bosonic control and quantum error correction. However, this always-on dispersive interaction propagates errors from the ancillary qubits to the bosonic systems both while idling and when performing operations, introducing a trade-off between control strength and fidelity. We break this trade-off by introducing a parametrically activated hybridization between the bosonic modes and ancilla qubits, keeping both elements decoupled when not active. When activated, this hybridization mediates a dynamic light-matter coupling with non-trivial engineered symmetries, permitting resilience to ancilla decay and dephasing. This dynamic coupling functions as a new control primitive that offers a route to bosonic processors whose performance is set by the oscillator, rather than the ancilla.
one_liner: Parametrically activated light–matter coupling enables bosonic control while suppressing ancilla-error propagation during gates and idle periods.
why_it_matters: This could shift superconducting bosonic-processor fidelity limits from short-lived ancillary qubits toward the longer-lived oscillator hardware.
detailed_summary: The work replaces an always-on dispersive interaction with parametrically activated hybridization between microwave bosonic modes and ancilla qubits. The components remain decoupled while idle, while engineered symmetries in the activated interaction provide resilience to ancilla decay and dephasing. The resulting primitive targets bosonic operations whose performance is governed mainly by oscillator coherence rather than ancilla quality.
platform_or_system: Superconducting bosonic circuits with ancilla qubits
main_result: A dynamically activated light–matter control primitive is introduced that combines strong bosonic control with tolerance to ancilla decay and dephasing.
application_angle: The approach offers a hardware path toward higher-fidelity bosonic processors and more robust oscillator-based quantum error correction.

title: Quantum Error Correction in Nearly Critical Toric Codes
abstract: We investigate quantum error correction protocols for topological codes deformed away from their stabilizer limits, particularly as they are pushed towards quantum phase transitions into trivial phases. Our focus is primarily on quantum information stored within the ground-state manifold of the transverse-field toric code (TFTC), subjected to independent bit-flip and phase-flip decoherence. Although the transverse field induces strong quantum fluctuations of $m$ anyons in the ground states, we show that projective measurements of the "bare" toric code stabilizers can nevertheless be used to construct an efficient decoding algorithm which exhibits a finite threshold to both types of decoherence, even when the transverse field is tuned infinitesimally close to the quantum critical point. Our construction of the optimal postmeasurement decoders---that is, the optimal decoders assuming that the stabilizers are first measured---crucially relies on the stoquastic nature of the TFTC Hamiltonian, which affords a description of its ground states in terms of a classical lattice gauge theory. Using stoquasticity, we first prove that stabilizer measurements act unitarily on the undecohered TFTC ground states to excellent approximation, and that the optimal postmeasurement decoder can be efficiently implemented via Monte Carlo simulation of a constrained lattice gauge theory. We then construct the optimal postmeasurement decoder for the TFTC states under bit-flip and phase-flip decoherence, where we numerically demonstrate a finite threshold close to the quantum critical point. We provide theoretical evidence (without a rigorous proof) that stabilizer measurements constitute an optimal decoding strategy in this setting. For phase-flip decoherence, we further prove that the optimal postmeasurement decoding threshold is independent of the transverse field strength throughout the topological phase.
one_liner: Bare stabilizer measurements retain finite error-correction thresholds in transverse-field toric codes arbitrarily near criticality.
why_it_matters: It shows that topological quantum information can remain efficiently decodable despite strong ground-state fluctuations close to a phase transition.
detailed_summary: The authors study bit- and phase-flip correction in the transverse-field toric code as it approaches the transition out of the topological phase. Stoquasticity maps the postmeasurement decoding problem to constrained classical lattice-gauge Monte Carlo sampling. Numerics show finite thresholds arbitrarily close to criticality, and the phase-flip threshold is proven independent of transverse-field strength throughout the topological phase.
main_result: Efficient postmeasurement decoders based on bare toric-code stabilizers maintain finite bit- and phase-flip thresholds near the quantum critical point.
application_angle: The results broaden the operating regime in which imperfect, non-stabilizer topological-code hardware could still support practical error correction.

title: Superconducting Qubits as Quantum Targets for Direct Particle Scattering
abstract: We introduce a novel approach to particle detection in which a superconducting qubit itself serves as the scattering target and a resolved transition between circuit eigenstates constitutes the observable final state. The scattering amplitude factorizes into the incident-particle current and a finite-momentum electromagnetic transition response of the qubit. This momentum dependence is essential in that the energy transfer is fixed by the microwave-scale level spacing, whereas a nonrelativistic incident particle can transfer a spatial momentum parametrically larger than that energy and thereby resolve the device geometry. For charge-dominated processes, we recast the response as an induced-offset-charge kernel obtained from an auxiliary electrostatic weighting potential, providing a practical route from circuit geometry to a differential scattering cross section. We illustrate the framework with an Xmon-style transmon and photon-mediated scattering of dark matter. The exceptionally small qubit transition threshold opens sensitivity to an eV-to-keV mass regime that is largely unexplored by existing direct-detection experiments.
one_liner: A superconducting qubit is proposed as both the microscopic scattering target and resolved detector for low-mass incident particles.
why_it_matters: Microwave-scale qubit transitions could open direct-detection sensitivity to eV–keV dark matter masses that conventional detectors poorly cover.
detailed_summary: The framework treats a resolved transition between circuit eigenstates as the final state of direct particle scattering from a superconducting qubit. It factorizes the amplitude into an incident current and the qubit’s finite-momentum electromagnetic response, retaining geometric information absent from a purely energy-based treatment. For charge-mediated interactions, an auxiliary electrostatic weighting potential yields a practical offset-charge kernel, illustrated for photon-mediated dark-matter scattering from an Xmon-style transmon.
main_result: The paper derives a geometry-aware differential scattering framework showing how qubit transitions can detect particles in the eV-to-keV mass regime.
application_angle: The method could repurpose quantum-circuit hardware as an ultrasensitive direct-detection platform for low-mass dark matter and other weakly coupled particles.

title: Noise-Induced Topology in Chiral Quantum Walks
abstract: Noise typically destroys quantum coherence and washes out transport phenomena that rely on interference. Chiral quantum walks are a case in point: a particle hopping on a lattice threaded by a magnetic flux can spread asymmetrically due to interference between paths, an asymmetry that noise is expected to erase. Remarkably, we find that the most ubiquitous noise -- random fluctuations of on-site energies (dephasing) -- instead renders this asymmetry topologically robust. The density profile develops a skewness that grows in time while its center stays fixed, and in a finite chain the late-time relaxation modes pile up at one edge: a skin effect lacking the drift of conventional non-Hermitian skin effects. With multiple sites per unit cell, the dephasing strength alone can cause a topological phase transition, reversing the asymmetry. On a flux ladder with noisy rung hopping, the noise causes a drift of rung coherences, a quantum ratchet with no classical counterpart. Underlying these effects, the noise-averaged dynamics is an interacting (generically non-integrable) Lindbladian that remains analytically tractable. The modes governing late-time relaxation are bound states of the noise-induced interaction and form a band with a point gap, absent both without noise and under postselection, whose winding number fixes the direction of the asymmetry. These effects are within reach of several experimental platforms, including synthetic lattices, superconducting qubits, and optical lattices.
one_liner: Dephasing creates topologically protected asymmetric transport and an unconventional skin effect in chiral quantum walks.
why_it_matters: It turns a ubiquitous noise source into a controllable resource for robust transport, topology, and coherence ratchets across synthetic quantum lattices.
detailed_summary: Random on-site-energy fluctuations produce growing density skewness without center-of-mass drift and make finite-chain relaxation modes accumulate at one edge. The late-time modes are interaction-bound states of the noise-averaged Lindbladian, forming a point-gapped band whose winding fixes the asymmetry direction. Dephasing strength can reverse the topology in multi-site unit cells, while noisy rung hopping on a flux ladder produces a coherence drift with no classical analogue.
platform_or_system: Synthetic chiral lattices and flux ladders
main_result: Dephasing is shown to induce point-gap topology, edge-localized relaxation, switchable transport asymmetry, and a purely quantum coherence ratchet.
application_angle: The predicted effects are testable in superconducting-qubit arrays, optical lattices, and other synthetic-lattice platforms for noise-engineered transport.

title: Fermionic Porter-Thomas statistics and their emergence in random matchgate circuits
abstract: For Haar-random quantum states, measurement probabilities follow the universal Porter--Thomas distribution. This implies anticoncentration, i.e.\ the spreading of probability over exponentially many outcomes, a key property underlying random-circuit-sampling experiments. We derive the exact analogue of the Porter--Thomas law for random fermionic Gaussian states, both with and without particle-number conservation. We also consider Clifford Gaussian states, for which the problem maps onto a simple model of arcs and loops. For large systems the probabilities become log-normally distributed, with moments growing polynomially in system size. Free-fermion states thus anticoncentrate only up to polynomial factors. We then show how this fermionic Porter--Thomas law emerges in random one-dimensional brickwork matchgate circuits. A simple single-arc approximation accurately describes the full distribution of probabilities, revealing an early diffusive regime followed by a slow relaxation on times scaling as the square of the system size. We rigorously prove that depths growing almost quadratically with system size are required for the collision probability to converge. Finally, we show that ideal free-fermion sampling yields large linear cross-entropy scores, and propose a log-based benchmark with an exact fermionic normalization.
one_liner: The work derives fermionic Porter–Thomas statistics and their slow emergence in random one-dimensional matchgate circuits.
why_it_matters: It supplies platform-specific anticoncentration laws and benchmarks for validating free-fermion photonic or quantum-circuit sampling experiments.
detailed_summary: The authors derive exact measurement-probability statistics for random fermionic Gaussian states with and without particle-number conservation. Unlike Haar-random states, the probabilities become log-normal at large size and anticoncentrate only up to polynomial factors. In one-dimensional brickwork matchgate circuits, convergence of the collision probability requires nearly quadratic depth, motivating a log-based benchmark with exact fermionic normalization.
main_result: An exact fermionic analogue of Porter–Thomas statistics is established, with nearly quadratic circuit depth required for collision-probability convergence.
application_angle: The results provide calibrated tests for free-fermion sampling devices, including linear-optical and other Gaussian quantum-processing platforms.

title: Boosted Entanglement Swapping
abstract: Entanglement swapping entangles photons that never interacted directly. When implemented with linear optics, its success probability is upper bounded by $50\%$, due to the limited efficiency of linear-optical Bell-state measurements. Here, we demonstrate boosted entanglement swapping using an ancilla-assisted linear-optical Bell-state measurement, which raises the theoretical success probability to $62.5\%$ and allows all four Bell states to be identified. We measure an acceptance rate of $p_{\mathrm{a}}^{\mathrm{b}}=(69.39\pm0.39)\%$ with an average fidelity of the swapped states of $\langle F^{\mathrm{b}}\rangle=(76.6\pm1.0)\%$. We implement this protocol using photons at 1550 nm, making it well suited for quantum repeaters, where it could enable more efficient entanglement distribution. Beyond quantum communication, it could also enhance fusion-based quantum computing.
one_liner: Ancilla-assisted linear optics boosts 1550-nm entanglement swapping beyond the conventional 50% Bell-measurement limit.
why_it_matters: Higher Bell-measurement efficiency can directly improve repeater entanglement rates and reduce resource overhead in networked photonic systems.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses an ancilla-assisted linear-optical Bell-state measurement that identifies all four Bell states and has a theoretical success probability of 62.5%. At 1550 nm, the reported acceptance rate is 69.39±0.39%, with an average swapped-state fidelity of 76.6±1.0%. The telecom-band implementation directly targets fiber-compatible entanglement distribution.
main_result: Boosted entanglement swapping achieved a 69.39±0.39% acceptance rate and 76.6±1.0% average swapped-state fidelity at 1550 nm.
application_angle: The protocol can raise quantum-repeater throughput and may also reduce fusion overhead in photonic quantum computing.

title: Neuromorphic Camera for Multi-Target Pointing Acquisition and Tracking in Free Space Optical Communication
abstract: Pointing, Acquisition, and Tracking (PAT) in Free-Space Optical Communication (FSOC) applications must achieve both low jitter and a large Field of View (FoV) to support beacon acquisition and multi-target tracking. While conventional frame-based sensors provide the necessary angular coverage, their performance is limited by latency, available frame-rate, and motion blur. This work explores and demonstrates the application of an event-based vision sensor for PAT tasks in FSOC. The system employs a neuromorphic sensor that asynchronously records brightness changes (events) with microsecond-level temporal resolution. The main contribution of this paper is a comparative analysis of event-based tracking algorithms for the simultaneous acquisition and tracking of multiple optical beacons that operate directly on this asynchronous stream. The performance of these strategies is validated on an experimental dataset representing realistic operational conditions for dynamic High-Altitude Platform (HAP) and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks. The analysis compares key metrics, such as tracking accuracy and processing latency, under various signal-to-background conditions.
one_liner: An event-based neuromorphic camera enables low-latency simultaneous acquisition and tracking of multiple optical beacons for free-space links.
why_it_matters: Microsecond-resolved sensing could improve wide-field pointing and tracking for dynamic UAV and high-altitude-platform optical communication networks.
detailed_summary: The work applies an asynchronous event-based vision sensor to pointing, acquisition, and tracking of multiple optical beacons. Several algorithms operating directly on the event stream are compared using an experimental dataset representing dynamic UAV and high-altitude-platform links. Tracking accuracy and processing latency are evaluated across different signal-to-background conditions.
main_result: The study experimentally validates and compares event-stream algorithms for low-latency acquisition and simultaneous tracking of multiple optical beacons.
application_angle: The approach targets robust beam alignment in mobile free-space optical and prospective airborne quantum-communication links where latency, jitter, and field of view are critical.

title: From Claws to Conferences: Device-Independent Key Agreement Beyond Non-Signaling
abstract: Device-independent conference key agreement (DI-CKA) allows a group of users to establish a common secret key without trusting the internal operation of their quantum devices. Existing DI-CKA protocols derive their security from multipartite Bell tests and therefore require the device components not to communicate during each round. We present, to the best of our knowledge, the first DI-CKA protocol that removes this non-signaling assumption: all interfaces and their mutual communication are treated as one untrusted device, which only has to be quantum polynomial-time while the protocol runs. Assuming that the Learning With Errors (LWE) problem is hard for quantum algorithms with quantum advice during the execution, we prove finite-size security against coherent attacks, in which the device may keep quantum memory and correlate and adapt its behavior across rounds. For two parties the protocol is a computational DI-QKD protocol with an explicit finite-size proof against coherent attacks. Technically, we lift the claw state underlying the classical-verifier test of Brakerski et al.\ (FOCS 2018) to multipartite entanglement, obtaining a \emph{GHZ-correlated claw state}. %that is prepared with one coherent claw-free function evaluation and $N-1$ CNOT gates. We then introduce the \emph{collective adaptive hardcore bit}, a multiparty generalization of the adaptive hardcore bit of Brakerski et al.\ and show that it follows from the original property by a tight reduction. Combined with Jordan's lemma, an entropic uncertainty relation, and entropy accumulation, this certifies smooth min-entropy of the key against an external quantum adversary. Our protocol achieves \emph{everlasting security}: LWE needs to hold only during the execution, because the final key is statistically secure and its secrecy persists even if LWE is broken after the protocol ends.
one_liner: A computational device-independent conference-key protocol removes the usual requirement that device components cannot communicate during each round.
why_it_matters: It broadens device-independent security to internally communicating, fully untrusted hardware while retaining finite-size and everlasting key secrecy.
detailed_summary: The protocol treats all interfaces and their internal communication as one untrusted quantum-polynomial-time device, replacing the usual non-signaling assumption with quantum hardness of Learning With Errors during execution. A multipartite GHZ-correlated claw state and collective adaptive hardcore-bit property support finite-size security against coherent, memory-bearing attacks. After execution, the key is statistically secure even if LWE is later broken.
main_result: The authors prove finite-size computational DI conference-key security against coherent attacks without imposing non-signaling between device components.
application_angle: This framework could make device-independent group key distribution more compatible with integrated or networked hardware whose internal modules cannot be reliably isolated.

title: Quantum error correcting codes from quiver moduli: Grassmannians, cyclic monodromy, and argyle collision divisors
abstract: Building on aspects of a recent diagrammatic field-theory programme for quantum error correction put forward by the first-named author (arXiv:2607.08911), we construct exact finite-dimensional codes from twisted cyclic and argyle quiver moduli on the projective line. A regular fibre of the node-labelled cyclic Hitchin map records the ways to distribute simple spectral zeroes among the arrows with prescribed degrees. The Hilbert space spanned by these allocations is a Young permutation module. Root monodromy acts on its Specht factors and leaves their multiplicity spaces noiseless. Resetting the Specht factor therefore recovers the encoded state for every channel in the monodromy noise model. We prove that the largest Kostka multiplicity is the optimal dimension of a subspace code correcting the full monodromy algebra, even among codes spanning several isotypic blocks. Quantizing an argyle master space recovers the cyclic sheet space as a weight sector of a tensor power, with the identification preserving monodromy. For the balanced three-cycle with $t$ zeroes per arrow, the multiplicity of a partition $(a,b,c)$ of $3t$ is $1+\min(a-b,b-c)$. The optimal logical dimension is thus $t+1$, attained uniquely by the block indexed by $(2t,t)$. At $t=1$ we give explicit codewords for a qubit on six sheets. The commuting right action generates its full logical algebra, yielding errors outside the monodromy model that leave the measured footprint statistics unchanged yet require different recoveries. We also compute collision-parity ranks, give a higher-rank Grassmannian example, and derive a conditional criterion for recovery across splitting types.
one_liner: Quiver-moduli constructions yield exact finite-dimensional quantum codes whose noiseless multiplicity spaces correct a full cyclic-monodromy noise algebra.
why_it_matters: The work identifies provably optimal code dimensions for a structured noise model and supplies an explicit six-dimensional physical encoding of one logical qubit.
detailed_summary: Spectral-zero allocations in twisted cyclic quiver moduli form Young permutation modules, with root monodromy acting only on Specht factors and leaving multiplicity spaces noiseless. The largest Kostka multiplicity is proved to give the optimal subspace-code dimension for the full monodromy algebra. For a balanced three-cycle the optimal logical dimension is t+1, and at t=1 the authors provide explicit codewords encoding a qubit on six sheets.
main_result: The paper derives optimal monodromy-correcting codes and explicitly realizes a logical qubit in a six-sheet code at the smallest balanced instance.
application_angle: The construction offers mathematically exact encodings for hardware or simulators exhibiting structured permutation and monodromy errors, while clarifying failures beyond that model.

title: Quantum theory of damping: A new approach to temporal evolution of density operator without the rotating wave approximation
abstract: The Lindblad master equation is the standard framework for describing dissipative dynamics of the open quantum system context. Its conventional derivation, however, relies on the rotating-wave approximation (RWA), which neglects the counter rotating terms in the system-reservoir interaction. Here, we derive a generalized Lindblad master equation beyond the RWA within the density operator formalism, retaining the full systemreservoir coupling. We consider two prototypical open quantum systems, a two-level atom and a single-mode quantized field, each interacting with thermal or squeezed reservoirs described by the Wigner-Weisskopf theory. The resulting master equations are applied to the evolution of representative physical observables and compared with the conventional RWA based formulation. We show that counter-rotating terms produce significant modifications to the dissipative dynamics and therefore cannot, in general, be neglected. For a thermal reservoir, increasing the mean thermal photon number, nth, enhances the decay of hσ^yi beyond the RWA but suppresses it within the RWA. Likewise, the evolution of hσ^zi exhibits opposite damping behavior with increasing Γt and squeezing parameter r. These findings demonstrate the importance of including counter rotating terms for an accurate description of open quantum systems.
one_liner: A generalized Lindblad treatment retains counter-rotating system–reservoir terms and predicts dissipative dynamics that can differ qualitatively from RWA models.
why_it_matters: Beyond-RWA damping models may be essential for accurately designing and interpreting strongly coupled quantum-optical and circuit-QED experiments.
detailed_summary: The authors derive generalized master equations without the rotating-wave approximation for a two-level atom and a single quantized field mode coupled to thermal or squeezed reservoirs. Retaining the full interaction changes the predicted evolution of representative atomic observables. In particular, thermal occupation and reservoir squeezing can produce damping trends opposite to those obtained under the conventional RWA.
platform_or_system: Atom–reservoir and cavity-mode open quantum systems
main_result: The beyond-RWA equations predict substantial, and sometimes opposite, damping responses to thermal occupation and squeezing compared with standard RWA dynamics.
application_angle: The model can improve parameter extraction and control predictions in regimes where ultrastrong coupling or engineered reservoirs make counter-rotating interactions non-negligible.

title: Multipartite entanglement swapping with homodyne and single photon detection
abstract: Establishing multipartite entanglement across lossy optical networks remains a central challenge for distributed quantum information processing. Here, we consider a non-Gaussian continuous-variable entanglement-swapping protocol combining a symmetric discrete Fourier transform (DFT) interferometer with photon-number-resolving detection. In the ideal limit, single-photon heralding generates a $W_N$-class state across remote modes, with Fourier symmetry rendering all single-click outcomes equivalent up to local phase corrections. We find that conditional pairwise entanglement can exceed that of conventional Gaussian homodyne swapping in weak-to-moderate squeezing and lossy regimes, remaining nonzero beyond the channel-loss thresholds at which Gaussian pairwise entanglement vanishes. These results demonstrate that combining non-Gaussian measurements with symmetric interferometric mixing can improve both the resilience and operational efficiency of multipartite entanglement distribution in lossy quantum networks.
one_liner: A DFT interferometer with photon-number-resolving heralding swaps multipartite entanglement into remote W-class optical states resilient to channel loss.
why_it_matters: Non-Gaussian heralding preserves useful pairwise entanglement beyond loss thresholds where conventional Gaussian homodyne swapping fails.
detailed_summary: The protocol mixes optical modes in a symmetric discrete Fourier-transform interferometer and uses photon-number-resolving detection to herald remote multipartite states. In the ideal single-click limit it generates a W_N-class state, with all detector outcomes related by local phase corrections. Calculations show stronger conditional pairwise entanglement than Gaussian homodyne swapping for weak-to-moderate squeezing and lossy channels, including regimes where the Gaussian entanglement vanishes.
platform_or_system: Multimode optical DFT interferometer with photon-number-resolving detectors
main_result: Single-photon heralding distributes W-class entanglement and maintains nonzero pairwise entanglement beyond the loss threshold of Gaussian homodyne swapping.
application_angle: The scheme could improve loss-tolerant multipartite entanglement distribution for quantum repeaters, distributed sensing, and networked quantum processors.

title: Tensor-network simulation of strongly coupled multi-fluxonium circuits
abstract: Designing a superconducting quantum processor rests on predicting the low-lying spectrum of its coupled circuit. The Hilbert-space dimension of the circuit's lumped-element model grows exponentially with the number of circuit nodes. The usual methods split the circuit into subsystems, but that split is hard to choose when the elements are strongly coupled. We present a tensor-network method that chooses no subsystems and whose memory and run time per solve are set by the number of modes and two truncations, the Fock cutoff of each normal mode and the bond dimension of a matrix product state (MPS), not by the Hilbert-space dimension. From the capacitance matrix, the inverse-inductance matrix and the junction list alone, the linear circuit is diagonalized into normal modes. Each junction cosine is then a sum of two products of single-mode operators, so the complete lumped-element Hamiltonian is a matrix product operator (MPO) of small bond dimension with one site per mode, solved by the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG). The normal modes make the method generic, and the tensor network makes it affordable. For two fluxonia joined by a tunable coupler, the method agrees with exact diagonalization of the same truncated space to within 1 MHz. Our circuit of three fluxonia joined by two couplers has 11 normal modes and a truncated space of $10^9$ states, out of reach of exact diagonalization in dense or sparse storage. At a bond dimension of 32, its lowest eight levels are converged to within 1 MHz in both truncations, and each state is stored in a small fraction of the numbers a dense vector needs. One solve at that bond dimension takes 81 min and 1.3 GB of memory on one CPU node.
one_liner: A normal-mode tensor-network solver predicts spectra of strongly coupled multi-fluxonium circuits without choosing artificial circuit subsystems.
why_it_matters: It makes billion-state circuit models tractable on one CPU node, enabling practical spectral design of larger, strongly coupled superconducting processors.
detailed_summary: The method diagonalizes the linear circuit into normal modes and represents each Josephson cosine within a low-bond-dimension matrix product operator. DMRG then extracts low-energy eigenstates with costs governed by mode cutoff and MPS bond dimension rather than the full Hilbert-space size. It matches exact diagonalization within 1 MHz for two coupled fluxonia and converges eight levels of an 11-mode, 10^9-state three-fluxonium model within 1 MHz using 1.3 GB and 81 minutes on one CPU node.
main_result: The solver achieves megahertz-level spectral convergence for an 11-mode circuit with a nominal billion-state truncated Hilbert space using modest single-node resources.
application_angle: This provides an affordable design tool for optimizing strongly coupled fluxonium processors, tunable couplers, transition frequencies, and leakage before fabrication.

title: Efficient training of a 128-modes 3D continuously coupled photonic chip via limited quantum resources
abstract: Integrated photonics provides a promising route towards the development of large-scale, stable and low-loss quantum hardware. Existing implementations of universal quantum photonic chips generally rely on architectures consisting of localised interactions between the modes that can be programmed with known algorithms to implement specific operations. Recent advances have shown that interferometers based on 3D continuously coupled waveguide arrays may allow to significantly scale up the number of modes with reduced overhead. However, for this class of devices, optimal strategies to set the controllable parameters and obtain the desired transformation have not been demonstrated generally. In this work, we report the use of a machine learning algorithm driven by quantum data to program the operation of a reconfigurable three-dimensional continuously coupled photonic device comprising 128 modes. We show experimentally the capability of reaching a target unitary matrix, among those achievable by the device, through a limited number of one- and two-photon measurements. Our results demonstrate that this approach results to be effective in the presence of noise and with a limited amount of resources, also allowing to partially compensate imperfections in the experimental setup. This method can thus represent a viable route towards programming large scale integrated photonic devices, unlocking the possibility of controlling photonic systems for which an analytical decomposition is not trivial.
one_liner: Quantum-data-driven training programs a reconfigurable 128-mode, continuously coupled 3D photonic chip using sparse one- and two-photon measurements.
why_it_matters: The method offers a noise-tolerant route to controlling large photonic processors whose transformations lack practical analytical decompositions.
detailed_summary: The authors experimentally train a reconfigurable 128-mode three-dimensional continuously coupled waveguide array to realize target unitary transformations accessible to the device. A machine-learning optimizer uses a limited set of one- and two-photon measurements as quantum training data. The procedure remains effective under noise and partially compensates imperfections in the optical setup.
main_result: The experiment reaches achievable target unitaries on a 128-mode chip with limited one- and two-photon measurement resources.
application_angle: This calibration strategy could make large, densely coupled photonic processors programmable for quantum information and optical sensing tasks.

title: Exact teleportation bounds for fermionic Hawking thermality beyond the single-mode approximation
abstract: Fermionic teleportation near a Schwarzschild horizon involves two physically distinct ingredients that are often varied together: Hawking thermal mixing and the relative composition of the right and left Unruh modes. We separate them by factorizing the reduced map of the detected exterior fermionic mode into a mode-preparation channel and a Hawking thermal channel. At fixed right-left Unruh-mode composition, we then solve a global constrained quantum-channel optimization over all two-qubit resource states whose fully entangled fraction remains at or below the standard teleportation threshold immediately before thermal mixing. A parity twirl and positivity reduce the arbitrary-state problem exactly to a two-variable quadratic optimization. The solution yields a necessary-and-sufficient activation boundary, a second exact boundary for attaining the universal optimum, and explicit optimizing states. The resulting phase diagram contains a strict no-go region, a composition-limited activation region, and a universal-bound region. The analysis converts state-specific observations of Hawking-assisted teleportation into exact channel-level bounds over the full two-qubit state space.
one_liner: Exact channel-level bounds map when Hawking thermal mixing can activate fermionic teleportation beyond the single-mode approximation.
why_it_matters: The work separates thermal and mode-composition effects, replacing state-specific examples with rigorous limits across all two-qubit resources.
detailed_summary: The detected exterior fermionic mode is modeled as a mode-preparation channel followed by a Hawking thermal channel. Parity twirling and positivity reduce a global optimization over threshold-limited two-qubit resource states to an exact two-variable quadratic problem. The resulting phase diagram identifies no-go, composition-limited activation, and universal-bound regimes, with explicit optimizing states.
platform_or_system: fermionic modes near a Schwarzschild horizon
main_result: The analysis derives necessary-and-sufficient activation and universal-optimum boundaries for Hawking-assisted fermionic teleportation.
application_angle: These bounds provide a rigorous benchmark for relativistic quantum-communication protocols exposed to horizon-induced thermal noise.

title: Coherence Spreading Law in Quenched Homogeneous Bose Gases
abstract: We investigate nonequilibrium coherence spreading in quenched homogeneous bosonic gases both analytically and numerically. Our ensemble-averaged Gross-Pitaevskii trajectory approach and kinetic analysis confirm the linear-in-time growth of the squared coherence length, and explicitly give the spreading-law dependence on the ratio of initial energy to healing energy. When the ratio is relatively small, the squared coherence length grows at a universal rate determined by the ratio of Planck's constant to the particle mass, insensitive to interaction strength and initial momentum distributions. However, our further calculations uncover fundamental limitations to such universality and establish its phase boundaries governed by low system energies, weak interparticle interactions and many-body integrability. Our theory fully reproduces the key experimental signatures and resolves the puzzle of the dynamical origin of the recently observed universal coherence-spreading speed limit [Nature 647, 608-612 (2025)]. Going beyond existing experimental observations, we provide some testable predictions for ultracold-atom experiments and clarify the conditions for the emergence of universal coherent dynamics in nonequilibrium bosonic many-body systems.
one_liner: A theory of quenched homogeneous Bose gases derives coherence-spreading rates and the boundaries limiting their apparent universality.
why_it_matters: It explains a recently observed coherence speed limit and supplies experimentally testable conditions for universal nonequilibrium dynamics.
detailed_summary: Ensemble-averaged Gross-Pitaevskii trajectories and kinetic analysis show that the squared coherence length grows linearly with time. At sufficiently low initial-to-healing-energy ratio, its rate depends only on Planck's constant divided by particle mass, not on interaction strength or the initial momentum distribution. The authors also identify phase boundaries set by low energy, weak interactions, and many-body integrability, reproducing key experimental signatures.
main_result: The work derives the coherence-spreading law, recovers the observed universal regime, and establishes where that universality breaks down.
application_angle: The predictions can guide ultracold-atom experiments that engineer and diagnose coherent nonequilibrium many-body dynamics.

title: Structural Lower Bounds for Quantum Property Estimation with Persistent Memory
abstract: In quantum property estimation, an experimenter estimates $\operatorname{Tr}(Oρ)$ for a family of observables from independent copies of an unknown state $ρ$ simultaneously to additive error $ε$. While quantum memory can dramatically reduce sample complexity, understanding the power of a modest register that remains coherent throughout an adaptive experiment has remained an open challenge because existing frameworks require optimizing over the infinite space of measurement trees. We overcome this barrier by developing a backward-induction framework based on operator resolvents. Rather than tracking path-dependent memory states across rounds, resolvent regularization cancels internal memory trajectories exactly, reducing the lower bound to an algebraic certificate computed directly from the target observables with sharp $Ω(1/ε^2)$ scaling. Our structural rule charges only the retained dimension $K$ under arbitrary adaptive instruments and unrestricted memory lifetime. Via symmetry reductions, it yields polynomial-size linear programs that establish the optimal linear $Ω(D/(Kε^2))$ trade-off for the $D^2-1$ Paulis, eliminating the cubic loss in prior bounds. For growing weight-$w$ Pauli strings ($w=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$) and quadratic Majorana cross-correlations, it proves lower bounds of $Ω(3^w/ε^2)$ and $Ω(n^2/(ε^2(1+\ln n)^2))$ against an indefinitely persistent memory of dimension $K=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$. These bounds match memoryless or commuting estimators within polylogarithmic factors, demonstrating that rank constraints on the persistent register fundamentally throttle observable overlap and prevent a modest coherent memory from overcoming the sample complexity barrier.
one_liner: Resolvent-based lower bounds quantify how persistent quantum memory limits sample efficiency in adaptive quantum property estimation.
why_it_matters: The framework replaces optimization over infinite measurement trees with tractable algebraic certificates and sharp memory-sample trade-offs.
detailed_summary: A backward-induction method based on operator resolvents cancels internal memory trajectories and produces algebraic lower-bound certificates directly from target observables. It proves the optimal linear trade-off Ω(D/(Kε²)) for the D²−1 Pauli observables under arbitrary adaptive instruments with retained dimension K. Further bounds for logarithmic-weight Pauli strings and quadratic Majorana correlations show that a modest persistent coherent register cannot remove the sample-complexity barrier.
platform_or_system: adaptive quantum measurement with a K-dimensional coherent register
main_result: The authors derive sharp structural lower bounds showing that retained memory dimension fundamentally constrains simultaneous observable estimation.
application_angle: The results set resource limits for memory-assisted tomography, shadow estimation, and adaptive characterization of quantum hardware.

title: Sympathetic Cooling of Ionic Fullerenes with Ultracold Atoms to Millikelvin Temperatures
abstract: Cooling complex molecular ions to millikelvin temperatures remains a major challenge because their intricate internal structures prevent laser cooling. Here, we propose to use an ultracold gas of Cd atoms to efficiently cool C$_{60}^+$ ions to average kinetic energies of approximately 20 mK, following an initial precooling stage with He buffer gas. Our approach is based on full molecular dynamics simulations using accurate ion-atom interaction potentials derived from high-level electronic structure methods. Furthermore, using a Monte Carlo approach, we predict the formation of C$_{60}^+$ Coulomb crystals supported solely by collisions with the buffer gas. The probability of reaching these cold states shows a pronounced dependence on the number of trapped ions, revealing the competition between neutral-atom cooling and many-ion dynamics in radio-frequency traps.
one_liner: Molecular-dynamics simulations predict that ultracold cadmium atoms can sympathetically cool trapped C60+ ions to about 20 mK.
why_it_matters: The proposal offers a cooling route for complex molecular ions that cannot be directly laser cooled and predicts buffer-gas-supported Coulomb crystals.
detailed_summary: The study models C60+ ions precooled by helium and subsequently sympathetically cooled through collisions with an ultracold Cd gas. Full molecular-dynamics simulations use ion-atom potentials obtained from high-level electronic-structure calculations and predict average kinetic energies near 20 mK. Monte Carlo calculations also indicate Coulomb-crystal formation, with success probability strongly dependent on trapped-ion number.
platform_or_system: C60+ ions and ultracold Cd atoms in an RF trap
main_result: The simulations predict cooling of C60+ to roughly 20 mK and collision-supported formation of ionic fullerene Coulomb crystals.
application_angle: Millikelvin complex ions could enable precision spectroscopy, controlled ion-atom chemistry, and cold-molecule quantum experiments.

title: Efficiently tracking errors and outcomes in universal quantum circuits
authors: Julio C. Magdalena de la Fuente
abstract: We present a method for efficient simulation of error propagation and decoding in universal fault-tolerant quantum circuits under stochastic Pauli noise, requiring only that the circuit has a high fault distance and that all logical non-Clifford operations are implemented by physical T, CS and CCZ gates. This is achieved using modified Pauli frame-based error tracking in which the frame contains no logical information. Decoding success is identified by verifying that the Pauli frame is still logically trivial after decoding. Using the results of Ref. [1] and the observation that the distribution of non-logical measurement outcomes in the circuit is independent of the logical state, we show that we can accurately sample all detector outcomes. Our approach can also simulate circuits containing adaptive operations conditioned on logical measurements, provided these measurements have a known outcome distribution. This applies to the majority of adaptive operations such as state teleportation and preparation by measurement. Our method only detects decoding failures and so is consistent with complexity-theoretic expectations as it cannot be used to sample from the noiseless outcome distribution of the logical circuit.
one_liner: A modified Pauli-frame method efficiently simulates stochastic errors, detector outcomes, and decoding failures in universal fault-tolerant circuits.
why_it_matters: It extends efficient error tracking beyond Clifford circuits while respecting the hardness of sampling noiseless logical computation outcomes.
detailed_summary: The method tracks stochastic Pauli errors through high-distance fault-tolerant circuits whose logical non-Clifford operations use physical T, CS, and CCZ gates. Its Pauli frame carries no logical information, and decoding succeeds when the post-decoding frame remains logically trivial. Independence of nonlogical measurement outcomes from the logical state enables accurate detector sampling, including many adaptive teleportation and measurement-based preparation operations.
platform_or_system: universal fault-tolerant quantum circuits under Pauli noise
main_result: The approach efficiently samples detector records and identifies decoding failures in universal circuits with supported non-Clifford and adaptive operations.
application_angle: It can accelerate realistic benchmarking and decoder studies for fault-tolerant processors and teleportation-based quantum communication modules.

title: Hardware Demonstration of Neural-Surrogated Quantum-Enhanced MCMC for Large-Scale Constrained Boltzmann Sampling
abstract: Neural-surrogated quantum-enhanced Markov chain Monte Carlo (QeMCMC) uses neural networks trained on samples from the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) to accelerate Boltzmann sampling. A divide-and-conquer strategy extends this approach to larger systems, but independently optimizing QAOA parameters for each subproblem is costly. In this paper, we develop a hardware-efficient implementation of neural-surrogated QeMCMC and demonstrate it using an IBM Quantum Heron r2 processor. Experiments with $N=144$ binary variables reveal faster autocorrelation decay for appropriate subproblem sizes while exposing challenges in neural-surrogate learning for larger blocks. We then extend the demonstration to a system with $N=1064$, where the autocorrelation decay rate per MCMC step is approximately $5.2$ and $12.3$ times those of global and local Kawasaki dynamics, respectively. These results demonstrate faster autocorrelation decay in a system exceeding one thousand variables using samples generated on quantum hardware.
one_liner: IBM Heron hardware accelerates constrained Boltzmann sampling for systems containing up to 1,064 binary variables.
why_it_matters: The experiment shows a quantum-assisted sampling workflow operating beyond 1,000 variables while identifying block-size limits in neural-surrogate learning.
detailed_summary: The authors implement neural-surrogated quantum-enhanced MCMC using QAOA samples generated by an IBM Quantum Heron r2 processor. Tests on 144 variables show faster autocorrelation decay for suitable divide-and-conquer block sizes, although surrogate learning degrades for larger blocks. At 1,064 variables, the decay rate per MCMC step is approximately 5.2 times that of global Kawasaki dynamics and 12.3 times that of local Kawasaki dynamics.
main_result: Quantum-hardware-derived surrogates produced substantially faster autocorrelation decay for constrained sampling with 1,064 binary variables.
application_angle: The method targets faster sampling for large constrained optimization and statistical-physics problems while reducing repeated QAOA parameter optimization overhead.

title: Norm Bounds on Sums of Positive Operators with Applications to Monogamy Games and Quantum Key Distribution
abstract: Bounding the acceptance probabilities of quantum measurements is a recurring task in quantum information theory. An acceptance probability averaged over a random measurement setting can be bounded uniformly over the input state by the operator norm of an average of positive semidefinite operators. We prove a general inequality for such norms, valid for arbitrary finite families of positive semidefinite operators and averaging distributions. We give two applications of our operator-norm inequality. First, we determine the sharp robustness threshold for the parallel BB84 monogamy-of-entanglement game. For error thresholds $β,γ\in[0,1/2]$, when the two players may make at most $βn$ and $γn$ errors, respectively, the optimal winning probability decays exponentially if $(1-2β)^2+(1-2γ)^2>1$, tends to one exponentially fast under the reverse strict inequality, and remains bounded away from zero on the boundary. Second, we establish the achievability of every asymptotic key rate $0<R<1- 2h_2(γ)$ for one-sided device-independent BB84 quantum key distribution with tolerated bit-error rate $γ$ and asymptotically optimal reconciliation, where $h_2(\cdot)$ is the binary entropy function. Alice's measurements are trusted, while Bob may perform an arbitrary joint measurement depending on the entire basis string, subject to the protocol's receipt and isolation requirements. This recovers the usual BB84 rate in this model.
one_liner: A general operator-norm bound yields sharp parallel-BB84 monogamy thresholds and optimal one-sided device-independent QKD rates.
why_it_matters: The results strengthen security analysis against jointly optimized measurements and recover the usual BB84 key-rate expression with only Alice's devices trusted.
detailed_summary: The paper proves an operator-norm inequality for averages of arbitrary finite families of positive semidefinite operators. Applied to parallel BB84 monogamy games, it identifies the sharp transition governed by (1−2β)^2+(1−2γ)^2=1. It also establishes every asymptotic one-sided device-independent BB84 key rate below 1−2h2(γ), even when Bob performs an arbitrary joint measurement conditioned on the full basis string.
main_result: The analysis recovers asymptotically optimal BB84 key rates and determines the exact robustness threshold for parallel BB84 monogamy games.
application_angle: These bounds support rigorous QKD security guarantees when the receiver is untrusted but receipt and isolation requirements can be enforced.

title: Collectively pumped superradiant laser with coherence scaling beyond the standard quantum limit
abstract: For more than half a century, the standard quantum limit (SQL) was thought to limit the laser coherence $\mathfrak{C}$ -- the number of photons emitted from the laser into the beam in one coherence time -- to a scaling $Θ(μ^2)$, where $μ$ is the mean number of optical-frequency excitations stored inside the laser. However, recently it has been shown [Baker et al., Nat. Phys. 17, 179 (2021)] that the Heisenberg limit -- an achievable ultimate limit set by quantum mechanics for the task of producing a beam with the standard properties of a laser beam -- is $\mathfrak{C}=Θ(μ^4)$, a quadratic enhancement. So far, proposals to demonstrate beyond-SQL scaling of $\mathfrak{C}$ have been limited to circuit QED, at microwave frequencies (i.e., a maser). Here, we introduce a class of generalized far-above-threshold (FAT) laser models, obtained by replacing the ordinary bosonic lowering operator $\hat{a}$ by a general lowering operator $\hat{L}$ in the superoperators appearing in the master equation that governs the FAT laser dynamics. We then show that an optical-frequency superradiant laser in the bad-cavity limit, with feedback-controlled collective pumping, realizes one such model, in which $\hat{L}$ is identified with the collective superradiant lowering operator $\hat{J}$. This model can surpass the SQL scaling, with the coherence exhibiting a scaling as large as $\mathfrak{C}= Θ(μ^{8/3})$ in the optimal parameter regime. Here, in the bad-cavity limit, $μ\approx N/2$, where $N$ is the number of superradiant atoms.
one_liner: A feedback-controlled optical superradiant laser is predicted to achieve coherence scaling of Θ(μ^(8/3)), surpassing the SQL.
why_it_matters: The proposal moves beyond-standard-quantum-limit laser coherence from microwave circuit-QED concepts toward an optical-frequency atomic platform.
detailed_summary: The authors generalize far-above-threshold laser models by replacing the bosonic lowering operator with an arbitrary lowering operator. They show that a bad-cavity optical superradiant laser with feedback-controlled collective pumping realizes such a model through the collective operator J. In the optimal regime, its coherence scales as Θ(μ^(8/3)), beyond the conventional Θ(μ^2) standard quantum limit, with μ approximately N/2 for N atoms.
main_result: The proposed optical superradiant laser can theoretically surpass SQL coherence scaling and reach Θ(μ^(8/3)).
application_angle: Beyond-SQL optical coherence could benefit precision spectroscopy, optical frequency references, and low-linewidth quantum light sources.

title: Classical Clifford+T Sampling without Computing Marginals
abstract: We introduce a new exact classical sampling algorithm for Clifford+T circuits, called T-by-T sampling. For a circuit with T-count t, it reduces sampling to evaluating 2t amplitudes of circuits with successively increasing T-counts 1,2,...,t, without the need to compute costly marginal probabilities. Crucially, the number of amplitude evaluations is completely independent of the surrounding Clifford structure. This makes T-by-T sampling well suited for use together with low-rank stabiliser decompositions, which enable efficient amplitude evaluations as long as the T-count is not too high. In that sense, T-by-T sampling is an improvement over the gate-by-gate sampling technique introduced by Bravyi, Gosset, and Liu (Phys. Rev. Lett. 128, 2022), where the number of amplitudes instead scales with the number of non-monomial operations such as Hadamard gates, which can remain large even in circuits with low stabiliser rank. Concretely, T-by-T sampling offers significant speedups in regimes where T gates are embedded within large Clifford computations. This makes it well suited for applications such as simulating quantum error correction experiments, which typically have lower T complexity but involve extensive Clifford operations and measurements. In particular, we show how T-by-T sampling allows us to take samples from recent end-to-end magic state cultivation circuits with escape up to distance 19 in a couple of seconds.
one_liner: T-by-T sampling exactly simulates Clifford+T circuits using only 2t amplitude evaluations, independent of the surrounding Clifford structure.
why_it_matters: The algorithm makes low-T-count circuits with extensive Clifford processing much cheaper to sample, directly aiding error-correction experiment simulation.
detailed_summary: T-by-T sampling constructs an exact sample by evaluating two amplitudes at each successive T-count from one through t, eliminating explicit marginal-probability calculations. Its 2t amplitude count does not depend on the number of Clifford or other non-monomial operations. Combined with low-rank stabilizer decompositions, it samples recent end-to-end magic-state cultivation circuits with escape up to distance 19 in a few seconds.
main_result: Exact samples require 2t amplitude evaluations and can be generated for distance-19 magic-state cultivation circuits within seconds.
application_angle: The method enables faster validation and benchmarking of fault-tolerant protocols dominated by Clifford gates but containing relatively few T gates.

title: Robust Geometric Gates for QCCD Architecture
abstract: The trapped-ion quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) is a promising route toward scalable quantum computing. However, the frequency offset during shuttling operations introduce significant decoherence and control errors, severely degrading gate fidelity on transported ions. Here, using a room-temperature planar chip trap, we demonstrate a robust and universal single-qubit gate set in the QCCD architecture. Based on a recently proposed path-optimizable noncyclic geometric scheme, we show that dynamic noise is strongly suppressed even when multiple shuttling operations are interleaved with gate execution, achieving substantially higher fidelities than conventional dynamical gates. This robustness is further validated in a multi-ion system containing up to 33 qubits. With inherent robustness and adaptability to varying shuttle distances and ion numbers, our work offers a plug-and-play solution for building robust quantum primitives for the QCCD platform.
one_liner: Noncyclic geometric gates preserve high single-qubit fidelity during repeated ion shuttling in a room-temperature QCCD trap.
why_it_matters: Robust gates that tolerate transport-induced frequency offsets address a central control bottleneck in scalable trapped-ion processors.
detailed_summary: The experiment implements a universal single-qubit gate set in a room-temperature planar-chip QCCD trap using a path-optimizable noncyclic geometric protocol. The gates suppress dynamic noise and outperform conventional dynamical gates when multiple shuttling operations are interleaved with execution. Robustness is demonstrated in multi-ion systems containing as many as 33 qubits and across varying shuttle distances.
main_result: Geometric single-qubit gates substantially improve robustness to shuttling-induced frequency offsets and remain effective in systems of up to 33 ions.
application_angle: The approach provides transport-tolerant control primitives that can be integrated into modular, scalable trapped-ion quantum processors.

title: Colloidal 2D WS2 nanosheets exhibiting high-purity single photon emission
abstract: The search for quantum emitters, delivering single photons "on demand" at cryogenic and elevated temperatures for photonic technologies is ever progressing. For example, micrometer-sized WS2 monolayers exhibit single photon emission by elaborated local defect or strain engineering. Here, we show that wet-chemically synthesised monolayered two-dimensional (2D) WS2 nano sheets (NSs) with lateral sizes of 14 (+/- 6 nm) readily emit single photons from exciton recombination without the need for substrate-induced patterning, strain/defect engineering or spectral filtering. Single particle spectroscopy of 70 individual NSs shows photoluminescence from excitons (2.02 eV), trios (1.94 eV) and defect-localized states (1.85 eV) with fast emission (t1<0.2 ns, t2=3.2 ns), allowing highly frequent excitation cycles. Pulsed at 80 MHz, colloidal WS2 NSs exhibit limited spectral diffusion, no blinking and distinct photon antibunching (g2(0)=0.07 at 5 K), thereby tackling challenges of established colloidal quantum dot systems (blinking, longer emission cycles), while retaining high single photon purity as key quality of deterministic quantum emitters.
one_liner: Colloidal 14-nm WS2 monolayer nanosheets emit high-purity single photons with g2(0)=0.07 under 80-MHz pulsed excitation at 5 K.
why_it_matters: Wet-chemical synthesis produces fast, nonblinking quantum emitters without patterned substrates, engineered strain or defects, or spectral filtering.
detailed_summary: Single-particle spectroscopy of 70 wet-chemically synthesized WS2 nanosheets resolves exciton, trion, and defect-localized emission near 2.02, 1.94, and 1.85 eV. The emitters show a sub-0.2-ns fast component, a 3.2-ns slower component, limited spectral diffusion, and no blinking. Under 80-MHz pulsed excitation at 5 K, they achieve strong antibunching with g2(0)=0.07 without spectral filtering.
main_result: Unpatterned colloidal WS2 nanosheets deliver fast, nonblinking single-photon emission with g2(0)=0.07 at 5 K.
application_angle: Solution-processable, high-purity emitters could simplify fabrication and integration of deterministic single-photon sources for quantum photonic devices.

title: BIC-Engineered Silicon Nitride Microring Resonators Enabled by an Etch-Free Laser-Writing Approach
abstract: We report the initial experimental demonstration of a complementary, etch-free approach with fewer fabrication steps, in useful SU-8 ridges written by direct ultraviolet laser lithography on an unpatterned silicon nitride film define waveguides and microring resonators. Because the nitride film is never patterned, scattering at patterned nitride sidewalls does not arise, and the remaining radiative loss is engineered by design. The guided transverse-magnetic mode lies within the continuum of transverse-electric slab modes, and we use bound states in the continuum (BICs) as a design tool to control this radiation. Coupled-mode analysis and full-vectorial simulations show that radiation from the two ridge sidewalls cancels by destructive interference at discrete widths, with a first BIC at 2.25 micron and radiation below 1 dB/cm over a 0.3 micron width window and about 200 nm of bandwidth, and that curvature confines this cancellation to discrete bands of bending radius and width. Laser-written waveguides follow the predicted width dependence of the loss, reaching approximately 1.5 dB/cm near the BIC, where non-radiative loss dominates. A microring designed on a radius-selected BIC band exhibits loaded quality factors up to 1.6 \times 10^4 and, under the over-coupled assignment supported by a coupler model, an intrinsic quality factor of 3.3 \times 10^5. Because radiation is set by a patterned low-index layer on an unetched film, the same approach could be extended to other nanostructures. Optimization of the writing conditions and materials is ongoing.
one_liner: Etch-free laser-written SU-8 ridges create BIC-engineered waveguides and microrings on unpatterned silicon nitride.
why_it_matters: Avoiding nitride etching removes patterned-sidewall scattering and could simplify fabrication of low-loss integrated photonic devices.
detailed_summary: Direct ultraviolet laser lithography defines SU-8 ridges on an unetched silicon-nitride film, while destructive interference suppresses leakage of the guided TM mode into TE slab modes. Experiments reach approximately 1.5 dB/cm waveguide loss near the predicted BIC. A radius-selected microring shows a loaded quality factor up to 1.6×10^4 and an inferred intrinsic quality factor of 3.3×10^5 under the supported over-coupled model.
main_result: The etch-free platform experimentally achieved near-BIC waveguide loss of about 1.5 dB/cm and an inferred microring intrinsic Q of 3.3×10^5.
application_angle: The reduced-step process offers a route to rapidly written, low-scattering resonators and waveguides for integrated photonic and quantum-optical circuits.

title: Resetting a Superconducting Qubit with a Compact Colder Resistive Dissipator below the Qubit Frequency
abstract: Efficient qubit reset has become a key requirement for large-scale superconducting quantum processors, as initialization fidelity increasingly lags behind gate performance and quantum error correction demands rapid, high-fidelity state re-initialization. This work proposes a compact on-chip dissipator consisting of two transmon dissipation modes and a thin-film resistor, and experimentally demonstrates an unconditional reset protocol. With no additional control lines and negligible impact on the qubit $T_1$, the effective temperature of the transmon qubit is reduced from $49$~mK to $35$~mK. Quantum process tomography is employed to benchmark the reset process, achieving a process error of $0.0028$. This reset protocol is robust to pulse parameter deviations, thereby relaxing calibration requirements. The dissipator architecture provides a practical, calibration-friendly reset solution for large-scale superconducting quantum processors.
one_liner: A compact resistive dissipator resets a superconducting transmon without extra control lines or appreciable T1 degradation.
why_it_matters: Its low reset error, weak calibration sensitivity, and compact integration directly address fast reinitialization in scalable quantum processors.
detailed_summary: The on-chip dissipator combines two transmon dissipation modes with a thin-film resistor operating below the qubit frequency. An unconditional reset lowers the qubit effective temperature from 49 mK to 35 mK without additional control lines or a significant T1 penalty. Quantum process tomography measures a process error of 0.0028, and the protocol remains robust against pulse-parameter deviations.
platform_or_system: superconducting transmon with on-chip resistive dissipator
main_result: The device demonstrated unconditional reset with 0.0028 process error while reducing the qubit effective temperature by 14 mK.
application_angle: The architecture could provide compact, calibration-tolerant qubit initialization for error-corrected superconducting processors.

title: Hyperbolic Nanocavities for Single-Molecule Vibrational Strong Coupling
abstract: Hyperbolic phonon polaritons (HPhPs) in low-loss anisotropic materials such as hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) provide extreme sub-diffractional field confinement in the mid-infrared, making them attractive for enhancing the interaction of light with molecular vibrations. Collective vibrational strong coupling between molecular ensembles and HPhPs has already been demonstrated in extended slabs. Reaching this regime with a single molecule, however, remains a major challenge, and would provide a platform for investigating how vacuum electromagnetic fields influence molecular dynamics and chemical reactivity. Here, we show theoretically that single-molecule vibrational strong coupling can be reached in hBN nanocavities that laterally confine HPhPs within a finite volume. Combining full-wave electromagnetic simulations with the few-mode quantization approach, we find that these nanocavities support a rich set of asymmetric resonances that strongly enhance the local spectral density, with frequencies that follow from simple HPhP ray trajectories and can be tuned through the cavity aspect ratio. We identify resonances with quality factors of about $600$ and effective mode volumes of $|V_{\mathrm{eff}}| \sim 10^{-7}λ^{3}$, sufficient for single-molecule strong coupling with vibrational transitions with dipole moments on the order of $1\,\mathrm{D}$. These results establish hyperbolic nanocavities as a promising platform for single-molecule vibrational strong coupling and open new routes toward the local control of vibrational dynamics and molecular energy flow.
one_liner: Simulations predict that hBN hyperbolic nanocavities can reach vibrational strong coupling with a single molecule.
why_it_matters: Single-molecule coupling to confined mid-infrared fields could enable local control of vibrational dynamics, energy flow, and chemical reactivity.
detailed_summary: Full-wave simulations combined with few-mode quantization reveal asymmetric hyperbolic phonon-polariton resonances tunable through cavity aspect ratio. Selected modes have quality factors near 600 and effective mode volumes around 10^-7 λ^3. The predicted confinement is sufficient for strong coupling to a single vibrational transition with a dipole moment of order 1 D.
main_result: The theory predicts single-molecule vibrational strong coupling using cavity modes with Q≈600 and effective volume near 10^-7 λ^3.
application_angle: Such nanocavities could support nanoscale spectroscopy and vacuum-field control of molecular vibrations and reaction pathways.

title: Connection of surface code patches based on entanglement distillation without postselection
abstract: Distributed quantum computing is a promising approach for overcoming the scalability limitations of fault-tolerant quantum computing. Entanglement distillation, a process that extracts higher-fidelity entangled states from noisy ones, plays a key role in distributed quantum computing. However, simple distillation protocols typically rely on postselection, which poses practical challenges for implementation. Here, we propose a scheme for distributed surface-code quantum computing that benefits from entanglement distillation even without postselection. Numerical simulations show that the logical error rates in the proposed scheme are lower than those in the setting without distillation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the logical error rates can be suppressed further by exploiting the asymmetry between spacelike and timelike errors in the surface code. The proposed scheme offers a practical and simple approach to distributed quantum computing with surface codes.
