one_liner: A simulated protocol connects surface-code patches using entanglement distillation without discarding failed outcomes.
why_it_matters: Removing postselection simplifies distributed fault-tolerant operation while retaining a logical-error advantage from distilled network entanglement.
detailed_summary: The proposed distributed surface-code scheme incorporates entanglement distillation without conditioning execution on postselected outcomes. Numerical simulations show lower logical error rates than an otherwise comparable connection scheme without distillation. Further suppression is obtained by exploiting the differing effects of spacelike and timelike errors in the surface code.
main_result: Simulations show that non-postselected entanglement distillation reduces logical error rates, with additional gains from asymmetric error handling.
application_angle: The protocol offers a simpler route to linking fault-tolerant quantum-computing modules across imperfect entanglement channels.

title: Bridging Pulse and Circuit Levels: A Geometric Framework for Deterministic Error Suppression
abstract: Quantum errors in noisy environments remain a major obstacle to advancing quantum information technology. Standard quantum error correction requires massive ancillary qubit overhead, motivating the need for hardware-efficient mitigation strategies. In this work, we propose a framework for dynamical quantum error correction at the circuit level, requiring no logical encoding or ancillary qubits. By extending a geometric framework (originally developed for creating dynamical error-correcting gates at the control pulse level) to the discrete dynamics of digital circuits, we map the accumulation of coherent errors to trajectories in a high-dimensional error space. We demonstrate that inserting deterministically optimized twirling gate sequences actively shapes these trajectories, utilizing destructive interference to keep the accumulated error bounded with error scaling $\mathcal{O}(1)$. This deterministic path-shaping suppresses circuit errors fundamentally differently than the stochastic random-walk behavior of standard randomized compiling with error scaling $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})$. Furthermore, we show that this circuit-level dynamical correction synergizes with pulse-level robust control, providing an analytical bridge between continuous noise dynamics and discrete quantum compilation. This research illuminates pathways to achieving highly noise-resistant quantum circuits prior to the era of fault tolerance.
one_liner: Deterministic twirling sequences geometrically shape coherent-error trajectories to keep circuit-level error accumulation bounded.
why_it_matters: The framework promises ancilla-free error suppression before full fault tolerance and analytically connects robust pulses with circuit compilation.
detailed_summary: The framework maps coherent-error accumulation in digital circuits onto trajectories in a high-dimensional error space. Deterministically optimized twirling gates create destructive interference that bounds accumulated error with O(1) scaling, rather than the O(√N) stochastic scaling associated with randomized compiling. The analysis also shows how circuit-level path shaping can be combined with pulse-level robust control without logical encoding or ancillary qubits.
main_result: The proposed deterministic compilation method theoretically bounds coherent-error accumulation at O(1) through optimized twirling sequences.
application_angle: It could extend useful circuit depths on noisy processors using compilation and control updates rather than additional qubit hardware.

title: Spatial Path Superposition: A No-Cloning Perspective on MIMO-Inspired Spatial Diversity
abstract: Spatial diversity is a key mechanism in classical Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) communications, where multiple propagation alternatives provide redundant observations that improve reliability in noisy environments. A direct translation of this principle to quantum communications is forbidden by the no-cloning theorem, since an unknown quantum state cannot be copied and transmitted through independent links. In this Perspective article, we argue that spatial path superposition provides a no-cloning-compatible analogue of the spatial-diversity principle of MIMO. Rather than duplicating the transmitted quantum state, a quantum carrier is coherently delocalized over multiple communication links, so that alternative spatial evolutions are experienced in quantum superposition. In this framework, classical redundancy is replaced by spatial coherence, and the communication link itself becomes part of the quantum dynamics. Indeed, spatial coherence can enhance the fidelity of the received quantum state, providing the quantum counterpart of the classical diversity gain, and can be converted into bipartite and multipartite entanglement during propagation. This implies that, under suitable coherent path control, noisy channel evolutions can contribute constructively to entanglement generation. This Perspective identifies spatial path superposition as a quantum-native primitive for the Quantum Internet, linking no-cloning-compatible spatial diversity, fidelity enhancement, entanglement generation, and coherent path control.
one_liner: This Perspective frames coherent spatial path superposition as a no-cloning-compatible analogue of MIMO diversity.
why_it_matters: It unifies path coherence, fidelity enhancement, and propagation-induced entanglement as design principles for quantum networks.
detailed_summary: Instead of copying an unknown quantum state across independent links, the carrier is coherently delocalized over multiple spatial paths. The authors argue that interference among alternative channel evolutions can improve received-state fidelity and convert spatial coherence into bipartite or multipartite entanglement. As a Perspective, the work develops a conceptual framework rather than reporting a new experimental demonstration.
main_result: The paper establishes spatial path superposition as a quantum-native diversity primitive compatible with the no-cloning theorem.
application_angle: Coherent routing across multiple links could improve network robustness and generate entanglement during propagation in a future quantum internet.

title: Semi-Device-Independent Certification of multi-qubit Entangled Basis Measurement
abstract: The entangled basis measurement plays a pivotal role in fundamental information-processing tasks, such as dense coding, quantum teleportation, and entanglement swapping. Consequently, certifying such measurements in a device-independent manner remains an important task. In this work, we present a semi-device-independent (SDI) protocol in a prepare-and-measure (PM) scenario for certifying a class of m-qubit entangled basis measurements. Specifically, we consider a tripartite PM scenario featuring two senders and one receiver, where each sender sends an arbitrary number of 2^m inputs and the receiver performs a measurement with 2^m outcomes. We adopt a classical causal model framework to demonstrate the non-classicality of quantum measurements. We introduce nonlinear witnesses in classical causal models and demonstrate that the optimal quantum value exceeds the classical bounds. Further, we demonstrate that the optimal quantum value of the witness SDI certify the entangled basis measurement and the prepared states of the two senders.
one_liner: A prepare-and-measure protocol semi-device-independently certifies multi-qubit entangled-basis measurements and sender states.
why_it_matters: Reliable certification of entangled measurements supports trustworthy teleportation, dense coding, and entanglement swapping without fully characterized devices.
detailed_summary: The protocol uses a tripartite prepare-and-measure scenario with two senders and one receiver performing a 2^m-outcome measurement. Nonlinear witnesses derived from classical causal models separate quantum behavior from classical bounds. Achieving the optimal quantum value certifies both the m-qubit entangled-basis measurement and the states prepared by the senders under semi-device-independent assumptions.
main_result: The optimal quantum witness value semi-device-independently certifies a class of multi-qubit entangled-basis measurements and both senders' prepared states.
application_angle: The method offers a practical trust layer for quantum-network primitives based on teleportation and entanglement swapping.

title: Constraining Lorentz Invariance Violation via Precision Atomic Spectroscopy
abstract: This paper investigates Lorentz violation arising from quantum gravity effects in electronic and muonic hydrogen atoms. The violation is modeled through a modified dispersion relation parameterized by a dimensionless coefficient $ξ$ and suppressed by the Planck scale. Using high-precision spectroscopic data and a chi-squared fitting procedure that carefully accounts for theoretical uncertainties in the Rydberg constant and the proton radius, the analysis yields a 95% confidence level constraint $ξ\in [-14.3,\; 1.37] \times 10^5$. The mass scaling of the effect reveals two distinct regimes: for the lowest-order deformation, the heavy nucleus amplifies the signal, while for higher-order corrections, the lepton dominates the sensitivity. These bounds approach Planck-scale sensitivity using the simplest atomic systems, thereby circumventing ambiguities inherent in more complex quantum systems.
one_liner: Precision hydrogen spectroscopy constrains Planck-suppressed Lorentz violation through a modified particle dispersion relation.
why_it_matters: Simple atomic systems provide clean probes of quantum-gravity signatures while avoiding modeling ambiguities found in more complex platforms.
detailed_summary: The study models Lorentz violation with a Planck-suppressed modified dispersion relation parameterized by a dimensionless coefficient ξ. A chi-squared fit to electronic- and muonic-hydrogen spectroscopy includes theoretical uncertainties in the Rydberg constant and proton radius. It obtains the 95% confidence interval ξ ∈ [-14.3, 1.37] × 10^5 and identifies different nucleus- and lepton-dominated mass-scaling regimes.
main_result: High-precision spectra constrain the Lorentz-violation coefficient to ξ ∈ [-14.3, 1.37] × 10^5 at 95% confidence.
application_angle: The analysis positions precision atomic spectroscopy as a tabletop probe of Planck-suppressed new physics.

title: Phase matching and mode coupling in photonic-crystal ring resonators
abstract: Photonic-crystal ring resonators, in which periodic refractive-index modulations couple counter-propagating modes, have become a widely used platform for nonlinear photonics, offering mode-by-mode dispersion engineering. When several modulation components are superimposed, their relative angular alignment (phase) is an additional degree of freedom whose impact on the nonlinear dynamics has remained unclear. Here we show that the relative phases between the modulation patterns have a decisive impact. Through the interference of the nonlinear processes in forward and backward direction, they add a phase and mode selection rule to the established phase-matching conditions, which can fully suppress nonlinear coupling. They also impose a relative spectral chirp between forward- and backward-propagating waveforms. We illustrate these effects for parametric oscillation and dissipative Kerr solitons. Our results extend the concept of phase matching to resonators with interfering nonlinear pathways and establish the alignment of index gratings as a design dimension for nonlinear microresonators.
one_liner: Relative grating phases in photonic-crystal ring resonators control nonlinear mode selection, coupling suppression, and spectral chirp.
why_it_matters: Angular grating alignment becomes a powerful design knob for parametric oscillators, Kerr solitons, and dispersion-engineered microcombs.
detailed_summary: Superimposed refractive-index modulations couple counter-propagating modes in a photonic-crystal ring resonator. The work shows that their relative angular phases create an additional phase and mode-selection rule through interference between forward and backward nonlinear pathways. These phases can completely suppress nonlinear coupling and impose a relative spectral chirp, as illustrated for parametric oscillation and dissipative Kerr solitons.
main_result: Grating alignment controls interference between nonlinear pathways, enabling complete coupling suppression and direction-dependent spectral chirp.
application_angle: Phase-engineered gratings can improve the design and control of nonlinear microresonators, soliton sources, and frequency combs.

title: Spectral properties of twisted soft waveguides
abstract: We discuss a model of a soft waveguide described by Schrödinger operator whose potential is a twisted straight channel of non-circular profile. We show that a compactly supported twist makes the operator subcritical, the property being expressed in terms of a Hardy-type inequality. On the other hand, a periodic twist raises the essential spectrum and its local slowdown may give rise to isolated eigenvalues below the essential spectrum threshold.
one_liner: Twisting a soft non-circular waveguide changes spectral stability and can create bound states through localized slowdowns in periodic twist.
why_it_matters: The results clarify how geometric twisting can engineer confinement and spectral thresholds in waveguides and analogous quantum channels.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes a Schrödinger operator whose confining potential forms a twisted straight channel with a non-circular cross-section. A compactly supported twist makes the operator subcritical, expressed through a Hardy-type inequality. Periodic twisting raises the essential-spectrum threshold, while a local reduction in twist can generate isolated eigenvalues below that threshold.
main_result: Compact twisting produces subcriticality, whereas periodic twisting raises the continuum threshold and localized slowdown can create discrete bound states.
application_angle: The spectral principles may guide geometry-based confinement and mode engineering in soft waveguides and matter-wave structures.

title: Discovering correlated error mechanisms: data-driven augmentation of detector error models improving decoding
abstract: Accurate decoder priors are essential for high-performance quantum error correction. Theoretical noise models inevitably omit physically relevant error mechanisms, most notably correlated errors, which appear consistently in experimental error budgets yet are absent from standard models. We introduce a data-driven method for augmenting detector error models (DEMs) by discovering entirely new error mechanisms directly from experimental detector-firing statistics, going beyond most existing approaches that merely refine the probabilities of already-known mechanisms. Our method generates candidates by combining pairs of existing mechanisms as building blocks, then filters and validates them using pairwise and higher-order detector correlations. Crucially, this construction provides each newly discovered mechanism with a well-defined logical effect derived from the constituent error mechanisms, enabling its direct use in decoding. Furthermore, each mechanism is accompanied by a natural decomposition into lower-order components, preserving compatibility with the original decoder. This is particularly valuable in settings that rely on correlated graph-based decoders such as correlated matching. We evaluate the method on surface-code simulations with correlated noise and correlated-matching decoding, demonstrating that, in a realistic near-term noise scenario, DEM augmentation increases the Lambda parameter by 20% across code distances 7-15 and reduces the logical error rate by 75% at code distance 15 relative to the unaugmented DEM. On experimental data from Google's superconducting device, the augmented DEM increases the Lambda parameter by 9% across code distances 5-7 and yields a reduction of 14% in logical error rate over the baseline for distance 7. To our knowledge, this is the first data-driven DEM augmentation method that produces decomposed hyperedges with assigned logical effects.
one_liner: A data-driven method discovers missing correlated error mechanisms and augments detector models to improve surface-code decoding.
why_it_matters: Learning correlations absent from theoretical noise models directly lowers logical error rates on simulated and experimental quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The method constructs candidate error mechanisms by combining known detector-model mechanisms, then filters them using pairwise and higher-order detector correlations. Each discovered mechanism receives a logical effect and a decomposition compatible with correlated graph-based decoders. In simulation it improves Lambda by 20% and reduces distance-15 logical error by 75%; on Google's superconducting data it improves Lambda by 9% and distance-7 logical error by 14%.
main_result: Data-driven detector-model augmentation reduces logical errors by 75% in a near-term simulation and 14% on distance-7 experimental data.
application_angle: The technique can upgrade decoder priors from measured syndrome data without requiring a complete microscopic hardware-noise model.

title: Cryogenic suppression of correlated loss in Rydberg atom arrays
abstract: Blackbody radiation (BBR) poses a central challenge for quantum science with Rydberg atoms. By driving transitions to nearby opposite-parity states, BBR shortens Rydberg lifetimes and has long been suspected to trigger "avalanche" events known to cause correlated atom loss. Here, we suppress avalanche decay and establish BBR as its dominant trigger using a Rydberg atom array that operates either cryogenically or at room temperature. A $45~\text{K}$ radiation shield reduces ambient BBR, extending Rydberg $nS$ lifetimes for $n$ ranging from 50 to 75. BBR-induced decay rates are suppressed by 30%-50%, corresponding to an effective blackbody temperature $T_{\rm eff}\approx190~\text{K}$. This enables controlled comparisons of Rydberg-dressed atom arrays operating in different BBR environments. Arrays of up to 70 atoms demonstrate cryogenically suppressed avalanche rates, tracking the suppression in BBR-induced decay, for both $n=50$ and $n=60$ dressing. A parameter-free rate model agrees with the measured avalanche rates after accounting for frequency-dependent cryogenic shielding, photoionization-triggered avalanches, laser phase noise, BBR decay channels, and Rydberg interaction effects. We demonstrate a quantitative description of avalanche decay and show that improved BBR shielding should further suppress correlated loss to the $T_\text{eff}=45~\text{K}$ achievable in the current apparatus. Our results establish a route to mitigating correlated errors that otherwise impede fault-tolerant operation in neutral-atom quantum processors.
one_liner: A 45 K radiation shield suppresses blackbody-triggered avalanche loss in Rydberg-dressed arrays of up to 70 atoms.
why_it_matters: Reducing correlated atom loss addresses a key obstacle to scalable, fault-tolerant neutral-atom quantum processors.
detailed_summary: A Rydberg atom array is operated with either cryogenic or room-temperature radiation environments to isolate the role of blackbody radiation. The 45 K shield suppresses blackbody-induced decay rates by 30–50%, corresponding to an effective temperature near 190 K, and extends nS lifetimes for n = 50–75. Arrays of up to 70 atoms show matching suppression of avalanche rates, while a parameter-free model reproduces the data using shielding, photoionization, laser-noise, decay-channel, and interaction effects.
main_result: Cryogenic shielding suppresses blackbody decay by 30–50% and correspondingly reduces correlated avalanche loss in arrays of up to 70 atoms.
application_angle: Improved cryogenic shielding offers a direct route to lower correlated-error rates in neutral-atom quantum computers.

title: Precision Limits and Non-Gaussian Advantage in Optical Phase Estimation under Preparation Constraints
abstract: In optical quantum metrology, the scaling of the quantum Fisher information (QFI) with the mean photon number is a standard benchmark for relating precision to probe resources. For phase estimation, Heisenberg scaling corresponds to a quadratic growth of the QFI with the mean photon number, which Gaussian probes can approach. Interestingly, certain non-Gaussian probes can exhibit arbitrarily large QFI even at fixed mean photon number. Here, we clarify the resource requirements underlying this behavior by introducing a constraint that separates physically admissible states from inadmissible ones: an envelope on the photon-number distribution that arises naturally from the physical limitations of state-generation methods. Building on this constraint and considering pure single-mode probes, we define a resource quantity, $N_\mathrm{RMS}$, fixed by the preparation constraints, and derive a finite bound on the QFI whose Heisenberg scaling is attainable. We identify a genuine metrological advantage of non-Gaussian states over Gaussian probes subject to the same constraints. Finally, we illustrate these results with an optical preparation model based on a universal gate set.
one_liner: Preparation-aware bounds reveal a finite, attainable non-Gaussian advantage for single-mode optical phase estimation.
why_it_matters: The framework replaces unphysical fixed-mean-photon-number claims with precision limits tied to realistic state-generation constraints.
detailed_summary: The work constrains pure single-mode probes using an envelope on their photon-number distributions, motivated by physical state-preparation limits. It defines a preparation resource, N_RMS, and derives a finite QFI bound with attainable Heisenberg scaling. Under equal constraints, non-Gaussian probes retain a genuine advantage over Gaussian states, illustrated using a universal optical gate-set model.
main_result: A preparation-constrained QFI bound is derived, with attainable Heisenberg scaling and a certified non-Gaussian advantage over Gaussian probes.
application_angle: The result supports realistic resource accounting when designing high-precision optical sensors with engineered non-Gaussian states.

title: Experimental activation of hidden metrological steerability in quantum channels via stochastic filtering
abstract: Quantum steering-assisted metrology allows a trusted party (Bob) to improve local phase estimation by exploiting classical information communicated by an untrusted party (Alice). In realistic scenarios, however, the channel is subject to noise that degrades steerability and suppresses the associated metrological advantage. Here, we demonstrate that stochastic pre- and post-filtering operations can revive the violation of the metrological steering inequality (MSI) in phase-covariant amplitude-damping channels where it is initially absent, thereby activating a hidden metrological steerability and restoring their usefulness for quantum metrology. Specifically, the critical damping parameter beyond which the MSI violation is suppressed is raised from $γ_c \approx 0.5$ to $γ_c \approx 0.75$ for the largest filter strength considered. We verify this in a photonic experiment, where polarization qubits carrying the encoded phase are transmitted through an amplitude-damping channel implemented with a two-path Sagnac interferometer, and the stochastic operations are realized with glass plates at the Brewster angle. By tuning the filter strength and scanning the damping parameter over its full range, we observe the revival of the MSI violation, obtained at the cost of a reduced success probability inherent to the stochastic nature of the filtering operations. Our results establish that metrological utility and steerability can be activated through stochastic operations even when these properties are absent in the original noisy channel, extending filtering-based activation from witnesses of nonclassicality to a certified and operationally quantified metrological advantage.
one_liner: Stochastic optical filtering revives steering-certified phase sensitivity after amplitude damping suppresses it.
why_it_matters: The experiment shows that noisy quantum channels can recover operational metrological value, trading higher noise tolerance for probabilistic success.
detailed_summary: Polarization qubits carrying an encoded phase traverse a phase-covariant amplitude-damping channel implemented with a two-path Sagnac interferometer. Brewster-angle glass plates provide stochastic pre- and post-filtering that restores violation of the metrological steering inequality. At the largest tested filter strength, the critical damping parameter rises from about 0.5 to about 0.75, with reduced success probability.
main_result: Stochastic filtering experimentally extends steering-certified metrological operation from a damping threshold near 0.5 to near 0.75.
application_angle: The method offers a practical probabilistic route to recover sensing performance across lossy or dissipative photonic links.

title: Photoionization rates of oxygen and nitrogen at 800 nm measured by Thomson coherent microwave scattering
abstract: In this study, we report on the use of Thomson coherent microwave scattering (CMS) to characterize photoionization rates in oxygen and nitrogen at 800 nm over a range spanning approximately three orders of magnitude, from about mid-10$^9$ s$^{-1}$ range to the to mid-10$^{12}$ s$^{-1}$ range, corresponding to laser intensities in the vicinity of 10$^{13}$-10$^{14}$ W/cm$^2$, a range of significant practical relevance to filamentation physics.
one_liner: Coherent microwave scattering measures oxygen and nitrogen photoionization rates driven by intense 800 nm laser pulses.
why_it_matters: Direct rate measurements across a filamentation-relevant intensity range can improve strong-field ionization and plasma-propagation models.
detailed_summary: The study applies Thomson coherent microwave scattering to characterize photoionization in oxygen and nitrogen under 800 nm illumination. It covers rates from the mid-10^9 to mid-10^12 s^-1 range at laser intensities around 10^13–10^14 W/cm². This regime is directly relevant to the formation and evolution of laser-induced filaments.
main_result: Photoionization rates in oxygen and nitrogen are measured over roughly three orders of magnitude using coherent microwave scattering.
application_angle: The measurements provide experimental inputs for atmospheric filamentation, strong-field plasma modeling, and laser-plasma diagnostics.

title: A Quantum Lower Bound for Triangle Finding
abstract: Triangle finding is a fundamental problem in graph theory that has played a central role in the development of quantum algorithmic techniques. For $N$-vertex graphs given by their adjacency matrices, a long line of work has improved the quantum query upper bound from $O(N^{3/2})$ to $O(N^{5/4})$. However, the best known lower bound has remained the elementary $Ω(N)$ bound obtained from unstructured search. We prove the first superlinear quantum query lower bound for triangle finding, showing that $Ω(N^{13/12})$ queries are necessary. Our result also implies the same lower bound for triangle detection and for detecting every fixed connected non-bipartite graph. The proof builds on the compressed oracle approach of Zhandry and the transfer approaches of Belovs. It compares the computation on graphs with a planted triangle to the computation on random graphs conditioned to be triangle-free, through a map on the input registers that almost commutes with every query. We average over local changes to the input while preserving its distribution, through a procedure known as conditional resampling. Our main technical contribution is a set of estimates that let us control the query error under this averaging, despite the dependence introduced by conditioning a dense graph to be triangle-free.
one_liner: A compressed-oracle proof establishes the first superlinear quantum query lower bound for triangle finding.
why_it_matters: The Ω(N^13/12) bound narrows a longstanding complexity gap and constrains achievable speedups for graph-analysis quantum algorithms.
detailed_summary: The paper proves that triangle finding in an N-vertex adjacency-matrix graph requires Ω(N^13/12) quantum queries, improving on the elementary Ω(N) bound. The proof compares planted-triangle graphs with random triangle-free graphs using compressed-oracle and transfer techniques. Conditional resampling controls query errors despite correlations induced by conditioning, and the bound extends to detecting any fixed connected non-bipartite graph.
platform_or_system: Quantum query model for graph oracles
main_result: Triangle finding, triangle detection, and fixed connected non-bipartite subgraph detection require Ω(N^13/12) quantum queries.
application_angle: The bound provides a sharper benchmark for assessing quantum accelerators and algorithms targeting graph analytics.

title: Near-Quantum-Limited Readout for the Princeton Axion Search using a sub-GHz Kinetic Inductance Traveling Wave Parametric Amplifier
abstract: Parametric amplifiers are a workhorse for near-quantum-limited measurements above 1 GHz. However, amplifier development has been more limited below 1 GHz. We present a kinetic inductance traveling-wave parametric amplifier (KI-TWPA) operating over 300-700 MHz, with gain exceeding 30 dB and pump powers of a few hundred nanowatts. The system noise performance, as measured by a variable-temperature noise source, is 2.5-3.5 quanta. This device is a versatile new tool for precision measurements of sub-GHz signals, with applications including readout of semiconductor spin qubits, superconducting detector arrays, and searches for new physics beyond the Standard Model. We characterize aspects of the amplifier performance relevant to axion searches, including gain drift, compression point, amplifier noise at various operating temperatures, readout with an input circulator, and magnetic field insensitivity.
one_liner: A 300–700 MHz kinetic-inductance traveling-wave amplifier delivers over 30 dB gain with 2.5–3.5 quanta system noise.
why_it_matters: Near-quantum-limited amplification below 1 GHz enables more sensitive axion searches and readout of low-frequency quantum devices.
detailed_summary: The kinetic-inductance traveling-wave parametric amplifier operates from 300 to 700 MHz with more than 30 dB gain and pump powers of a few hundred nanowatts. Variable-temperature measurements give a system noise of 2.5–3.5 quanta. The study also characterizes gain drift, compression, temperature-dependent noise, circulator-assisted readout, and magnetic-field insensitivity for axion-search operation.
main_result: The amplifier achieves greater than 30 dB gain across 300–700 MHz with measured system noise of 2.5–3.5 quanta.
application_angle: It supplies a low-noise readout front end for axion haloscopes, semiconductor spin qubits, and superconducting detector arrays.

title: GFlowQEC: Generative Flow Networks that Learn to Sample Quantum LDPC Codes
abstract: Choosing a quantum error-correcting code for a real device means scoring candidates with circuit-level simulations so slow that only a few hundred can be run. So every evaluation counts, and a search is judged by how many good codes it finds per paid evaluation. Quantum LDPC codes built from a few group elements protect many logical qubits, but good ones are rare in a huge space. We introduce GFlowQEC, to our knowledge the first generative flow network (GFlowNet) for quantum code design. It builds a code one group element at a time and learns to propose codes in proportion to a power of their score. We train it once on scores from earlier searches, freeze it, and let it propose lifted-product codes with 180 physical qubits, scored by their distances. Ranking ten of its draws per paid call, it finds more than twice as many new top-scoring codes (inequivalent to any it was trained on) as tuned parallel tempering, even when tempering starts from GFlowQEC's training codes. It finds more than three and a half times as many as a supervised screen ranking ten random candidates per call. When both rank a hundred, the screen beats GFlowQEC, and does best ranking GFlowQEC's draws. Soft Q-learning, which shares the GFlowNet's optimal policy, does as well at one noise bias and better at the other, so the gain does not depend on the GFlowNet's training loss. Trained proposers can make a budget of expensive evaluations go further when good codes are rare.
one_liner: A learned generative proposer finds high-scoring 180-qubit lifted-product LDPC codes with fewer expensive evaluations.
why_it_matters: Data-driven code search can stretch limited circuit-level simulation budgets when useful hardware-compatible QEC candidates are rare.
detailed_summary: GFlowQEC builds quantum LDPC codes one group element at a time and learns to sample candidates according to a powered score distribution. After training on prior search results, it proposes 180-physical-qubit lifted-product codes evaluated by distance. Ranking ten draws per paid evaluation yields over twice as many new top-scoring codes as tuned parallel tempering and over 3.5 times as many as a supervised screen of random candidates, although screening becomes stronger at a ranking depth of 100.
main_result: GFlowQEC more than doubles the yield of new top-scoring codes versus tuned parallel tempering under the reported ten-candidate evaluation protocol.
application_angle: The approach can reduce costly simulation overhead when selecting error-correcting codes for constrained quantum hardware.

title: Optimal Holding Times for Entanglement Swapping
abstract: We revisit the optimization of entanglement holding times in memory-based quantum repeaters for maximizing entanglement swapping throughput under different fidelity constraints - strict, probabilistic, and mean. We consider two heterogeneous quantum links that are equipped with single or multiple memories and differ in decoherence rates, memory capacities, entanglement attempt rates and success probabilities, as well as classical communication latencies. Efficient models are developed to estimate the expected entanglement throughput and the probability density functions of the conditional wait time to swap. The models are then used to satisfy different fidelity requirements by optimizing the maximum holding times for the two links. Finally, our proposed model and approach are validated with a discrete-event quantum network simulator.
one_liner: Optimized memory holding times improve entanglement-swapping throughput across heterogeneous quantum-repeater links under multiple fidelity constraints.
why_it_matters: The framework translates realistic memory decay, link asymmetry, and communication latency into actionable timing policies for quantum-network nodes.
detailed_summary: The work models entanglement swapping between heterogeneous links with unequal decoherence, memory capacity, generation rates, success probabilities, and classical latency. It derives throughput and conditional waiting-time estimates, then optimizes separate maximum holding times under strict, probabilistic, or mean-fidelity requirements. Discrete-event quantum-network simulations validate the analytical optimization approach.
main_result: The authors obtain and simulation-validate link-specific holding-time policies that maximize swapping throughput while satisfying prescribed fidelity constraints.
application_angle: The method can guide buffer-control and scheduling policies in practical repeater nodes built from nonidentical links and quantum memories.

title: FNO-Based Inverse Co-Design of Semiconducting Quantum-Dot Devices
abstract: Gate-defined semiconductor quantum dots are promising building blocks for scalable spin-based quantum processors, however their operational properties depend on several fabrication and control parameters, such as lithographic gate layout and applied voltages. Existing device architectures have been refined through repeated fabrication and experimental testing, producing layouts that support reliable device operation. However, this process does not exhaustively explore the design space, limiting the ability to obtain qubits with targeted properties. We address these challenges by presenting a differentiable inverse co-design framework for electrostatically defined quantum dots that jointly optimises gate voltages and the gate electrode layout. A semiclassical Thomas--Fermi electrostatic simulator provides reference data for a Fourier neural operator (FNO) surrogate, which predicts the two-dimensional charge-density field. The desired spatial distribution of the confined charge defines the target quantum-dot geometry for inverse design. The FNO reproduces charge densities with a relative $L^2$ test error of just 0.6\% and enables millisecond-scale differentiable evaluations. Relative to the CPU-based physics simulator, the FNO achieves a 17,000-fold speed-up on GPU for a single design, with further performance gains enabled by batched inference. When embedded in a gradient-based design loop with fabrication constraints, the FNO can produce both vertically and horizontally elongated double-dot confinement geometries from the same initial conditions. The ability to engineer these distinct confinement configurations demonstrates control over quantum-dot shape and position, providing a route towards designing devices with distinct qubit-relevant operating properties prior to fabrication.
one_liner: A differentiable FNO surrogate jointly designs quantum-dot gate layouts and voltages while predicting charge density at millisecond scale.
why_it_matters: Fast inverse co-design could reduce costly fabrication iterations and tailor semiconductor confinement geometries before devices reach the cleanroom.
detailed_summary: A Fourier neural operator is trained on charge-density fields generated by a semiclassical Thomas–Fermi electrostatic simulator. The surrogate reaches 0.6% relative L2 test error and provides millisecond-scale differentiable evaluations, corresponding to a reported 17,000-fold GPU speed-up over the CPU simulator for one design. With fabrication constraints included, gradient optimization produces both vertically and horizontally elongated double-dot geometries from identical initial conditions.
main_result: The framework jointly optimizes electrode geometry and control voltages to realize targeted double-dot shapes and positions with fast differentiable inference.
application_angle: It offers a pre-fabrication route to engineering confinement profiles associated with desired spin-qubit operating properties.

title: 3D Printed Monolithic Optomechanical Chassis for an Unbalanced Field-Widened Interferometer
abstract: Additive manufacturing is increasingly being explored as an approach for producing complex structures for optical hardware. In this work, we present a fully monolithic optomechanical chassis fabricated using laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing. The structure was fabricated from thermally stable Invar36, a low-thermal-expansion alloy that enables high dimensional stability under varying environmental conditions. Our monolithic design incorporates embedded optical mounts, flexures, and alignment features directly into the chassis geometry that exceed the practical limits of conventional subtractive manufacturing. By integrating the optomechanical support structure into a single compact unit, the system achieves a reduced footprint compared to traditional optomechanical assemblies. The results demonstrate the potential of additive manufacturing to produce lightweight, and highly customized optical systems, opening the possibility of new pathways for next-generation quantum sensors and optical instrumentation.
one_liner: Laser powder-bed fusion produces a compact monolithic Invar36 chassis with integrated mounts and flexures for a field-widened interferometer.
why_it_matters: Combining low thermal expansion with monolithic alignment features could make precision interferometers smaller, more stable, and easier to deploy.
detailed_summary: The authors fabricate a fully monolithic optomechanical chassis in low-expansion Invar36 using laser powder-bed fusion. Optical mounts, flexures, and alignment features are incorporated directly into the printed geometry, including structures difficult to realize through conventional subtractive machining. The integrated architecture reduces the footprint relative to traditional assemblies and targets improved dimensional stability under environmental variation.
main_result: A compact Invar36 optomechanical structure with embedded mounting, flexure, and alignment functions is demonstrated as a single additively manufactured component.
application_angle: The manufacturing approach supports customized, lightweight, and environmentally stable interferometers for fieldable quantum sensors and optical instruments.

title: On Entanglement Dynamics in Holographic Theories
abstract: Entanglement entropy (EE) is central to modern theoretical physics, yet its calculation in interacting theories with nontrivial time dependence remains challenging. In this thesis, we investigate the real-time dynamics of EE in strongly coupled quantum field theories (QFTs) using the Anti-de Sitter/Conformal Field Theory (AdS/CFT) correspondence. We first examine EE evolution in an exactly solvable two-dimensional conformal field theory (CFT) with an inhomogeneous sine-square deformation (SSD). We argue that the unconventional time evolution driven by the SSD Hamiltonian can be viewed as a change in spacetime foliation, producing new horizons in the dual three-dimensional bulk. Holographic EE calculations agree with CFT results in all comparable cases. We then study entanglement dynamics in generic chaotic quantum many-body systems. In the limit of late time and large regions, these dynamics are believed to admit an effective entanglement membrane description. In 2d CFTs, a degenerate membrane tension reproduces several entropy dynamics results, unlike the non-degenerate tension in higher dimensions. Using holography, we show that capturing reflected entropy in 2d CFT requires an additional degree of freedom in the membrane description. We further show that a conventional non-degenerate tension emerges when the CFT undergoes a relevant deformation, holographically dual to a planar Banados-Teitelboim-Zanelli (BTZ) black hole with scalar hair and an interior Kasner universe. We then develop a membrane effective theory for reflected entropy dynamics in higher dimensions. Finally, we apply the membrane theories for reflected entropy to study the time evolution of multipartite entanglement signals. We found that scrambling dynamics generate multipartite entanglement with rich structures.
one_liner: Holographic calculations develop effective membrane descriptions of entanglement and reflected-entropy dynamics in strongly coupled quantum systems.
why_it_matters: The results sharpen theoretical tools for tracking scrambling and multipartite entanglement where direct many-body calculations are difficult.
detailed_summary: This thesis studies real-time entanglement entropy using AdS/CFT, including an exactly solvable sine-square-deformed two-dimensional conformal field theory whose evolution is interpreted through altered bulk foliation and horizons. Holographic results reproduce available CFT calculations and show that reflected entropy in two dimensions requires an additional membrane degree of freedom. Relevant deformations restore a nondegenerate membrane tension, while higher-dimensional extensions reveal structured multipartite entanglement during scrambling.
platform_or_system: holographic strongly coupled quantum field theories
main_result: The work constructs and extends membrane theories that capture entanglement, reflected entropy, and multipartite scrambling signals across several holographic settings.
application_angle: Although primarily theoretical, the framework supplies benchmarks for interpreting entanglement growth and information scrambling in controllable quantum simulators.

title: Threshold-Free Symmetry-Enriched Topological Quantum Memory
abstract: We show that non-Abelian symmetry enrichment can protect a toric code memory against incoherent electric noise at any bond error probability $p\in[0,1]$. For a toric code on the honeycomb lattice coupled to $Sp(N)$ rotors, with electric anyons carrying the fundamental representation, we construct an efficient minimum-weight decoder whose logical error probability decays exponentially with system size for $N\ge40$, a conservative sufficient bound. The same decoder also rules out strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking in the fundamental channel of $Sp(N)$ under the corresponding local decoherence in two dimensions. The construction extends to other symmetries, including $SU(N)$.
one_liner: Non-Abelian symmetry enrichment yields a toric-code memory whose decoded logical error falls exponentially at every electric bond-error probability.
why_it_matters: Threshold-free protection suggests a new route to robust quantum memory that does not rely on operating below a conventional finite noise threshold.
detailed_summary: The proposal couples a honeycomb-lattice toric code to Sp(N) rotors so that electric anyons transform in the fundamental representation. For N at least 40, an efficient minimum-weight decoder is proven to suppress logical failure exponentially with system size for any bond-error probability from zero to one. The construction also constrains symmetry breaking under local decoherence and is argued to extend to groups including SU(N).
main_result: For a conservative bound of N≥40, the decoder achieves exponentially decreasing logical error with system size across the full electric-noise probability range.
application_angle: The mechanism could inspire quantum-memory architectures with unusually broad tolerance to incoherent errors, though physical implementation remains to be established.

title: Ground-State Dressing and Delayed Feedback of a Chiral Giant Atom in Ultrastrong Waveguide QED
abstract: We study a chiral giant atom ultrastrongly coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide at two spatially separated points. At a relative coupling phase π/2, the total spectral density is independent of the distance between the coupling points, whereas its directional components are not. Using a variational polaron transformation, we show that the renormalized transition frequency and the total ground-state dressing inherit this independence, while the virtual-photon cloud remains chiral. A sudden switch-off of the coupling releases this cloud as directional radiation. We also derive the spontaneous-emission dynamics in the polaron frame, showing that, after neglecting the local photonic potential, the memory kernel becomes distance independent at the same phase.
one_liner: A two-point chiral giant atom in ultrastrong waveguide QED supports distance-independent dressing but a directional virtual-photon cloud and emission.
why_it_matters: Phase-controlled chirality offers a way to shape vacuum dressing, delayed feedback, and directional photon release in waveguide-based quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The study considers a giant atom ultrastrongly coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide at two separated points with relative phase π/2. A variational polaron treatment shows that the renormalized transition frequency and total ground-state dressing become independent of separation, although the virtual-photon cloud remains chiral. Switching off the interaction releases directional radiation, and the approximate polaron-frame memory kernel exhibits the same distance independence.
platform_or_system: chiral giant atom in a 1D waveguide
main_result: At phase π/2, global dressing and an approximate emission kernel lose their distance dependence while virtual photons and released radiation remain directional.
application_angle: The predicted effects could enable directional photon sources and engineered non-Markovian feedback in superconducting or other waveguide-QED circuits.

title: Quantum Noise Engineering in Advanced LIGO
abstract: Advanced LIGO is a gravitational-wave detector with extreme sensitivity, operating close to the quantum limits of optical measurement. The quantum noise in this system arises from vacuum fluctuations entering the interferometer readout port: phase-like fluctuations produce measurement imprecision, while amplitude-like fluctuations drive radiation-pressure back-action. In this review, we present an intuitive description in terms of complex fields and quadratures, and follow squeezed vacuum from its generation, through its interaction with the filter cavity and propagation through the interferometer, to the readout. We discuss how frequency-independent and frequency-dependent squeezing engineer quantum noise, and how correlations between optical quadratures map onto correlations between measurement imprecision and back-action. We conclude that LIGO is both a gravitational-wave observatory and a kilometre-scale platform for quantum measurement science.
one_liner: Reviews how squeezed vacuum and filter cavities reshape quantum measurement noise across Advanced LIGO’s kilometre-scale interferometer.
why_it_matters: Advanced LIGO demonstrates quantum-noise engineering at unprecedented scale, directly improving gravitational-wave sensitivity while testing measurement and back-action physics.
detailed_summary: The review tracks squeezed vacuum from generation through a filter cavity, kilometre-scale interferometer, and optical readout. It explains how frequency-dependent quadrature rotation balances phase-noise imprecision against amplitude-noise radiation-pressure back-action. The treatment highlights correlations between these noise channels and their role in broadband sensitivity enhancement.
main_result: Frequency-dependent squeezing enables engineered correlations between optical measurement imprecision and radiation-pressure back-action in Advanced LIGO.
application_angle: The techniques support more sensitive gravitational-wave observatories and inform quantum-enhanced precision measurements at large scale.

title: Particle-loss error correction using $2^l$-step states generated via particle-number-resolving measurement schemes
abstract: We present an iterative scheme for generating finite superpositions of Fock states whose photon numbers differ by $2^l$ ($2^l$-step states). We derive an upper bound on the probability of generating such states. Based on the proposed class of states, we construct several bosonic encodings and compare their performance in correcting particle-loss errors. Our results identify the most efficient encoding, which achieves a higher channel fidelity than previously studied bosonic encodings.
one_liner: Introduces particle-number-resolved generation of finite Fock superpositions with spacings of 2^l for loss-correcting bosonic codes.
why_it_matters: The proposed encoding improves particle-loss channel fidelity over previously studied bosonic codes and offers a measurement-based state-preparation route.
detailed_summary: The authors construct an iterative particle-number-resolving measurement scheme that generates finite superpositions of Fock states separated by 2^l quanta. They derive an upper bound on the state-generation probability and use the resulting family to define several bosonic encodings. Performance comparisons identify an encoding with higher channel fidelity under particle loss than earlier bosonic constructions.
main_result: A 2^l-step bosonic encoding achieves higher particle-loss channel fidelity than the previously studied encodings used for comparison.
application_angle: Measurement-generated code states could improve loss-tolerant photonic or oscillator-based quantum memories and processors.

title: Dithered Belief Propagation for Real-Time Quantum Memory Decoding
abstract: We introduce dithered belief-propagation decoding for circuit-level quantum memory to mitigate the oscillations and trapping behavior that limit standard belief-propagation (BP) decoders for qLDPC codes. Our approach combines a quantum-adapted sign-flip mechanism with chained randomized prior perturbation. Evaluated under circuit-level noise on the distance-11 rotated surface code and the distance-12 bivariate-bicycle code, the proposed dithered decoder significantly outperforms BP and BP+OSD+CS-10. The proposed decoder achieves accuracy comparable to or better than state-of-the-art Relay-BP, especially at higher physical error rates, while trading a moderate increase in additions for about 98% fewer multiplications on average and eliminating node-level RNGs. These results suggest that dithering is a promising approach toward real-time decoding of quantum memories.
one_liner: Dithered belief propagation suppresses decoder trapping and oscillations for real-time circuit-level quantum-memory error correction.
why_it_matters: It approaches leading decoding accuracy with about 98% fewer multiplications, making fast qLDPC memory decoding more practical for hardware controllers.
detailed_summary: The decoder combines quantum-adapted sign flips with chained randomized perturbations of belief-propagation priors. Circuit-level simulations on a distance-11 rotated surface code and a distance-12 bivariate-bicycle code show substantial gains over BP and BP+OSD+CS-10. Accuracy is comparable to or better than Relay-BP, especially at higher physical error rates, while eliminating node-level random-number generators and cutting multiplications by roughly 98%.
main_result: Dithered BP delivers near-state-of-the-art circuit-level decoding accuracy with a moderate addition overhead but approximately 98% fewer multiplications.
application_angle: The reduced arithmetic and RNG requirements suit low-latency FPGA or ASIC decoders for fault-tolerant quantum memories and communication nodes.

title: Upper and lower bounds for few-copy Gaussian tomography, and the absence of a fermionic warm regime
abstract: Chen, Mele, Mele and Preskill proved a crossover for bosonic Gaussian tomography: cold states need $Θ(m^3/ε^2)$ copies under single-copy or few-copy measurements, warm ones $Θ(m^2/ε^2)$. The author proved $Ω(m^3/ε^2)$ for adaptive single-copy tomography of mixed fermionic Gaussian states. This note shows the crossover has no fermionic counterpart and extends the fermionic bound to blocks of $k$ copies. There is no warm regime: on the quadratic Gibbs balls $β\|h\|_F\leβ_0$ of unknown Hamiltonian $h$, the single-copy rate is $Θ(m^3/ε^2)$ for every fixed $β_0>0$, at accuracies that resolve the ball, with a lower-bound constant independent of $β_0$. At the maximally mixed state a replicated-parameter Fisher budget gives $N>m^3/(8{,}553{,}600\,k\,ε^2)$ for blocks of at most $k$ copies and all $ε\le1/3600$; an exact formula for the maximal block Fisher information, via spinor tensor powers of $\mathfrak{so}(2m)$, shows that the budget $mt^2$ behind it is asymptotically attained for every fixed block size; whether $1/k$ is the true rate is open. Near the vacuum, block protocols need $Ω(m^3/(ε^2\min\{\sqrt k,m\}))$ copies, with no logarithm, via an exterior-power embedding of qudit tomography; parity superselection changes no rate, and number superselection costs nothing on number-conserving inputs. The embedding also carries upper bounds: a particle-number measurement followed by the $k$-copy qudit protocol of Nayak and Zhou attains the lower bound for every $k$ on number-conserving fermionic Gaussian states with bounded fugacity trace and on passive bosonic Gaussian states with bounded photon number, and a heterodyne stage that undoes displacement and squeezing extends this to all cold bosonic Gaussian states. This closes their $k$-entangled gap on the cold class; intermediate temperatures remain open.
one_liner: Establishes few-copy tomography bounds for Gaussian states, ruling out a warm-regime advantage for fermions and closing a cold bosonic gap.
why_it_matters: The results quantify how collective measurement size affects the experimental sample cost of characterizing fermionic and photonic Gaussian systems.
detailed_summary: For mixed fermionic Gaussian states, the work extends the Ω(m^3/ε^2) single-copy limitation to measurements on blocks of at most k copies and shows that no bosonic-like warm crossover occurs. Near the vacuum it proves an Ω(m^3/[ε^2 min{√k,m}]) copy bound using an exterior-power embedding. Matching protocols based on particle-number measurements and few-copy qudit tomography close the entangled-measurement gap for number-conserving fermionic states and cold bosonic Gaussian states, with heterodyne preprocessing covering displacement and squeezing.
main_result: Fermionic Gaussian tomography retains cubic mode scaling without a warm regime, while matching few-copy bounds are obtained for important cold Gaussian classes.
application_angle: The bounds guide measurement design and resource estimates for calibrating Gaussian photonic devices, many-body platforms, and continuous-variable processors.

title: Unifying First-Order Coherence, Concurrence, and Bell Correlations in Three-Flavor Neutrino Oscillations
abstract: Neutrino oscillations provide a natural setting for investigating the quantum character of flavor conversion and the distribution of quantum resources over macroscopic distances. Here, we study exact relations among purity-based first-order coherence, pairwise concurrence, and the maximal Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) value in coherent three-flavor neutrino oscillations. By expressing the evolving neutrino as a three-qubit single-excitation state, we derive the generally mixed two-qubit reductions and show that the squared first-order coherence of each flavor mode and its two associated squared concurrences sum to unity. Furthermore, a closed two-branch relation is obtained, showing that the maximal CHSH value of any reduced pair is determined by its average first-order coherence and concurrence. The branch structure follows from the correlation-tensor spectrum and yields exact conditions for CHSH violation. For the vacuum parameters and propagation ranges considered, electron preparation gives weak CHSH violations in electroncontaining pairs, while muon preparation produces a dominant utau pair with substantially stronger concurrence and Bell correlations. The comparison also identifies the thirdflavor contribution responsible for the different locations of concurrence and CHSH maxima. These results clarify the distribution of quantum correlations during flavor evolution and provide a basis for extensions to coherent matter propagation and wave-packet-induced mixed states.
one_liner: Derives exact links among coherence, concurrence, and maximal CHSH correlations during coherent three-flavor neutrino oscillations.
why_it_matters: The analysis gives closed resource identities for macroscopic flavor evolution, but it is primarily foundational rather than a near-term photonic experiment.
detailed_summary: The evolving three-flavor neutrino is represented as a three-qubit single-excitation state, allowing exact treatment of generally mixed two-mode reductions. For each flavor, squared first-order coherence plus the two associated squared concurrences equals unity. A two-branch formula connects each pair’s maximal CHSH value to its mean coherence and concurrence, predicting preparation-dependent Bell-violation patterns.
main_result: Exact conservation-like identities and a two-branch CHSH relation determine how coherence and pairwise entanglement are distributed during flavor evolution.
application_angle: The framework can inform quantum-resource analyses of neutrino propagation in matter and future oscillation measurements including wave-packet decoherence.

title: Dark-State Coherent Control of Excitons in TMD Monolayers: A Reduced Intravalley Lindblad Framework for WSe$_2$
abstract: Dark-state coherence in driven three-level systems underlies electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) and stimulated Raman adiabatic passage (STIRAP). Their performance depends on the coupling topology: in a ladder ($Ξ$) scheme the coherence can bypass a lossy intermediate state, whereas in a $V$ scheme it is carried by two excited states that both decay. We develop a topology-resolved Lindblad framework for driven three-level excitonic manifolds at fixed center-of-mass momentum, in which a single exciton couples to phonons, the radiation field and a dilute exciton gas. The $Ξ$ and $V$ manifolds are selected from the exciton spectrum by systematically screening optical brightness, intra-excitonic dipole strength and state compactness, making the selection reproducible and transferable to other materials. Within this framework, in the $Ξ$ manifold of hBN-encapsulated WSe$_2$, a weak optical pulse, preceded by a terahertz pulse in the counterintuitive STIRAP order, converts the excitation it creates into an optically dark exciton by dark-state following, while the lossy bright intermediate exciton stays nearly empty. The conversion is limited by emission from that intermediate state rather than by non-adiabatic coupling, and is controlled by a single adiabaticity parameter of the terahertz leg. The exchange mean field of the exciton gas shifts the two-photon resonance by more than the conversion tolerates at moderate densities; the center of the cascade transparency window provides an in situ calibration, and we identify the control strengths at which it is true EIT rather than Autler--Townes splitting. The $V$ manifold loses its coherence on the radiative timescale and serves as the unprotected reference. These results provide a minimal, material-specific baseline for dark-state coherent control of excitons in two-dimensional semiconductors in the radiative limit.
one_liner: A WSe2-specific Lindblad model predicts STIRAP transfer from optically created bright excitons into dark excitons using terahertz control.
why_it_matters: Dark-state transfer could enable coherent storage and manipulation of excitonic states in atomically thin optoelectronic and quantum-photonic devices.
detailed_summary: A topology-resolved Lindblad framework includes exciton coupling to phonons, radiation, and a dilute exciton gas at fixed momentum. In an hBN-encapsulated WSe2 ladder manifold, counterintuitive terahertz and optical pulses transfer excitation into a dark exciton while keeping the lossy bright intermediate nearly empty. The study identifies emission and density-dependent exchange shifts as practical limits and distinguishes genuine EIT from Autler–Townes splitting.
main_result: Counterintuitive terahertz–optical pulse ordering enables dark-state-following conversion to an optically dark exciton with minimal bright-state occupation.
application_angle: The scheme offers a route to coherent exciton preparation, storage, and switching in two-dimensional semiconductor photonic hardware.

title: A nonlinear interface for phase transduction
abstract: Broadband nonlinear frequency conversion mixes multiple input frequencies, complicating the transfer of programmed spectral phase between widely separated spectral bands. Here we identify and experimentally realize a quasi-linear phase-transduction regime enabled by broad phase-matching acceptance and effective localization of the complex frequency-mixing response. This selectivity can arise from coherent interference without narrowing the pump spectrum. We implement this regime through dispersive four-wave mixing in an argon-filled hollow-capillary fiber, transferring spectral phase from 1032-nm near-infrared signals to 344-nm ultraviolet idlers. Transient-grating frequency-resolved optical gating reveals frequency-inverted, phase-conjugating transfer of quadratic dispersion, localized phase steps, and low-frequency sinusoidal modulation. After correction for the modeled pump-induced phase background, the quadratic and step responses exhibit approximately linear point-by-point correlations. With increasing pump chirp, the transferred phase steps become more sharply preserved, and the fitted phase-transfer gains approach unity, consistent with enhanced effective localization. These results demonstrate quasi-linear spectral-phase transduction in a co-propagating broadband nonlinear interaction without spatially separating its spectral components.
one_liner: An argon-filled hollow-capillary fiber transfers programmed spectral phase from 1032-nm signals to phase-conjugated 344-nm idlers.
why_it_matters: The demonstrated interface could translate complex optical waveforms between distant spectral bands without spatially separating their spectral components.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses dispersive four-wave mixing in an argon-filled hollow-capillary fiber to transfer spectral phase from 1032-nm near-infrared signals to 344-nm ultraviolet idlers. Transient-grating FROG measurements resolve frequency-inverted, phase-conjugating transfer of quadratic dispersion, localized phase steps, and sinusoidal modulation. Corrected quadratic and step phases show approximately linear point-by-point correlations, while increased pump chirp sharpens step preservation and drives fitted transfer gains toward unity.
main_result: Broadband four-wave mixing achieved quasi-linear, frequency-inverted spectral-phase transfer from the near infrared to the ultraviolet.
application_angle: The method supports programmable ultraviolet pulse shaping and coherent waveform translation across otherwise difficult-to-bridge spectral bands.

title: Spin-Exchange-Controlled Nonclassical Light in Cavity Electromagnetically Induced Transparency
abstract: Controlling nonclassical light while maintaining a finite cavity response requires selective suppression of unwanted multiphoton excitation. We investigate a ring-cavity system containing two three-level emitters coupled by a coherent spin-exchange interaction, where electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) provides resonant access to a dark-state polariton. The exchange interaction shifts the polariton resonance while modifying the dressed two-photon excitation pathways. Strong photon antibunching emerges when the one-polariton resonance nearly coincides with a destructive-interference minimum of the second-photon transition amplitude. By jointly tuning the exchange interaction and control-field strength, pronounced photon blockade with a finite intracavity population can be sustained over an extended interaction range. We further show that the relative cavity-coupling phase redistributes optical coupling between symmetric and antisymmetric collective channels with opposite exchange shifts, allowing the photon statistics to switch between antibunching and bunching at fixed exchange strength. This mechanism provides a possible route to tunable nonclassical-light sources based on coherent control of collective excitation pathways.
one_liner: Spin exchange and cavity-coupling phase provide tunable photon blockade in a two-emitter cavity-EIT system with finite intracavity population.
why_it_matters: The mechanism offers a controllable route to switching photon statistics while retaining useful cavity response, a key requirement for nonclassical-light sources.
detailed_summary: The study analyzes a ring cavity containing two three-level emitters coupled by coherent spin exchange, with EIT enabling resonant excitation of a dark-state polariton. Strong antibunching occurs when the one-polariton resonance aligns with a destructive-interference minimum in the second-photon transition amplitude. Joint tuning of exchange strength, control-field amplitude, and relative cavity-coupling phase sustains blockade over an extended range and switches the output between antibunched and bunched statistics.
main_result: Coherent spin exchange enables robust, tunable photon blockade with finite cavity occupation and phase-controlled switching between antibunching and bunching.
application_angle: The proposed controls could enable adjustable single-photon sources and nonlinear quantum-optical elements for photonic information processing.

title: Certifying the Rydberg-exposure limit of a globally driven controlled-Z gate
abstract: Rydberg excitation enables entangling gates in neutral-atom quantum processors but also exposes them to spontaneous decay. Whether this exposure can be made arbitrarily small through pulse shaping and longer gate times has remained unresolved. We show that an exact controlled-$Z$ gate driven by a single global laser has an irreducible Rydberg-exposure cost in the perfect-blockade regime. The product of the maximum Rabi frequency $Ω_{\max}$ and the average time $T_R$ spent in the Rydberg state is bounded below by $2.9312$, independent of pulse shape and duration. We derive this bound using a sum-of-squares certificate, strengthened by constraints imposed by the shared drive. Using interval arithmetic, we also certify the existence of an exact gate pulse with $Ω_{max} T_R<2.9359$. The unrounded bounds differ by less than $0.16\%$. The bound identifies a fundamental cost of shared-drive entangling dynamics and establishes a benchmark against which future gate-control strategies can be assessed.
one_liner: A certified bound shows that globally driven neutral-atom CZ gates have an irreducible Rydberg-exposure cost of ΩmaxTR ≥ 2.9312.
why_it_matters: The nearly tight limit establishes a hardware-relevant benchmark for decay exposure that no pulse shaping or longer gate duration can evade under shared global driving.
detailed_summary: For perfect Rydberg blockade and a single global laser, the authors prove that every exact controlled-Z gate satisfies ΩmaxTR ≥ 2.9312, where TR is the average Rydberg-state dwell time. A sum-of-squares certificate incorporates constraints imposed by the shared drive. Interval arithmetic also certifies an exact pulse with ΩmaxTR below 2.9359, leaving less than a 0.16% gap between the lower and upper bounds.
main_result: The work establishes and nearly saturates a pulse-shape-independent lower bound on Rydberg exposure for an exact global-drive CZ gate.
application_angle: The bound quantifies an unavoidable spontaneous-decay vulnerability and provides a reference for evaluating neutral-atom gate protocols and control architectures.

title: Weak Values in Postselected Quantum Trajectories
abstract: Weak value (WV) describes the amplified response of a meter when the measured system undergoes postselection. While conventional WV theory mainly rests on a single system-meter interaction setting, it remains unexplored whether WV can act as an effective pointer for sequential quantum measurements under postselection. Here we introduce the concept of WVs to the setting of sequential quantum measurements and quantum trajectories. We find that WV naturally emerges in postselected quantum trajectories of sequential weak measurements, by establishing a connection between the WV of the measured observable and the postselected statistics of quantum trajectories. Using sequential weak measurements on a qubit or an oscillator implemented by Ramsey interferometry with an ancilla qubit, we show that postselection shifts the collective record polarization away from the unconditioned ones, with an effective bias described by the WV. Our predictions are feasible to test in various platforms.
one_liner: Weak values emerge as effective biases in postselected records from sequential qubit or oscillator measurements implemented by Ramsey interferometry.
why_it_matters: Connecting weak values to full measurement trajectories extends postselected sensing concepts from single interactions to experimentally accessible sequential readout.
detailed_summary: The authors extend weak-value theory to postselected quantum trajectories generated by sequential weak measurements. For a qubit or oscillator probed through Ramsey interferometry with an ancilla qubit, postselection shifts the collective record polarization relative to its unconditioned value. The effective bias is governed by the weak value of the measured observable, connecting trajectory statistics to conventional weak-value amplification.
main_result: The work shows that weak values quantitatively describe postselection-induced polarization shifts across sequential quantum-measurement records.
application_angle: The framework could guide postselected sensing and trajectory-based estimation protocols on qubit, oscillator, and hybrid quantum platforms.

title: Information flow control in hybrid quantum networks
abstract: Quantum resources can change the dynamical features and operational behaviors of conventional networks. Long-distance entanglement supports information transfer between nodes lacking a direct connection. This entanglement link not only modifies the stationary effective connectivity of the network but can also be used to suppress undesirable classical dynamics. By examining information flow control mechanism, we demonstrate that classical collective behavior can be well-balanced by altering the initially distributed entanglement. We show the entanglement thresholds for two distinct control approaches: linear response control and Lyapunov functional controllability.
one_liner: Distributed entanglement is proposed as a control resource for reshaping information flow and suppressing unwanted collective dynamics in hybrid networks.
why_it_matters: The analysis links entanglement distribution to explicit control thresholds, suggesting that quantum links can regulate classical network behavior beyond carrying information.
detailed_summary: The paper studies hybrid networks in which long-distance entanglement creates effective connections between nodes without direct classical links. By changing the initially distributed entanglement, the framework balances or suppresses undesirable classical collective dynamics. Entanglement thresholds are derived for both linear-response control and controllability based on a Lyapunov functional.
main_result: The analysis identifies entanglement thresholds under which nonlocal quantum links can control classical information flow and collective network dynamics.
application_angle: The approach could inform resource allocation and stability control in distributed quantum-classical communication networks.

title: Bell Test and Quantum State-Space Geometry
abstract: We explore a minimal phenomenological model of coupling between the geometry of the classical spacetime and the quantum state space. Assuming a simple structure of the combined manifold, bilinear interaction between the corresponding geometric scalars and the simplest case of the two-qubit entanglement dynamics, we derive an illustrative upper bound on the geometric coupling constant from the requirement of the Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) inequality violation over a finite time interval.
one_liner: A phenomenological two-qubit model uses finite-duration CHSH violation to bound a proposed coupling between spacetime and quantum-state-space geometry.
why_it_matters: Although conceptual rather than experimental, the model illustrates how Bell-test observations could constrain speculative geometric modifications of entanglement dynamics.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces a minimal phenomenological manifold combining classical spacetime geometry with quantum state-space geometry through a bilinear interaction of geometric scalars. It applies the construction to a simple two-qubit entanglement model. Requiring CHSH-inequality violation to persist over a finite interval yields an illustrative upper bound on the proposed geometric coupling constant.
main_result: Finite-time preservation of CHSH violation is translated into an upper bound on a phenomenological spacetime–quantum-geometry coupling.
application_angle: The result suggests a Bell-test-based route for constraining speculative geometry-induced modifications of quantum correlations.

title: Ultrafast Moiré Exciton Dynamics Revealed by Two-Dimensional Coherent Spectroscopy
abstract: Moiré superlattices of van der Waals heterostructures confine excitons into discrete energy levels in finite-sized samples, yet their internal relaxation pathways remain obscured by inhomogeneous broadening. Here, using two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy (2DCS), we directly resolve seven discrete energy levels of the moiré-confined intralayer $\mathrm{WS}_{2}$ A exciton in an hBN-encapsulated $\mathrm{WS}_{2}/\mathrm{WSe}_{2}$ heterostructure, corresponding to a confinement depth of 57.02 meV. By tracking the population of these levels over picosecond delays, we uncover a two-stage thermalization process: an effective exciton temperature drops from 171.8 to 99.3 K within 1.2 ps through rapid intra-manifold population redistribution, followed by a slower recovery toward quasi-equilibrium mediated by exciton--environment interactions. Kullback--Leibler divergence analysis confirms the progressive transition from a non-equilibrium to a Boltzmann-distributed population. Our results establish state-resolved access to moiré exciton dynamics and provide a foundation for exploring nonequilibrium many-body phenomena in moiré quantum materials.
one_liner: 2D coherent spectroscopy resolves seven confined moiré-exciton levels and their ultrafast, two-stage thermalization.
why_it_matters: State-resolved relaxation measurements enable controlled studies of nonequilibrium excitons and many-body physics in moiré quantum materials.
detailed_summary: Two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy resolves seven discrete levels of the moiré-confined intralayer WS2 A exciton despite inhomogeneous broadening. The levels span a 57.02 meV confinement depth. Population tracking reveals rapid cooling from 171.8 K to 99.3 K within 1.2 ps, followed by slower environment-mediated recovery toward a Boltzmann distribution.
main_result: The experiment achieves state-resolved measurement of seven moiré-exciton levels and identifies a two-stage picosecond thermalization process.
application_angle: The method supports characterization and engineering of excitonic states for moiré photonics and quantum-material devices.

title: Efficient Pauli Truncation from Operator Stabilizer Rényi Entropy
abstract: Operator stabilizer Rényi entropy (OSE) quantifies the magic of Heisenberg operators and serves as a diagnostic of their compressibility in the Pauli basis. We establish rigorous bounds showing when an operator can be efficiently approximated by Pauli truncation in terms of the scaling of its OSE. Specifically, we prove that volume-law scaling of OSE for $α\geq1$ prevents efficient Pauli truncation from reproducing expectation values for all states at sufficiently small fixed error. On the other hand, logarithmic growth of OSE for $0<α<1/2$ guarantees efficient Pauli truncation approximability uniformly over all states. A counterexample shows that this sufficient range cannot be extended on the basis of OSE scaling alone. If we restrict to correlations over suitable low-average state ensembles, then the sufficient range extends to $0<α<1$. We further derive cumulative error bounds for iterative Pauli propagation and approximation guarantees for fixed-order out-of-time-ordered correlators.
