Moreover, under an independent-sign assumption, we show that logarithmic OSE for $0<α<1$ guarantees efficient Pauli truncation with the prescribed accuracy for all input states with high probability. Our results provide a theoretical framework for understanding when operator magic constrains or enables efficient Pauli truncation and for guiding the development of classical simulation methods.
one_liner: Rigorous entropy bounds identify when Heisenberg operators admit efficient approximation by truncated Pauli expansions.
why_it_matters: The results clarify when quantum dynamics and sensing observables can be simulated classically with controlled error.
detailed_summary: The work connects operator stabilizer Rényi entropy scaling to uniform and ensemble-dependent Pauli-truncation guarantees. Volume-law entropy for α≥1 obstructs efficient approximation at sufficiently small fixed error, whereas logarithmic growth for 0<α<1/2 guarantees it uniformly over states. The authors also bound errors in iterative Pauli propagation and fixed-order out-of-time-ordered correlators, with stronger probabilistic guarantees under an independent-sign assumption.
main_result: The paper establishes necessary obstructions and sufficient entropy-scaling conditions for efficient Pauli truncation with prescribed accuracy.
application_angle: These criteria can guide tractable classical modeling of quantum-control, sensing, and many-body experiments.

title: Experimental demonstration of dual-polarization nonreciprocal thermal emission at moderate magnetic fields
abstract: Conventional thermal emitters obey Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation, which requires emissivity and absorptivity to be equal at each wavelength, angle, and polarization. This in turn places a fundamental limit on a range of radiative energy technologies as well as heat transfer. This constraint can however be overcome using magneto-optic semiconductors, which break Lorentz reciprocity under an applied magnetic field. However, in most prior experimental demonstrations, nonreciprocity has been restricted to TM polarization, since the electric field of TE-polarized light is parallel to the applied magnetic field. Here, we experimentally demonstrate nonreciprocal absorption in both polarizations at the same wavelengths and angles from a single structure, wherein a germanium Mie-resonant metasurface on a doped InAs layer scatters TE-polarized light into near fields with components perpendicular to the magnetic field, allowing the magneto-optic response of the InAs to act on them. Under a 0.48 T field from a permanent Halbach array, this structure exhibits a difference in absorptivity between $+B$ and $-B$ of 0.035 in both TE and TM polarization at 16.6 $μ$m. Our approach shows that the magneto-optic response of a planar semiconductor and the resonances of a dielectric metasurface can be designed together, offering a potential route to dual-polarization nonreciprocity at fields available from permanent magnets for emerging energy and heat transfer technologies.
one_liner: A Ge/InAs metasurface demonstrates dual-polarization nonreciprocal absorption using a 0.48 T permanent-magnet field.
why_it_matters: Dual-polarization operation at moderate fields makes nonreciprocal thermal photonics more practical for heat and energy systems.
detailed_summary: A germanium Mie-resonant metasurface converts TE illumination into near fields that couple to the magneto-optic response of doped InAs. With a 0.48 T Halbach-array field, the structure shows a +B versus −B absorptivity difference of 0.035 for both TE and TM polarization at 16.6 μm. The co-design overcomes the usual restriction of planar magneto-optic emitters to TM nonreciprocity.
main_result: The device demonstrates equal-magnitude nonreciprocal absorption for TE and TM light at the same wavelength and angle under a moderate magnetic field.
application_angle: Permanent-magnet-compatible nonreciprocity could improve thermal management, radiative heat transfer, and energy-conversion devices.

title: Optimal quantum metrology with restricted controls
abstract: Quantum control can enhance sensing precision, but practical protocols are constrained by probe preparation and the available control resources. Optimizing the sensing protocol within these constraints helps establish what precision is experimentally attainable. We study quantum metrology from a fixed initial probe state under restricted Hamiltonian controls with bounded amplitudes. Building on Pontryagin's maximum principle, we formulate quantum Fisher information maximization at a prescribed interrogation time for multiple control channels subject to a weighted amplitude constraint. The formulation also accommodates stochastic Hamiltonian evolution and time-local master equations. A geometric description of sensitivity accumulation reveals the mechanisms underlying the optimized protocols. Two spin-$1/2$ examples demonstrate the resulting enhancement: time-dependent control outperforms optimized constant control in transverse-field sensing, while optimized waveforms improve upon CPMG pulses for AC-field sensing under strong colored noise. These findings highlight the importance of optimizing sensing protocols within available control resources to improve experimentally attainable precision.
one_liner: Bounded-control optimization maximizes quantum Fisher information for realistic sensing protocols under coherent and noisy dynamics.
why_it_matters: It provides a principled route to sensing waveforms that outperform standard controls without assuming unavailable preparation or drive resources.
detailed_summary: The authors formulate fixed-time quantum Fisher information maximization from a fixed probe state with multiple bounded Hamiltonian controls using Pontryagin's maximum principle. The framework includes stochastic Hamiltonians and time-local master equations. Spin-1/2 examples show time-dependent control beating optimized constant driving for transverse-field sensing and optimized waveforms outperforming CPMG under strong colored noise.
main_result: Optimized bounded waveforms improve attainable precision over constant controls and CPMG sequences in representative field-sensing problems.
application_angle: The approach can tailor experimentally feasible pulse sequences to actual control limits and measured noise environments.

title: Multi-Channel Non-Abelian Edge Pumping via Multi-Degeneracy Encircling
abstract: Non-Abelian operations enable sequence-dependent control of light, yet experimental realizations in wave systems have remained confined to local bulk or same-boundary modes and have often required fragile gap-closing degeneracies. Conventional Thouless pumps, meanwhile, support only two-channel edge transfer across a single gap. Here we demonstrate multi-channel non-Abelian edge pumping on a silicon photonic chip by adiabatically encircling multiple band degeneracies in a multi-gap lattice. In a minimal three-band band-triangle, two opposite-charge Weyl points and one zero-charge degeneracy are linked by global band connectivity, yielding both opposite-boundary and same-boundary edge channels. Sequencing these channels produces non-Abelian braiding of three topologically protected edge modes that reside on distinct physical boundaries. The process remains fully gapped and is protected by topological winding rather than by maintained spectral degeneracies. The same band-triangle principle extends systematically to an arbitrary number of channels, establishing a scalable route to collective, sequence-controlled routing of topological states in integrated photonic circuits.
one_liner: A silicon photonic chip realizes fully gapped, three-channel non-Abelian pumping of topological edge modes.
why_it_matters: Scalable sequence-dependent routing across distinct boundaries expands the control toolbox for robust integrated photonic circuits.
detailed_summary: The experiment adiabatically encircles multiple degeneracies in a three-band, multi-gap photonic lattice containing two opposite-charge Weyl points and one zero-charge degeneracy. Global band connectivity provides both opposite-boundary and same-boundary transfer channels. Ordered channel sequences braid three edge modes noncommutatively while the spectrum remains gapped, with protection supplied by topological winding.
main_result: The chip demonstrates non-Abelian braiding and sequence-controlled routing of three protected edge modes residing on distinct physical boundaries.
application_angle: The extensible band-triangle design offers a route to robust multi-channel switching and routing in integrated photonics.

title: Universal Phase Locking from Slowly Varying Inhomogeneity in Tunnel-Coupled One-Dimensional Condensates
abstract: The sine-Gordon model can be experimentally realised by tunnel-coupled one-dimensional Bose condensates. However, the experiments show relaxation to a phase-locked state, which conflicts with the predictions of the homogeneous integrable theory. Here we combine the truncated Wigner approximation with an asymptotic analysis, and show that this locking is produced by a slowly varying density profile through a universal mechanism, whereby the relative phase near the density maximum drifts towards zero. We show that this drift is already present in the linearised theory and its timescale is determined by the density curvature alone, while it is independent of the tunnel coupling. Rescaling time by the relaxation time scale collapses the dynamics for different system sizes and density profiles, while non-linearity suppresses the excitation returning from the edges.
one_liner: Slow density inhomogeneity drives universal phase locking in tunnel-coupled one-dimensional Bose condensates.
why_it_matters: The mechanism reconciles phase-locking experiments with homogeneous sine-Gordon theory and identifies density curvature as the key timescale.
detailed_summary: Truncated-Wigner simulations and asymptotic analysis show that a slowly varying density profile drives the relative phase near the density maximum toward zero. The drift exists already in the linearized theory, and its timescale depends on density curvature rather than tunnel coupling. Rescaling by this relaxation time collapses dynamics across system sizes and profiles, while nonlinear effects suppress excitations returning from the edges.
main_result: The study identifies a universal, density-curvature-controlled mechanism for phase locking in inhomogeneous coupled condensates.
application_angle: The result informs trap design, coherence control, and interpretation of atom-chip quantum-simulation experiments.

title: Unified design of short mode-evolution couplers
abstract: Short mode-evolution couplers have been designed with several seemingly different approaches, including fast quasi-adiabatic dynamics (FAQUAD), counter-diabatic (CD) driving realized by tailoring waveguide widths and spacing, CD driving realized by axis bending, and numerical optimization of the coupler geometry. Using exact two-mode coupled-mode theory in the Kramers--Henneberger frame of the bent coupler, we show that these approaches belong to the same design space. The three geometric parameters, width difference, spacing, and axis tilt, act on the light through two functions only: the coupling strength, set by the spacing, and an effective detuning, set by the width difference and the axis curvature. The gauge, bent, and mixed realizations of a CD coupler are therefore the same device and have the same bandwidth. The bandwidth is set by the angle $χ$ between the light and the field that steers it on the Bloch sphere, integrated along the device as $\int\sin^2χdz$, and for a CD coupler this integral is set by the reference alone. This leads to a lithography-aware design rule: make the reference as adiabatic as the minimum gap allows, by narrowing its spacing at the anticrossing, and let exact CD suppress the remaining nonadiabatic coupling. In beam propagation method (BPM) simulations on a polymer platform, a 500\um{} coupler designed this way, without numerical optimization, maintains ${>}99\%$ transfer over 274~nm at a minimum edge gap of 1.05\um, compared with 150~nm for the CD coupler of a fixed-spacing reference at nearly the same gap. Particle swarm optimization of the geometry with BPM in the loop does not exceed the design rule. Three-dimensional BPM of the BCB channel waveguides also confirms these conclusions.
one_liner: A unified coupled-mode framework yields compact waveguide couplers with broadband, near-unity mode transfer.
why_it_matters: The lithography-aware rule replaces costly geometry optimization while substantially expanding bandwidth in a fabrication-constrained device.
detailed_summary: Exact two-mode coupled-mode theory in the Kramers–Henneberger frame shows that FAQUAD, geometric counter-diabatic driving, axis bending, and numerical optimization occupy the same design space. In polymer-waveguide BPM simulations, a 500 µm coupler achieves over 99% transfer across 274 nm with a 1.05 µm minimum edge gap, versus 150 nm for a fixed-spacing reference. Three-dimensional BCB simulations support the design rule, and particle-swarm optimization provides no improvement.
main_result: A non-optimized 500 µm coupler maintains over 99% transfer across 274 nm under realistic lithographic constraints.
application_angle: The method enables compact, broadband integrated-photonic mode converters with reduced design and optimization overhead.

title: Bringing Dark States to Light after Frustrated Tunneling Ionization
abstract: High-harmonic generation (HHG) in gases is typically regarded as a sub-laser-cycle process, well described by the semiclassical three-step model. In this work, we report the extreme-ultraviolet (XUV) emission observed in an HHG experiment arising from a longer temporal process associated with dark states populated through frustrated tunneling ionization. The emission exhibits a larger spatial divergence than typical high-order harmonics, resembling the polarization decay of optically bright states. Supported by the time-frequency analysis of the theoretical calculations, we show that the emission originates from the nonradiative capture of the tunneling electrons into excited dark states of the neutral atom, followed by Floquet-like laser-dressing effects induced by the extended tail of the driving pulse. Our results reveal a largely unexplored pathway for XUV generation through laser-dressed dark states, thereby enabling the enhancement of coherent XUV emission at targeted wavelengths with high repetition rates.
one_liner: Laser-dressed dark atomic states populated by frustrated tunneling produce delayed, targeted coherent XUV emission.
why_it_matters: The identified emission pathway could extend high-repetition-rate XUV sources beyond conventional sub-cycle high-harmonic generation.
detailed_summary: The experiment observes a divergent XUV component associated with a longer-lived process than standard high-order harmonic emission. Time-frequency calculations attribute it to tunneling electrons captured nonradiatively into neutral-atom dark states and subsequently dressed by the driving pulse tail. The resulting Floquet-like dynamics open a distinct route to coherent emission at selected XUV wavelengths.
main_result: The study identifies coherent XUV emission from laser-dressed dark states populated through frustrated tunneling ionization.
application_angle: This mechanism offers a route to wavelength-selective, high-repetition-rate coherent XUV generation.

title: Efficient preparation of spin-squeezed states with Grover's algorithm
abstract: We propose a scheme for preparing spin-squeezed states in an ensemble of $N$ spin-$1/2$ particles based on Grover's algorithm. With only a few oracles, the scheme can exactly prepare superpositions of a few neighboring Dicke states with the Wineland squeezing parameter scaling as $N^{-1}$. The scheme requires only global rotations and Dicke-selective phase shifts, thus avoiding the need to engineer a dedicated many-body Hamiltonian for the squeezing dynamics. We further discuss the feasibility of realizing the scheme in cavity QED systems, with the phase-matched Grover iterations realized by single-photon reflection from a dispersively coupled cavity. Full-sequence scattering calculations accounting for finite photon bandwidth and loss show that appreciable spin squeezing can be achieved with high fidelity for suitable system parameters.
one_liner: Grover iterations prepare strongly spin-squeezed Dicke-state superpositions using global control and selective phases.
why_it_matters: The protocol reaches N^-1 Wineland squeezing without engineering a dedicated many-body squeezing Hamiltonian.
detailed_summary: The protocol uses a few Grover oracles to exactly prepare superpositions of neighboring Dicke states with a Wineland parameter scaling as N^-1. Its controls are limited to global rotations and Dicke-selective phase shifts. A cavity-QED implementation based on single-photon reflection is analyzed with full scattering calculations that include finite photon bandwidth and loss, yielding appreciable squeezing at high fidelity for suitable parameters.
main_result: A few phase-matched Grover iterations can prepare Dicke superpositions with N^-1 spin-squeezing scaling.
application_angle: The approach could provide metrologically useful entangled ensembles using experimentally accessible cavity controls.

title: Detecting Nonbilocal Correlations via Parameterized Elegant Joint Measurement
abstract: Quantum networks constitute a defining resource for quantum information processing; however, their nonclassical behavior is jointly governed by the choice of measurement basis and the independence of the distributed sources. We study a bilocal entanglement-swapping network in which the central node performs a three-parameter elegant joint measurement (EJM). For two independent Bell-state sources, we construct two binary edge observables and then derive a quantum prediction involving three parameters, which surpasses the classical constraints. In particular, the parameter θ controls both the degree of entanglement of the EJM basis states and the maximum value of the quantum prediction. These results provide an analytic and directly reproducible route for tuning nonbilocal correlations in an experimentally relevant two-source network.
one_liner: A tunable elegant joint measurement analytically exposes nonbilocal correlations in a two-source entanglement-swapping network.
why_it_matters: The construction gives experiments a reproducible way to tune and certify network nonclassicality under source-independence assumptions.
detailed_summary: The work considers two independent Bell-state sources connected through a central node performing a three-parameter elegant joint measurement. Two binary edge observables produce a quantum prediction that exceeds the corresponding bilocal classical constraints. A parameter θ jointly controls the entanglement of the measurement basis and the maximum quantum value, providing a direct experimental tuning knob.
main_result: The parameterized joint measurement produces analytically tunable correlations that violate bilocal classical constraints.
application_angle: The scheme supports experimental certification and calibration of nonclassical correlations in elementary quantum-network links.

title: Development of time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy using heralded emission spectroscopy for organic light-emitting materials
abstract: Organic light-emitting materials are widely used in optoelectronics and bioimaging, but sometimes conventional fluorescence spectroscopy techniques can be limited by scattering, background fluorescence, photon pile-up and photobleaching. We report a quantum-spectroscopic approach using frequency-entangled, nondegenerate photon pairs generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion with heralded detection, to perform photoluminescence lifetime measurements at low excitation intensities. We demonstrate this approach across three organic light-emitting material classes: the fluorescent dye Rhodamine 6G, an organic semiconducting conjugated polymer poly[2-methoxy-5-(2-ethylhexyloxy)-1,4-phenylenevinylene] (MEH-PPV), and a fluorescent protein mOrange. The intrinsic timing correlation between signal and idler photons enables coincidence gating that suppresses uncorrelated background counts. Across all materials and integration times of 500, 1000 and 3600 seconds, heralded detection yields signal-to-noise ratios 1.6-3.0 times higher than classical pulsed-laser excitation attenuated to match heralded photon counts in the fitting range. For MEH-PPV, this roughly halves the noise amplitude. Our measured lifetimes closely match long-integration classical pulsed-laser reference values.
one_liner: Heralded entangled-photon spectroscopy improves low-flux fluorescence-lifetime measurements across three organic emitters.
why_it_matters: Coincidence gating raises signal-to-noise at low excitation, benefiting samples limited by background, pile-up, or photobleaching.
detailed_summary: Frequency-entangled, nondegenerate SPDC photon pairs provide heralded excitation and coincidence-timed fluorescence detection. Measurements on Rhodamine 6G, MEH-PPV, and mOrange deliver signal-to-noise ratios 1.6–3.0 times those of photon-count-matched attenuated pulsed-laser excitation over 500–3600 s integrations. The extracted lifetimes agree closely with long-integration classical references, while MEH-PPV shows roughly half the noise amplitude.
main_result: Heralded detection improves fluorescence-lifetime signal-to-noise by 1.6–3.0 times while preserving reference-consistent lifetimes.
application_angle: The technique enables sensitive lifetime spectroscopy of fragile or weakly emitting materials at reduced excitation dose.

title: Discrete quadrature spectrum of composite bosons: Weyl relation, intensity correlations, and binned homodyne detection
abstract: A composite boson made of two fermions can look elementary under one measurement and composite under another. In an exactly solvable paired-mode model we compare three probes: classical drives, periodically binned quadrature statistics, and intensity correlations $g^{(2)}$. The Weyl defect has an exact product formula and a controlled dilute expansion in the Schmidt moments. The binned observables are instead piecewise constant in the Schmidt weights and sensitive to single eigenvalues crossing bin edges; on the flat-spectrum ladder they converge slowly and nonmonotonically over the computed range. A spectral filter and a polar correction recover an exact Pauli algebra; a heralded joint projection then extracts a logical singlet from the vacua of two independent copies of the composite, with probability set by the accepted weight and the mixedness of the filtered reduced qubit. Finite-mode examples with Schmidt number about three succeed at the percent level despite order-one Weyl defects; near-unit $g^{(2)}$ does not control the binned algebra. For flat spectra the construction converges strongly to its oscillator counterpart, whose vacuum overlap is strictly positive at every scale; for infinite spectra with summable Schmidt amplitudes it converges at all but countably many filter cutoffs, positivity at the cutoffs studied remaining open.
one_liner: Discrete homodyne-like observables reveal composite-boson structure missed by near-unity intensity correlations.
why_it_matters: The results clarify which optical measurements can certify fermionic compositeness and support filtered logical-state extraction.
detailed_summary: An exactly solvable paired-mode model compares Weyl defects, periodically binned quadratures, and g^(2) as probes of two-fermion composite bosons. Binned observables depend discontinuously on individual Schmidt weights, so near-unity g^(2) does not guarantee oscillator-like algebra. Spectral filtering and polar correction restore an exact Pauli algebra, enabling heralded logical-singlet extraction at percent-level probability in finite examples with Schmidt number near three.
main_result: Filtered binned-quadrature measurements recover an exact qubit algebra and permit heralded singlet extraction despite large Weyl defects.
application_angle: The framework informs measurement design for identifying composite-particle behavior and encoding logical photonic or excitonic states.

title: Multirobust Control Pulses Designed by Iterative Quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser Algorithm
abstract: We introduce a multi-robust quantum control strategy designed to suppress multilevel leakage outside the computational qubit space while simultaneously ensuring robustness against unknown inhomogeneities in control parameters. It is based on a reformulation of the Derivative Removal by Adiabatic Gate (DRAG) technique which allows for the full incorporation of control pulses originally designed for two-level models by using the iterative quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser (KAM) algorithm. We apply it for optimal robust control designed by inverse optimization (RIO), referred to as RDK pulses. We analyze the performance of RDK pulses on various durations, iterations, and robustness types. We show that the two-level robustness is restored after only a few iterations with an asymptotic exponential approximation (i.e. as a superasymptotic series), even for relatively short pulse durations and that the resulting pulses are near optimal in terms of energy compared to the optimal RIO pulses defined in the qubit subspace. Such pulses are well suited for superconducting transmons as well as other forms of qubits embedded in a multi-level structure. By effectively reproducing a two-level dynamics within a multi-level system, this approach is versatile thanks to its compatibility with two-level control strategies under conditions (smoothness, duration) that are analyzed.
one_liner: Iterative KAM corrections turn robust two-level control pulses into low-leakage pulses for multilevel qubits.
why_it_matters: The method preserves robustness to control inhomogeneity while suppressing leakage, addressing a central gate-control problem in transmons and other weakly anharmonic qubits.
detailed_summary: The work reformulates DRAG using an iterative quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser algorithm so that pulses designed for an ideal two-level system can be deployed in a multilevel device. Applied to robust inverse-optimized control, the resulting RDK pulses recover two-level robustness after only a few iterations, with asymptotically exponential convergence. They remain near the energy optimum of the original qubit-subspace pulses, including at relatively short durations.
main_result: Iterative KAM pulse corrections simultaneously suppress multilevel leakage and restore robustness to unknown control inhomogeneities with near-optimal pulse energy.
application_angle: The approach can retrofit established two-level pulse designs for higher-fidelity control of transmons and other qubits embedded in multilevel spectra.

title: Continuous variable payload transmitter for the SPOQC mission
abstract: The continuous variable (CV) quantum key distribution (QKD) scheme enables two parties to share a secret key separated by a certain distance. Here we propose, design, build, test and show results of a CV payload transmitter, intended to demonstrate downlink based QKD from a CubeSat in low earth orbit. This is part of the SPOQC mission by Quantum Communications Hub, UK which was successfully launched on March 2026.
one_liner: A CubeSat-ready continuous-variable transmitter was built and tested for quantum-key-distribution downlinks from low Earth orbit.
why_it_matters: The payload advances CV-QKD from laboratory links toward compact space hardware capable of extending secure quantum communication over satellite distances.
detailed_summary: The authors propose, design, construct, and test a continuous-variable QKD transmitter intended for a low-Earth-orbit CubeSat. The payload belongs to the UK Quantum Communications Hub's SPOQC mission, reported as launched in March 2026. The paper presents transmitter test results aimed at validating a space-to-ground CV-QKD downlink architecture.
main_result: A compact continuous-variable QKD payload transmitter was realized and tested for operation in a CubeSat downlink mission.
application_angle: The hardware targets deployable satellite QKD, potentially enabling secure key distribution across geographic ranges impractical for direct terrestrial optical links.

title: Continuum Photonic Axion Insulators
abstract: Here, I study the conditions for realizing an axion topology in a homogeneous inversion-symmetric electromagnetic continuum, in the absence of a crystalline lattice. I introduce a continuum inversion invariant expressed solely in terms of the spectral properties of the material response in the zero- and infinite-wave-vector limits. Surprisingly, it is found that standard gyrotropic-type material responses are strongly constrained and, under fairly general conditions, cannot open an axion gap within first-order perturbation theory. Based on an analogy between the effective response of crystalline photonic axion insulators and the optical response of centrosymmetric altermagnets, a class of spatially dispersive odd magnetoelectric couplings that can open an axion gap is identified. These findings suggest an interesting hierarchy of nonreciprocal mechanisms in electromagnetic continua: while uniform gyrotropy relates to Chern phases, odd magnetoelectric coupling relates to axion phases.
one_liner: A continuum invariant and odd magnetoelectric response are proposed for realizing photonic axion phases without a crystal lattice.
why_it_matters: The analysis identifies which nonreciprocal material responses can produce axion topology, offering design guidance for homogeneous topological photonic media.
detailed_summary: The paper derives an inversion invariant for homogeneous electromagnetic continua from the material-response spectra at zero and infinite wave vector. It finds that conventional gyrotropic responses are generally unable to open an axion gap at first order. Spatially dispersive odd magnetoelectric couplings, motivated by centrosymmetric altermagnets, are instead identified as a viable mechanism for continuum photonic axion phases.
main_result: Odd spatially dispersive magnetoelectric coupling can open a photonic axion gap, whereas standard uniform gyrotropy is strongly constrained at first order.
application_angle: The response criteria can guide the design of nonreciprocal topological photonic materials and interfaces without relying on a periodic lattice.

title: A Passive Intelligent Metasurface: A Network Model
abstract: Intelligent metasurfaces enable advanced wave manipulation, including negative refraction, focusing, beam splitting and beam steering, with significant potential for practical applications. However, conventional approaches often rely on active metamaterials with gain, or demand computationally intensive solutions of inverse problems to find the optimal configuration. In this work, we use the scattering framework of quantum graph theory to derive an exact, analytic expression for configuration of a passive metasurface that produces a prescribed reflected wave field. The metasurface terminates a periodic lattice of waveguides and consists of an array of channels, each a tube of length $\ell_m$ ending in a vertex whose scattering parameter $λ_m$ sets how much of the wave is lost to the wall. For any prescribed incident and reflected field, the exact lengths and scattering parameters follow channel by channel, in closed form, from the ratio of the wave amplitudes returning to and leaving the lattice, and the metasurface is passive whenever this ratio does not exceed unity in modulus. We demonstrate the construction for both a one-dimensional and a two-dimensional metasurface. The one-dimensional metasurface terminates a two-dimensional lattice and steers, splits or perfectly absorbs Gaussian beams. The two-dimensional metasurface terminates a three-dimensional lattice and generates a prescribed image in a plane inside the lattice. In each case, we obtain the exact boundary properties that produce the effect.
one_liner: Quantum-graph scattering yields closed-form passive metasurface parameters for prescribed reflection, absorption, beam control, and imaging.
why_it_matters: An exact channel-by-channel construction could replace costly inverse optimization when designing passive wavefront-shaping boundaries.
detailed_summary: The authors model a metasurface terminating a periodic waveguide lattice as an array of lossy, closed-end channels. For arbitrary incident and target reflected fields, each channel's length and wall-loss parameter are obtained analytically from the local ratio of returning to outgoing amplitudes; passivity holds when its modulus is at most one. Demonstrations include Gaussian-beam steering, splitting and perfect absorption in two dimensions, plus prescribed-image formation inside a three-dimensional lattice.
platform_or_system: Passive channel-array metasurface on a waveguide lattice
main_result: The model provides exact closed-form boundary parameters that generate prescribed reflected fields while explicitly enforcing passivity.
application_angle: It supports rapidly configurable passive designs for beam routing, absorption, focusing, and field-pattern generation without numerical inverse optimization.

title: Phase-Matched Design of Pinching-Antenna Elements on a 60-GHz Dielectric Rod Waveguide
abstract: The radiation of pinching antennas, dielectric elements placed on a dielectric waveguide, depends on the element shape. We explain it with a phase-matching, or prism-coupler, picture: the guided rod mode couples into the denser antenna plate at an angle set by the plate-mode effective index, about 31 degrees at 60 GHz, and radiates through the face it reaches first. This yields a simple sizing rule linking element height to contact length. Rectangular, isosceles and right-triangular elements of equal contact length and height are compared from 53 to 67 GHz in full-wave openEMS simulations including the waveguide-to-rod transitions. The rectangle peaks sharply at the rule, reaching 15.9 dBi. The right triangle keeps its gain within 0.7 dB and its side lobes at least 10 dB down over a two-to-one height range. At the rule, both outperform the isosceles element by 1.2 to 2.1 dB, and all remain matched.
one_liner: A phase-matching rule explains and optimizes 60-GHz pinching antennas, with a right-triangle element delivering broadband tolerance.
why_it_matters: The simple geometric rule and robust element shape can reduce design effort for practical millimeter-wave waveguide-fed antenna arrays.
detailed_summary: A prism-coupler picture links the guided dielectric-rod mode to a plate mode entering the antenna element at about 31 degrees, producing a sizing rule between element height and contact length. Full-wave openEMS simulations from 53 to 67 GHz compare rectangular, isosceles-triangular, and right-triangular elements including transitions. The rectangle reaches 15.9 dBi at the design point, while the right triangle stays within 0.7 dB gain and below −10 dB sidelobes across a two-to-one height range.
main_result: Phase-matched sizing produces high gain, while a right-triangular element provides substantially greater dimensional tolerance with controlled sidelobes.
application_angle: The results enable fabrication-tolerant, waveguide-fed millimeter-wave radiators for beamforming, wireless links, and distributed antenna systems.

title: Autler-townes energy-level engineering for high-quality all-microwave qubit gate
abstract: High-fidelity entangling gates are essential for realizing large-scale fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computing, yet existing approaches are limited: frequency-tuning techniques induce decoherence, while all-microwave-driven schemes suffer the trade-off between gate speed and leakage rate. Here, we introduce an energy-level engineering technique that employs the Autler-Townes effect to manipulate the nonlinearity of qubits without perturbing the computational subspace or degrading coherence time. This approach enables an experimentally validated, fast (97 ns) and high-fidelity (99.40(9)%) CZ gate, where error analysis reveals that gate errors arise mainly from static decoherence. The scheme facilitates fast, high-quality all-microwave gate operations with a simple topology and can be applied across various quantum platforms.
one_liner: Autler-Townes level engineering enables an experimentally validated 97-ns, 99.40(9)%-fidelity all-microwave CZ gate.
why_it_matters: The technique improves the speed-leakage trade-off without frequency tuning or measured coherence loss, simplifying scalable superconducting-qubit control.
detailed_summary: A microwave drive induces Autler-Townes splitting to reshape qubit nonlinearity while leaving the computational subspace and coherence time largely undisturbed. The engineered spectrum supports a 97 ns controlled-Z gate with measured fidelity of 99.40(9)%. Error analysis attributes the dominant residual error to static decoherence rather than drive-induced leakage or control imperfections.
main_result: Autler-Townes engineering realizes a 97 ns all-microwave CZ gate with 99.40(9)% experimental fidelity and no reported coherence degradation.
application_angle: The simple, fixed-frequency topology offers a practical route to faster entangling gates in scalable superconducting processors and may transfer to other platforms.

title: Crosstalk-Induced Row Hammer Attacks on Quantum Random Access Codes
abstract: Quantum processors remain susceptible to crosstalk-induced effects despite the continuous evolution of their underlying hardware architectures. In this work, we experimentally investigate the effectiveness of crosstalk-induced attacks across six IBM superconducting quantum processors and one IQM processor. Our results demonstrate that such attacks can be launched across all the platforms, due to persistance of crosstalk, although their effectiveness varies significantly between devices. The probability of a measurement outcome flip in the victim qubits reaches a maximum value of $60\%$. Also, it is seen that processors sharing identical coupling graphs exhibit different vulnerability profiles, indicating that connectivity alone is insufficient to predict attack efficiency. Finally, to demonstrate the practical relevance of these attacks, we study their impact on quantum random access codes (QRACs), observing a degradation in their average success probabilities.
one_liner: Crosstalk attacks altered victim-qubit outcomes by up to 60% across seven superconducting quantum processors and degraded QRAC performance.
why_it_matters: The results expose a hardware-level security risk that coupling graphs alone cannot predict, motivating device-specific crosstalk testing and mitigation.
detailed_summary: The authors experimentally launch crosstalk-induced attacks on six IBM superconducting processors and one IQM processor. All tested platforms were vulnerable, with victim-qubit measurement-flip probabilities reaching 60%, although susceptibility varied substantially among devices. Identical coupling graphs did not imply similar vulnerability, and attacks reduced the average success probability of quantum random access codes.
platform_or_system: IBM and IQM superconducting quantum processors
main_result: Crosstalk attacks were demonstrated on all seven processors, causing up to 60% victim-outcome flips and measurable QRAC degradation.
application_angle: The study provides an experimental basis for hardware-aware security audits, crosstalk isolation, and attack-resistant quantum-computing architectures.

title: Quantum Relative Entropy and Information Flux Resolve Wavefunction Collapse in Spacelike-Separated QED Waveguides
abstract: Resolving how first-order quantum coherence and definite measurement outcomes emerge from entangled vacuum fluctuations across spacelike-separated regions is unified here by the principle that quantum relative entropy governs the energy-information flux across causal boundaries [P.~Dorau and A.~Much, Phys.~Rev.~Lett.~\textbf{136}, 091602 (2026)]. We establish the exact quantum-optical realization of this principle using dual, spacelike-separated entangled nonlinear biphoton sources implemented in quantum electrodynamics waveguides pumped by an optical frequency comb and seeded by a continuous-wave laser in a coherent state $|α\rangle$. We demonstrate that single-photon-added coherent states (SPACS) generated via coherent seeding possess a quantum relative entropy that precisely quantifies the entanglement deficit between signal and idler fields. Tracing over the unmeasured idler continuum yields an exact spatial Lindblad master equation along the propagation axis, proving that spatial dephasing is driven by an information divergence flux determined by the SPACS overlap fidelity $F = |α|^2/(1+|α|^2)$. Uniting this relative-entropy flow with quotient measurement theory (detailed in Section~S3 of the Supplemental Material), we rigorously resolve nonlocal wavefunction collapse into local coset projections---explaining macroscopic state reduction without superluminal signaling. This exact open-system framework simultaneously saturates the wave-particle-entanglement triality [T.~H.~Yoon and M.~Cho, Sci.~Adv.~\textbf{7}, eabi9268 (2021)] and anchors hardware-native time--frequency Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill stabilizers to the comb symplectic structure.
one_liner: A theoretical QED-waveguide framework links relative-entropy flux, spatial dephasing, and local measurement projections in entangled biphoton sources.
why_it_matters: It proposes a unified open-system description connecting coherence loss, measurement locality, and time-frequency photonic encoding, though experimental validation remains open.
detailed_summary: The work analyzes dual spacelike-separated nonlinear biphoton sources driven by an optical frequency comb and coherently seeded by a continuous-wave laser. It derives a spatial Lindblad equation after tracing over the idler continuum and relates the dephasing rate to relative-entropy flow and the SPACS overlap fidelity F=|α|²/(1+|α|²). The framework also connects the comb structure to time-frequency GKP stabilizers and interprets measurement reduction through local coset projections.
main_result: The authors derive an exact open-system model in which SPACS information divergence governs spatial dephasing and local measurement projections.
application_angle: The proposed formalism may guide time-frequency photonic-state engineering and hardware-native bosonic encodings, pending physical implementation and validation.

title: Hybrid integration of a SESAM with a silicon nitride photonic integrated circuit
abstract: The realization of high-performance femtosecond lasers on photonic integrated circuits (PICs) requires robust, low-loss coupling between a saturable absorber and a photonic waveguide. In this work, we demonstrate the hybrid integration of a semiconductor saturable absorber mirror (SESAM) with a silicon nitride (SiN) PIC by micro-assembly. This micro-assembly strategy transfers the non-linear functionality of the absorber onto the PIC. We characterize the linear and non-linear performance of an unbonded SESAM and of a SESAM bonded to inverse-tapered SiN waveguides. At 1560~nm, the bonded device shows a waveguide-coupled modulation depth of 5.2\%, a maximum reflectivity of 37.2\%, and a saturation fluence of 47~\textmu J/cm$^2$. This work demonstrates that SESAMs can be integrated directly onto silicon nitride-based PIC platforms and provides a pathway towards fully integrated, self-starting, chip-scale ultrafast lasers.
one_liner: A micro-assembled SESAM bonded to inverse-tapered SiN waveguides delivered 5.2% modulation depth at 1560 nm.
why_it_matters: Directly integrating a saturable absorber with low-loss SiN photonics removes a key obstacle to self-starting chip-scale femtosecond lasers.
detailed_summary: The authors micro-assemble a semiconductor saturable absorber mirror onto inverse-tapered silicon-nitride waveguides and characterize it before and after bonding. At 1560 nm, the bonded device exhibits a waveguide-coupled modulation depth of 5.2%, maximum reflectivity of 37.2%, and saturation fluence of 47 µJ/cm². The experiment transfers nonlinear saturable-absorption functionality directly onto a SiN photonic integrated circuit.
main_result: The bonded SESAM-SiN device achieved 5.2% modulation depth, 37.2% maximum reflectivity, and 47 µJ/cm² saturation fluence at 1560 nm.
application_angle: The integration method supports compact, self-starting femtosecond sources for spectroscopy, frequency combs, communications, and quantum photonics.

title: Nonuniform Time-bins for Making Raw QRNG Outputs Uniform
abstract: Random numbers play a vital role in scientific simulations and cryptography. Both randomness and security are critical requirements for random number generators (RNGs). However, classical RNGs often rely on mathematical assumptions that can compromise security, while quantum RNGs (QRNGs) face challenges, including non-uniform output due to the lack of specialized single-photon sources. In this work, we propose a QRNG model that generates uniformly distributed random numbers using a standard coherent photon source, without requiring heavy attenuation or post-processing. Although the raw data is theoretically free of bias, post-processing, if any, may be required to suppress any classical noise and device imperfections. The proposed method analytically equalizes the output probabilities under the assumed photon-arrival-time model, potentially reducing the need for heavy attenuation and post-processing to correct binning bias. We evaluate the method using real photon-detection timestamps and compare its statistical performance with conventional uniform time binning using the NIST, Dieharder, and ENT test suites. The results demonstrate improved statistical performance for the proposed binning scheme under the tested conditions.
one_liner: Nonuniform arrival-time bins produced more uniform raw QRNG outputs from a coherent optical source without heavy attenuation or bias-correction processing.
why_it_matters: Reducing source and post-processing requirements could simplify practical photon-arrival-time QRNGs while retaining strong statistical output quality.
detailed_summary: The proposed QRNG assigns nonuniform time-bin widths so that detection probabilities are analytically equalized under an assumed photon-arrival-time model. It uses a standard coherent source without requiring heavy attenuation and aims to remove binning bias before post-processing. Tests on measured photon timestamps using NIST, Dieharder, and ENT suites show improved statistics over uniform time bins under the evaluated conditions, although classical noise and imperfections may still require processing.
main_result: Model-derived nonuniform bins improved the statistical uniformity of real timestamp data relative to conventional equal-width binning.
application_angle: The method could lower optical and computational overhead in compact QRNG modules for cryptography and quantum-communication systems.

title: Photonic Exceptional Topological Bound States in the Continuum
abstract: Exceptional bound states in the continuum (EBICs) arise when bound states in the continuum (BICs) with distinct intrinsic losses coalesce at exceptional points (EPs), combining continuum-embedded wave confinement with a non-analytic spectral response. However, conventional EBICs rely on precisely controlled modal coupling and intrinsic loss, making them fragile and difficult to realize experimentally. Here, we introduce bulk-band topology to mitigate this fragility and experimentally realize a photonic exceptional topological BIC (ETBIC) in spoof surface plasmon polariton waveguides by merging two symmetry-protected topological BICs (TBICs) to coalesce at an EP, with the topological design supporting robust localization under symmetry-preserving perturbations. By engineering an intrinsic loss contrast and tuning the intermodal coupling, we directly resolve the coalescence of the complex eigenfrequencies, accompanied by measured near-field distributions consistent with the exceptional eigenstate. Furthermore, weak perturbations induce approximately square-root eigenfrequency splitting, yielding an enhanced spectral response compared with the approximately linear frequency shift of an isolated TBIC. These results establish bulk-band topology as a design principle for exceptional BIC engineering and provide a foundation for EBIC-based photonic sensing.
one_liner: Two topological photonic BICs were merged at an exceptional point, producing robust localization and square-root spectral splitting.
why_it_matters: Topology makes exceptional BIC engineering less fragile while retaining the enhanced perturbation response sought in compact photonic sensors.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses spoof surface-plasmon-polariton waveguides to merge two symmetry-protected topological bound states in the continuum at an exceptional point. Engineered loss contrast and intermodal coupling produce coalescing complex eigenfrequencies, with measured near fields matching the exceptional eigenstate. Weak perturbations yield approximately square-root eigenfrequency splitting rather than the near-linear shift of an isolated topological BIC.
main_result: The authors experimentally realized an exceptional topological BIC with robust localization and enhanced square-root spectral response.
application_angle: The architecture offers a more robust route to exceptional-point photonic sensors with amplified responses to weak environmental perturbations.

title: Characterization and Suppression of Parasitic Back-Reflection Noise in Transponder-Type Heterodyne Interferometry
abstract: Transponder-type heterodyne interferometry is a versatile metrological technique for high-precision measurements, with applications in Earth's gravity-field recovery, space-based gravitational-wave detection, deep-space ranging, and Doppler tracking. However, parasitic back-reflections can contaminate phase readout and degrade measurement sensitivity. To characterize and suppress this noise, we constructed a transponder-type interferometer with coaxially aligned counter-propagating beams, achieving stable operation at a received optical power of 720 pW. An adjustable reflecting system was introduced into the master-side transmit path to simulate back-reflection under realistic conditions. Optical path scans and model fitting showed that phase errors vary periodically with the relative phase between the main and parasitic interference signals, which defines the working point. Assisted by π measurement, adjustment to low-sensitivity working points was combined with balanced detection to suppress back-reflection phase noise, achieving maximum suppression factors of 77 for single-frequency phase errors and 23 for band-limited phase-noise amplitude spectral density. π measurement also enabled working point diagnosis at 3.8 nW back-reflection power, confirming its applicability under weak back-reflection conditions. These results provide an effective approach for in situ back-reflection characterization and phase-noise suppression in transponder-type heterodyne interferometry.
one_liner: Working-point control plus balanced detection suppressed back-reflection phase errors by 77× and band-limited phase-noise amplitude by 23×.
why_it_matters: The method enables in situ diagnosis and strong suppression of a major noise source in ultraweak-light heterodyne metrology.
detailed_summary: A coaxial transponder-type heterodyne interferometer operated stably with 720 pW received optical power while an adjustable reflector emulated realistic parasitic feedback. Path scans and model fitting showed periodic phase errors determined by the relative phase of the desired and parasitic signals. π measurement identified low-sensitivity working points, and balanced detection then achieved suppression factors of 77 for single-frequency phase error and 23 for band-limited phase-noise amplitude spectral density.
main_result: The demonstrated control strategy suppressed back-reflection-induced phase error by up to 77× and phase-noise amplitude by up to 23×.
application_angle: The technique is directly relevant to gravity-field missions, space gravitational-wave detectors, deep-space ranging, and precision Doppler tracking.

title: Machine learning quantum data to accelerate quantum Monte Carlo
abstract: Simulating strongly correlated electrons in molecules and materials remains a central goal for quantum computing. A promising strategy uses quantum processors to prepare trial wavefunctions that guide classical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, the enormous computational cost of repeatedly processing quantum measurements has severely limited the practical scalability of this approach. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by compressing quantum measurement data into machine-learning models that efficiently provide the wavefunction overlaps needed by QMC. This accelerates quantum-classical QMC by orders of magnitude, enabling chemically accurate simulations on up to 40 qubits, more than doubling the scale of previous hardware demonstrations with comparable accuracy. We demonstrate our approach on hydrogen chains and strongly correlated iron-sulfur clusters using measurements from Google's Willow processor. By enabling efficient reuse of quantum-state information on the classical coprocessor, our framework addresses a fundamental bottleneck in hybrid quantum algorithms that will persist even into the fault-tolerant era.
one_liner: Machine-learned compression of Willow measurement data accelerates hybrid quantum Monte Carlo simulations on systems up to 40 qubits.
why_it_matters: Efficient reuse of quantum measurements removes a major classical-processing bottleneck in hybrid simulations of strongly correlated molecules and materials.
detailed_summary: The method trains machine-learning models on quantum measurement data to rapidly supply wavefunction overlaps required by classical quantum Monte Carlo. Measurements from Google's Willow processor enable chemically accurate calculations for hydrogen chains and strongly correlated iron-sulfur clusters at scales up to 40 qubits. This more than doubles the scale of prior hardware demonstrations at comparable accuracy while reducing repeated measurement-processing costs by orders of magnitude.
main_result: The hybrid workflow achieves chemically accurate QMC simulations on up to 40 qubits with orders-of-magnitude faster quantum-data processing.
application_angle: The approach improves the practical scalability of quantum-assisted simulations for molecular chemistry and correlated materials, including future fault-tolerant workflows.

title: Non-Unitary Quantum Butterfly Effect: Theory and Experiment
abstract: We present a generalization of the out of time order correlator (OTOC) for non-unitary systems. For a Haar-random brickwork qudit-circuit, peppered with local, projective measurement, we calculate the infinite-temperature, ensemble-average OTOC. Utilizing transfer matrix machinery, we find that the OTOC asymptotically decays exponentially and that the decay depends on the rate of measurement. In the thermodynamic limit, with sparse measurement, the OTOC approximately exhibits a Gaussian shape. Phenomenologically, this corresponds to the development of a causal scrambling front where unlike the unitary case, the signal decays in the bulk of the causal cone. We develop a Monte Carlo framework to compute the OTOC. We then estimate the OTOC directly via quantum simulation and on Quantinuum's trapped-ion quantum computer. We resolve the unitary and non-unitary OTOC phenomenology despite the presence of hardware noise. Our analytic results characterize how local nonunitary channels affect OTOC decay, providing a quantitative benchmark for the cumulative effects of a broad class of hardware noise on many-body dynamics.
one_liner: A generalized OTOC reveals measurement-dependent scrambling decay and is resolved experimentally on a Quantinuum trapped-ion processor.
why_it_matters: The framework turns non-unitary scrambling into a quantitative probe of how measurements and accumulated hardware noise alter many-body quantum dynamics.
detailed_summary: The authors derive the ensemble-averaged out-of-time-order correlator for Haar-random brickwork qudit circuits containing local projective measurements. Transfer-matrix analysis predicts exponential decay and, for sparse measurements in the thermodynamic limit, an approximately Gaussian scrambling profile with attenuation inside the causal cone. Monte Carlo simulations and experiments on a Quantinuum trapped-ion computer distinguish unitary and non-unitary behavior despite device noise.
main_result: The experiment resolves the predicted measurement-dependent non-unitary scrambling phenomenology on noisy trapped-ion hardware.
application_angle: The generalized OTOC provides a benchmark for diagnosing cumulative non-unitary errors and measurement effects in many-body quantum processors.

title: Analytical Modeling of the Admittance Tensor of Periodic Elliptical Meta-Atoms
abstract: A metasurface is an electrically thin interface that controls the phase, amplitude and polarization of a wave, upon reflection or transmission. Printed on a grounded dielectric substrate and spatially modulated across the aperture, it converts a guided surface wave into a radiated leaky wave, a mechanism used in holographic metasurface antennas. Controlling this conversion requires synthesizing a prescribed distribution of admittance tensors, each derived from the homogenization of a subwavelength unit cell. Many numerical and semi-analytical methods have been proposed to relate the geometry of a meta-atom to the tensor it produces. This paper presents, to the author's knowledge, the first analytical model, restricted to elliptical meta-atoms on a uniform lattice. The Galerkin method is applied directly to the geometry of the patches, without spatial meshing. An affine transformation maps any rotated ellipse onto the unit disk, so that a single formulation covers every configuration. A wideband response takes from minutes to tens of minutes with a periodic full-wave solver, while the proposed model evaluates it in a few tens of milliseconds on the same workstation, roughly three orders of magnitude faster. The predicted admittance agrees with a method-of-moments reference up to the fundamental resonance and captures the guided-mode anomaly of the substrate. Beyond the physical insight it brings, the model is a differentiable function of the geometry, which makes the quasi-real-time design of optimized metasurfaces possible.
one_liner: A differentiable analytical model predicts elliptical meta-atom admittance about three orders of magnitude faster than periodic full-wave simulation.
why_it_matters: Millisecond-scale tensor evaluation can enable quasi-real-time optimization of polarization- and wavefront-controlling metasurfaces.
detailed_summary: The model applies a Galerkin formulation directly to periodic elliptical patches on a grounded dielectric substrate, avoiding spatial meshing. An affine transformation maps rotated ellipses to a unit disk, providing one formulation across geometries and orientations. It agrees with a method-of-moments reference through the fundamental resonance, captures the substrate guided-mode anomaly, and evaluates a wideband response in tens of milliseconds.
main_result: The analytical model delivers differentiable, wideband admittance tensors roughly 1000 times faster than a periodic full-wave solver.
application_angle: Rapid differentiable evaluation supports optimized holographic metasurface antennas, leaky-wave apertures, and polarization-control devices.

title: Persistent level-resolved transmon population after dispersive readout, and the limits of its open-system description
abstract: We calculate the level-resolved transmon population remaining after dispersive readout with a converged open-system model. The drive and qubit-cavity coupling use the rotating-wave approximation, while the cavity is a quantized mode in a frame displaced by its classical trajectory. At a readout occupation of 80, the model leaves a persistent distribution across the first transmon levels, with p2 = 1.02 x 10^-3 and p3 = 4.10 x 10^-5 at the end of readout. These populations survive an additional drive-off wait: over 73 ns each level decays by less than 3 percent and follows its own relaxation rate, not the near-factor-of-two drop in residual cavity photons. This identifies the population as bare-level occupation rather than coherent dressing. Channel-removal and bath-model controls attribute p2 mainly to dephasing and p3 and above mainly to relaxation, unchanged across bath models though absolute values vary by up to 15 percent. We also test the coherent drive truncation. In dissipation-free transmon-only benchmarks driven by the classical cavity trajectory, the nearest-neighbour RWA drive underestimates the full charge-operator result while the drive is on. At switch-off for occupation 80, where coherent populations are hundreds of times larger than the residual values, p2(RWA)/p2(full) = 0.905 and p3(RWA)/p3(full) = 0.759, with larger discrepancies at deeper levels. One source is a parity-allowed non-nearest-neighbour charge matrix element omitted by the drive operator. A naive beyond-RWA extension with bare-basis Lindblad dissipators fails a zero-drive ground-state test and serves only as a diagnostic. A dressed-basis (secular) construction instead leaves the dressed ground state stationary at zero drive. The result is a converged RWA prediction of readout-induced population plus direct tests of where the approximation loses quantitative reliability.
one_liner: A converged open-system model finds persistent higher-level transmon populations after strong dispersive readout and quantifies RWA limitations.
why_it_matters: Residual leakage after measurement can degrade reset and error-correction cycles, while inaccurate drive models can misestimate the effect.
detailed_summary: At cavity occupation 80, the model predicts post-readout populations of p2=1.02×10^-3 and p3=4.10×10^-5 that decay by less than 3% during a further 73 ns wait. Channel-removal tests associate p2 mainly with dephasing and higher levels mainly with relaxation. Comparisons against the full charge operator show that nearest-neighbor RWA driving underestimates coherent excitation, particularly in deeper transmon levels.
main_result: The study identifies persistent bare-level transmon leakage after readout and establishes where the converged RWA treatment loses quantitative accuracy.
application_angle: The results inform readout-power selection, leakage-aware reset protocols, and more reliable error budgets for superconducting quantum processors.

title: Finite-Time Thermodynamic Routing in an Anharmonic Collective Quantum Otto Engine
abstract: The Gibbs state determined by a thermal reservoir does not determine how a working medium approaches it or how fluctuations accumulate over repeated cycles. We exploit this kinetic freedom in an anharmonic collective quantum Otto engine. A longitudinal interaction separates neighboring Dicke transition frequencies without changing their collective matrix elements, allowing passive spectral shaping to route finite-time transport among edges with different heat costs while preserving the contact Gibbs states. Exact edge-current identities and repeated-cycle counting statistics link this routing to mean work, hot heat, and intercycle work correlations. At fixed thermal-contact exposure, structured reservoirs can increase both mean work and long-time squared precision; equal-work controls distinguish these gains from uniform relaxation-rate changes. The useful regime is mesoscopic, bounded by spectral resolution and physical contact time. An equal-cooling example and a full-spin local-noise study test the mechanism beyond ideal engine operation, the latter retaining a one-cycle precision gain despite spin-sector mixing. In a six-transmon dressed-spectrum model, passive microwave filters at fixed integrated coupling achieve equal mean work with shorter thermal contacts, corresponding to higher contact-time-normalized output, and with long-time squared precision comparable to that of the fastest sampled flat reference. The transition pathways selected by a passive reservoir thus provide a control variable for finite-time performance and accumulated work fluctuations that is independent of thermal equilibrium.
one_liner: Passive spectral filtering routes finite-time heat transport in an anharmonic collective Otto engine, improving output and precision.
why_it_matters: Reservoir spectrum engineering offers a hardware-compatible control knob for quantum-engine performance without changing equilibrium Gibbs states.
detailed_summary: A longitudinal interaction separates adjacent Dicke transition frequencies while preserving collective matrix elements, allowing structured reservoirs to select transport pathways with different heat costs. Exact edge-current identities and counting statistics connect this routing to mean work and intercycle correlations. In a six-transmon dressed-spectrum model, passive microwave filters reach equal work with shorter thermal contacts and retain competitive long-time precision.
main_result: Passive filters improve contact-time-normalized engine output at equal work while maintaining long-time squared precision comparable to the fastest flat-reservoir reference.
application_angle: The scheme suggests practical microwave reservoir engineering for faster and more precise finite-time operation of superconducting quantum thermal machines.

title: Certifying quantum code and circuit distances at scale
abstract: Code and circuit distances characterize how strongly quantum error correction suppresses logical errors and guide code comparisons, schedule choices and resource estimates. Yet many published distances are only upper bounds from heuristic searches. Here, we express both distances as tropical partition functions and evaluate them with rank-based dynamic programming and weight-bounded search. Circuit reductions and relaxations shrink the problems, and proved lower bounds with explicit logical errors of matching weight certify exact values. On two benchmarks, our method certifies more instances than all other tested exact solvers combined. We certify distances for codes with up to 31,200 qubits, such as Google's modular hyperbolic codes, and for memory circuits with up to $8\times10^5$ fault mechanisms, such as those of high-rate Cornucopia codes. Our audit of 26 recent papers identifies overestimated distances and non-tight upper bounds in 10 papers, with a maximum discrepancy of at least eight. Certified distances also guide circuit design and show which defective chips remain usable. In particular, we certify circuit distance 16 for IBM's two-gross memory circuits with the standard schedule, not the assumed 18, whereas redesigned schedules reach 18 at one noisy cycle, at the cost of one more timestep per cycle. At 99.98% junction yield, keeping gross-code memory blocks with dead checks that are certified at distance 10 or more raises the estimated usable share from 53% for perfect blocks alone to 94% with an improved schedule.
one_liner: Exact algorithms certify code and circuit distances for systems reaching 31,200 qubits and 800,000 circuit fault mechanisms.
why_it_matters: Provable distances replace optimistic heuristic estimates, improving error-correction comparisons, resource forecasts, schedules, and defective-chip use.
detailed_summary: The authors formulate code and circuit distances as tropical partition functions evaluated using rank-based dynamic programming and weight-bounded search. Matching lower-bound proofs and explicit logical faults certify exact distances at scales including 31,200-qubit modular hyperbolic codes and memory circuits with 8×10^5 fault mechanisms. An audit finds overstated or non-tight distances in 10 of 26 recent papers and shows schedule redesign can recover lost circuit distance.
platform_or_system: Large-scale quantum error-correcting codes and memory circuits
main_result: The method certifies exact distances at unprecedented scale and revises IBM two-gross memory-circuit distance from an assumed 18 to 16 under the standard schedule.
application_angle: Certified distances enable trustworthy hardware resource estimates, improved syndrome schedules, and retention of defective code blocks that still meet reliability targets.

title: Entropic measures of quantum information
abstract: Entropy has played a pivotal role in physics ever since its inception by Clausius in the early industrial age. Shannon ushered the concept into the information age by using it to describe fundamental limits of information processing, founding the field of information theory. Today, a fruitful interaction between information theory and physics is pushing our understanding of entropy forward. It has revealed, in particular, that no single notion of entropy suffices to capture all relevant properties of physical systems, making it necessary to consider a variety of entropic measures of quantum information, each with distinct features and uses. This review surveys these recent advances in a structured way, covering a comprehensive array of information measures, including Rényi and smooth entropies, together with their interrelations. Starting with a systematic characterization of entropies that motivates their definitions from natural physical principles, we discuss their applications ranging from quantum communication and cryptography to resource theories, thermodynamics, and many-body physics.
one_liner: A structured review unifies Rényi, smooth, and other quantum entropies through their operational principles and uses.
why_it_matters: These measures underpin finite-resource analyses in quantum communication, cryptography, thermodynamics, and resource theories.
detailed_summary: This review organizes a broad family of quantum-information measures, including Rényi and smooth entropies, and explains their interrelations. It motivates entropy definitions from physical principles and surveys operational applications in communication, cryptography, thermodynamics, resource theories, and many-body physics.
main_result: The review provides a systematic framework connecting major quantum entropies to their defining principles and operational uses.
application_angle: It offers a reference framework for selecting appropriate entropy measures in finite-resource communication and security analyses.

title: Beyond Quantum Messages: Toward Quantum-Native Network Functioning
abstract: The Quantum Internet is commonly envisioned as a network that transports quantum states and distributes entanglement as the key resource underpinning distributed quantum applications. This view is necessary but incomplete if quantum phenomena are confined to what the network carries or manages, while network functionalities remain grounded predominantly in classical abstractions. This Perspective advances a broader thesis: quantum phenomena can also participate directly in the realization of network functionalities. We first establish the architectural baseline by introducing entanglement as a stateful network resource whose operational condition is non-locally distributed across remote nodes, evolves through manipulation or consumption, and degrades over time through decoherence. Its evolving state must therefore remain visible to the functionalities acting on it. We then move beyond resource visibility and use two mechanisms as proof points of a broader quantum-native functional design space: entanglement generation during propagation through coherent spatial-path superposition, and operational connectivity induced by shared entanglement that can depart from the physical graph. These examples show that paths, neighbors, or participating nodes may become operationally relevant in ways determined by quantum coherence and shared entanglement, rather than by physical connectivity alone. We identify Quantum Addressing as a transversal abstraction capable of representing such relations while complementing, rather than replacing, classical addressing and signaling. The resulting perspective broadens the Quantum Internet from transporting quantum information and distributing entanglement to exploiting quantum phenomena in network functioning, opening a coupled frontier spanning routing, forwarding, control, and functionality placement.
one_liner: A quantum-native networking perspective lets coherence and entanglement directly define paths, neighbors, and connectivity.
why_it_matters: It expands quantum-network design beyond state transport toward routing and control functions shaped by nonclassical resources.
detailed_summary: This Perspective treats entanglement as a stateful, nonlocally distributed network resource whose evolving condition must remain visible to network functions. It uses propagation through coherent spatial-path superposition and entanglement-induced connectivity as examples of quantum-native functionality. Quantum Addressing is proposed as an abstraction complementing classical addressing and signaling.
main_result: The work defines a design space in which quantum coherence and shared entanglement directly influence network topology and operation.
application_angle: The framework could guide quantum-native routing, forwarding, control, and placement of distributed network functions.

title: Reprogrammable polaritonic skyrmion and meron lattices based on the phase-change material In$_3$SbTe$_2$
abstract: Optical topological quasiparticles such as skyrmions and merons consist of engineered electromagnetic fields which can be realized via the controlled interference of polaritons. The resulting polaritonic topological lattices offer a promising platform for on-chip information encoding and nanoscale light-matter interaction. However, realizing these functionalities requires active tailoring of the polaritonic topological lattice. Although previous works have achieved tuning of the size of the polaritonic lattice sites, these methods relied on cumbersome and time-consuming fabrication processes and do not allow reconfiguration of the topological invariant. Here, we demonstrate fast optical prototyping of reconfigurable hexagonal and square coupling structures for the generation of polaritonic topological lattices with hyperbolic phonon polaritons in hBN using the phase-change material In$_3$SbTe$_2$. As In$_3$SbTe$_2$ can be switched reversibly between its dielectric ($\varepsilon$>0) amorphous and metallic ($\varepsilon$<0) crystalline phase by laser pulses, metallic In$_3$SbTe$_2$ coupling structures can be optically programmed and reconfigured. Our approach enables tailoring the size of the topological lattice sites by tuning the incident frequency. Moreover, In$_3$SbTe$_2$ allows for tailoring the topological invariant by reprogramming the coupling structure. Our platform enables reprogramming of robust optical topologies within minutes, opening a route toward rewritable on-chip photonic computing based on robust and on demand reconfigurable topological states.
one_liner: Laser-reprogrammable In3SbTe2 couplers create switchable skyrmion and meron lattices from hyperbolic phonon polaritons in hBN.
why_it_matters: Rewriting lattice geometry and topology within minutes supports adaptable, robust on-chip photonic information processing.
detailed_summary: The authors optically program hexagonal and square metallic coupling structures in phase-change In3SbTe2 to generate polaritonic topological lattices in hBN. Reversible switching between amorphous dielectric and crystalline metallic phases enables rapid structural reconfiguration. Frequency tuning changes lattice-site size, while rewriting the couplers changes the topological invariant.
main_result: The platform reprograms polaritonic skyrmion and meron lattice geometry and topological invariant within minutes.
application_angle: It provides a route to rewritable topological photonic circuits for robust on-demand information encoding and computing.

title: Polynomial-time classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss
abstract: Sampling experiments are a leading approach to demonstrating quantum computational advantage, yet their robustness to experimental noise is not completely understood. We develop a common framework for classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss, including pure loss. For Fock-state boson sampling, Gaussian boson sampling with fixed uniform squeezing, and fermion sampling with magic inputs, we obtain polynomial-time sampling at inverse-polynomial total variation error, for any fixed nonzero overall loss rate, and with high probability over Haar-random interferometers. A milder flatness assumption on the ideal output distribution suffices for quasipolynomial-time simulation without Haar randomness. With constant thermal loss per layer, the same flatness assumption gives polynomial-time simulation at logarithmic depth. Our bounds for Fock-state boson sampling cover both dilute and saturated regimes and become stronger near full input filling: when only a bounded number of input modes are empty, the noisy output for Haar-random interferometers converges, as the number of modes grows, to a distribution independent of the interferometer.
one_liner: Fixed nonzero thermal loss makes several boson- and fermion-sampling models classically simulable in polynomial time.
why_it_matters: The bounds sharpen experimental noise thresholds required for photonic sampling systems to sustain credible quantum advantage.
detailed_summary: A unified simulation framework covers Fock-state boson sampling, fixed-squeezing Gaussian boson sampling, and fermion sampling with magic inputs under thermal or pure loss. For Haar-random interferometers, any fixed nonzero overall loss permits polynomial-time sampling with inverse-polynomial total-variation error. Under a flat-output assumption, the authors also derive quasipolynomial general bounds and polynomial simulation at logarithmic depth with constant loss per layer.
main_result: Several noisy bosonic and fermionic sampling models become efficiently classically simulable under fixed nonzero loss.
application_angle: The result identifies loss regimes that experimental sampling hardware must avoid or outperform to support quantum-advantage claims.

title: Tailoring resonator geometry for astigmatism compensation with structured light in birefringent optical cavities
abstract: In this work, we experimentally investigate the astigmatism induced by a birefringent crystal inside an optical cavity and demonstrate a geometric compensation strategy for structured modes carrying orbital angular momentum (OAM). We show that the astigmatism observed in the semimonolithic configuration can be fully compensated by introducing a third mirror to fold the cavity, thereby exploiting the geometric astigmatism arising from oblique incidence on the curved mirror.
