By performing a study of the resonator geometry, both theoretical and experimental results confirm that this approach enables the preservation of OAM between the pump beam and the converted signal and idler modes, providing an effective design strategy for birefringent optical cavities.
one_liner: A folded three-mirror cavity geometrically cancels crystal-induced astigmatism and preserves orbital angular momentum during conversion.
why_it_matters: The method offers a practical cavity design for efficient structured-light frequency conversion without sacrificing OAM content.
detailed_summary: The study experimentally characterizes astigmatism caused by a birefringent crystal in a semimonolithic optical cavity. Adding a third mirror folds the resonator so oblique incidence on a curved mirror supplies compensating geometric astigmatism. Theory and experiment show that the optimized geometry preserves OAM from the pump into converted signal and idler modes.
main_result: Geometric cavity folding fully compensates crystal-induced astigmatism while preserving OAM in the converted fields.
application_angle: The approach supports structured-light parametric sources and mode-preserving frequency converters using standard cavity geometry.

title: Room-Temperature Quantum Emission from Boron Nitride Nanotubes
abstract: Quantum information systems such as quantum key distribution and quantum communications require bright, high-purity, stable sources of single photons to act as carriers of quantum information. As such, methods for obtaining single photon emitters (SPEs) in solid-state devices capable of articulating with quantum photonic circuits are a necessary obstacle that must be overcome. Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) flakes have been extensively studied as a host material for SPEs, though working in two dimensions is accompanied by engineering complexity. However, dimensionality can be reduced through the implementation of boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs). Here we investigate the potential of BNNTs as room-temperature SPEs using confocal photoluminescence microscopy and Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometry. Quantum emitters were found in BNNTs spanning the entirety of the visible spectrum, including spectral regions where SPEs within hBN have not been reported. Furthermore, each tube was found to possess multiple SPEs at varying emission wavelengths along the length, exhibiting lifetimes as fast as 0.5 ns, which is about two-fold faster than the fastest hBN SPEs. Additionally, we demonstrate that surface passivation/coating mitigates blinking events, therefore increasing the emitter stability. Thus, BNNTs can function as a single structure supporting a variety of multiwavelength SPE sources, while maintaining a compact radius of ~25 nm, making them ideally suited for deterministic placement and integration within nanophotonic devices such as waveguides and interferometric filters.
one_liner: Boron nitride nanotubes host multiple room-temperature single-photon emitters spanning the visible spectrum with lifetimes down to 0.5 ns.
why_it_matters: Compact, passivatable, multiwavelength nanotubes could simplify deterministic integration of stable emitters into nanophotonic circuits.
detailed_summary: Confocal photoluminescence microscopy and Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometry reveal room-temperature quantum emitters distributed along individual boron nitride nanotubes. The emitters span the visible spectrum, including regions not previously reported for hBN single-photon emitters, and show lifetimes as short as 0.5 ns. Surface coating suppresses blinking, while each approximately 25 nm-radius tube can host several emission wavelengths.
main_result: Individual BNNTs support multiple visible-wavelength room-temperature single-photon emitters with fast decay and improved stability after passivation.
application_angle: Their small footprint and multiwavelength emission favor deterministic placement in waveguides, interferometric filters, and quantum links.

title: Provable circuit-level thresholds for non-abelian topological phases
abstract: We provide an explicit scheme to realize a quantum memory in any 2D non-chiral topological order. For this, we construct syndrome extraction circuits based on the Turaev-Viro path integral as well as a classical algorithm for decoding on the fly. We prove that our scheme has a threshold under a local stochastic circuit-level noise model and discuss how to generalize it to implement topological logical gates.
one_liner: A fault-tolerant quantum-memory scheme is constructed for any 2D non-chiral topological order, with a proven circuit-level noise threshold.
why_it_matters: It extends rigorous fault-tolerance guarantees beyond abelian codes and supplies explicit syndrome extraction and online decoding procedures.
detailed_summary: The work constructs syndrome-extraction circuits from the Turaev-Viro path integral for arbitrary 2D non-chiral topological orders. It also provides an on-the-fly classical decoder and proves a threshold under local stochastic circuit-level noise. The framework is discussed as a basis for implementing topological logical gates.
main_result: The proposed memory architecture has a provable threshold against local stochastic circuit-level noise.
application_angle: The scheme offers a rigorous route toward fault-tolerant memories and logical gates based on non-abelian topological matter.

title: Exploring topological signatures of quantum Fisher information scaling in graph states
abstract: Graph states are a versatile resource for quantum metrology, and their quantum Fisher information (QFI) has a closed-form expression in terms of the underlying graph: it counts pairs of vertices with identical neighborhoods. It remains unclear, however, which global structural properties of a graph determine whether its QFI exceeds the standard quantum limit (SQL). Here we ask whether topological invariants, namely the Betti numbers of the graph's clique complex, capture this behavior, and we address the question numerically with two complementary approaches. First, we randomly add or delete edges in balanced complete multipartite graphs, which combine a QFI beyond the SQL with a single nonvanishing higher Betti number. Edge addition eventually destroys both the metrological advantage and the nontrivial topology. Under edge deletion, by contrast, higher Betti numbers persist well after the QFI has dropped to the SQL. Second, we start from Erdős--Rényi random graphs, whose QFI does not typically exceed the SQL, and maximize a chosen Betti number with a Monte Carlo search. The search drives the graphs toward near-extremal multipartite structures whose QFI lies well beyond the SQL. Our results show that topological optimization offers a route to metrologically useful graph states, but also that Betti numbers alone do not determine the QFI.
one_liner: Numerical studies connect graph-state metrological gain with clique-complex topology while showing that Betti numbers alone do not determine QFI.
why_it_matters: Topological optimization can steer graph states toward structures with quantum Fisher information beyond the standard quantum limit.
detailed_summary: For graph states, the authors examine how clique-complex Betti numbers relate to quantum Fisher information determined by repeated vertex neighborhoods. Perturbations of complete multipartite graphs show that topology can persist after metrological advantage is lost. Conversely, Monte Carlo maximization of selected Betti numbers drives random graphs toward near-extremal multipartite structures with QFI beyond the SQL.
main_result: Optimizing higher Betti numbers produces graph states with enhanced QFI, although the invariants are neither necessary nor sufficient predictors by themselves.
application_angle: The method provides a structural design heuristic for preparing entangled sensing resources with improved parameter-estimation performance.

title: Harnessing dimensional leakage for continuous-variable randomness certification
abstract: Semi-device-independent quantum protocols often rely on strict Hilbert-space dimension assumptions that are difficult to satisfy in realistic implementations, particularly with infinite-dimensional optical fields. The almost-qudit framework addresses this issue by quantifying the leakage of quantum states beyond a target subspace. Although such leakage can severely compromise randomness certification for fixed preparation and measurement inputs, we show that averaging over the full input ensemble can mitigate this vulnerability and extend the range of tolerable leakage. This enhanced robustness enables nonzero randomness certification using low-squeezing single-mode Gaussian states and homodyne detection, thus offering an experimentally accessible continuous-variable implementation.
one_liner: Input-ensemble averaging makes semi-device-independent randomness certification robust to dimensional leakage in continuous-variable optical systems.
why_it_matters: It enables nonzero certified randomness with experimentally accessible low-squeezing Gaussian states and homodyne detection.
detailed_summary: The study treats optical preparations as almost-qudits whose states can leak outside a designated finite-dimensional subspace. Although leakage can defeat certification for fixed inputs, averaging over the complete input ensemble substantially increases the tolerable leakage. The resulting protocol certifies nonzero randomness using low-squeezing single-mode Gaussian states measured by homodyne detection.
platform_or_system: single-mode Gaussian optics with homodyne detection
main_result: Full-ensemble averaging extends leakage tolerance enough to certify randomness from low-squeezing continuous-variable states.
application_angle: The approach relaxes unrealistic dimension assumptions in optical random-number generation and related semi-device-independent protocols.

title: Random encoders and expurgation improve 1,873 entries of the Grassl qubit code tables
abstract: I report 192 explicit binary stabilizer codes $[[n,k,d]]$ with $53\le n\le 254$ and $5\le d\le 13$ whose minimum distance exceeds the lower bound listed in Grassl's code tables at the same $(n,k)$: 161 codes by one and 31 by two. Through the standard propagation rules they raise 1,873 entries of the table. For 190 of the codes, a random Clifford encoder is followed by expurgation: every logical operator of weight below the target distance is enumerated, and a few logical operators are promoted to stabilizers so that each low-weight one anticommutes with at least one of them. The other two are obtained by puncturing a code from the table and repairing it in the same way. All 192 distances are exact: the lower bound is certified by exhaustive meet-in-the-middle enumeration of up to $4\times10^{13}$ Pauli operators, and the upper bound by an explicit logical operator of weight $d$. A first-moment count explains the results. Expurgated random codes have about eight more logical qubits than a typical random code of the same length and distance, so they beat the table wherever its best known codes are no better than random. The largest gains, up to nine logical qubits, are at $d\ge9$ and $n\gtrsim170$, where the table often gives a lower bound without an explicit code. The same count predicts improvements at 619 further pairs $(n,d)$. The search was run by AI agents. The codes, their certificates and an independent checker are public.
one_liner: Expurgated random stabilizer-code constructions improve 1,873 entries in the Grassl tables using 192 codes with exactly certified distances.
why_it_matters: The public codes and independently checkable certificates expand practical design options for medium- and large-block fault-tolerant quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The paper reports 192 explicit binary stabilizer codes with lengths 53–254 and distances 5–13, improving known lower bounds at fixed length and dimension. Most are generated with random Clifford encoders followed by expurgation that promotes selected logical operators to stabilizers. Exact distances are established through exhaustive meet-in-the-middle searches and explicit minimum-weight logical operators.
main_result: The constructions raise 1,873 Grassl-table entries, with some expurgated codes retaining up to nine more logical qubits than prior bounds.
application_angle: These explicit, verifiable codes can inform error-correction choices for quantum processors requiring moderate-distance block codes.

title: Laser-Direct-Written polymer WGM microring laser integrated on a fiber tip for refractive index sensing
abstract: Whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) microlasers are promising for refractometric sensing, but their practical implementation can be limited by the need for stable resonator-coupler alignment. Here, we demonstrate a Rhodamine B-doped polymer WGM microring laser directly fabricated on an optical-fiber tip, eliminating the external resonator-fiber coupling interface at the sensing head. Micro-droplet coating and UV laser direct writing are combined for fabrication, while finite-difference time-domain simulations guide the microring laser design. The microlasers operate in air and water with thresholds of 0.224 uJ and 0.458 uJ, respectively. Refractometric measurements in aqueous glucose solutions yield a bulk refractive index sensitivity of 364.95 nm/RIU and a detection limit of 2.47 x 10^(-4) RIU. Water-induced polymer changes and photobleaching are also investigated. This fiber-tip architecture provides a basis for probe-based refractometric sensing in environmental and biochemical applications.
one_liner: A polymer WGM microring laser written directly on a fiber tip achieves probe-format refractive-index sensing without an external coupling interface.
why_it_matters: The integrated architecture combines compact delivery and readout with 364.95 nm/RIU sensitivity for aqueous refractometry.
detailed_summary: A Rhodamine B-doped polymer microring is fabricated on an optical-fiber tip using micro-droplet coating and UV laser direct writing, guided by FDTD simulations. The WGM laser operates with pulse-energy thresholds of 0.224 µJ in air and 0.458 µJ in water. Glucose-solution tests yield 364.95 nm/RIU sensitivity and a 2.47×10^-4 RIU detection limit, while water-induced material changes and photobleaching are characterized.
main_result: The integrated microlaser performs aqueous refractometry with 364.95 nm/RIU sensitivity and a 2.47×10^-4 RIU detection limit.
application_angle: Its alignment-free probe geometry is suited to compact environmental and biochemical refractive-index measurements.

title: Neutral-atom quantum features as complementary structural encodings for graph learning
abstract: Structural descriptors provide graph neural networks (GNNs) with positional and topological inductive biases. However, widely used classical encodings based on random walks or Laplacian spectra emphasize specific structural statistics of a graph, leaving room for alternative descriptors. Neutral-atom quantum processing units (QPUs) can realize graph-dependent Rydberg Hamiltonians, allowing graph topology to be probed through dynamical correlation measurements. In this work, we use these measurements as quantum graph features (QGFs), providing a complementary, hardware-derived family of structural encoding that is not accurately described by classical features derived from Laplacian and adjacency matrices, even when supplemented with an extended set of random-walk, geometric descriptors and classical physical models. By appropriately selecting the quench parameters of the Hamiltonian, we access two characteristic correlation regimes with distinct structural signatures: antiferromagnetic-like and ferromagnetic-like. On an intrinsic information benchmark of 15 topological and spectral probing tasks, quantum and hybrid quantum-classical features match or surpass classical descriptors on local topological properties. When supplied to message-passing, attention, and graph-transformer backbones, hybrid quantum-classical features yield improvements that are within cross-fold noise on most cells but sign-consistent across architectures. When comparing noiseless, shot-sampled emulation-derived quantum features with a neutral-atom QPU implementation, the downstream hybrid results with compressed hardware features match their emulated counterparts within $0.01$ F$_1$ on all backbones. On a synthetic family of ladder graphs, QGFs distinguish two specific classes, outperforming the strongest classical structural descriptors by a margin exceeding cross-fold variability.
one_liner: Rydberg-quench correlations from a neutral-atom QPU provide graph features complementary to standard classical structural encodings.
why_it_matters: Hardware-derived features preserve useful graph information under shot noise and can distinguish structures missed by strong classical descriptors.
detailed_summary: Graph topology is encoded into Rydberg Hamiltonians and probed through dynamical correlations in antiferromagnetic-like and ferromagnetic-like quench regimes. Quantum and hybrid features match or exceed classical descriptors on several local-topology probes, while most downstream gains remain within cross-fold noise but are sign-consistent across architectures. Compressed QPU features reproduce emulated hybrid results within 0.01 F1 and separate selected ladder-graph classes beyond classical baselines.
main_result: Neutral-atom correlation features supply complementary structural information and retain downstream performance close to noiseless emulation.
application_angle: The results support near-term QPUs as hardware feature generators for hybrid graph-learning pipelines.

title: Kinetic Cluster Embedding for Qubit Decoherence in Dissipative Spin Baths
abstract: Interpreting the decoherence of a spin qubit requires knowing how the surrounding bath spins behave: whether they fluctuate independently, exchange polarization incoherently, or evolve as coherent groups. These processes can yield the same Hahn-echo coherence time yet produce different coherence signals under pulse control of the qubit. Existing theoretical approaches either capture bath correlations at a cost that grows combinatorially with spin-bath cluster size or neglect polarization transport altogether. We introduce kinetic cluster embedding (KCE), which uses a single dimensionless parameter, comparing the flip-flop coupling of a spin pair with its detuning and linewidth, to decide how each pair must be treated. Pairs that can complete an appreciable exchange oscillation are propagated with the full dissipative quantum dynamics. All other spins are treated as random-telegraph fluctuators coupled through a kinetic network of polarization-transfer rates. We show that for nitrogen-vacancy centers coupled to surface electron spins, KCE propagates about 7 four-spin clusters, compared to more than 10$^5$ propagated by fourth-order master-equation cluster-correlation (ME-CCE4); nevertheless it reproduces ME-CCE4 coherence times to within 15$\%$ for dipolar couplings of order $10^{2}$ times the bath relaxation rate. For a three-dimensional P1 bath, the agreement is within 16$\%$. Coherent multispin clusters emerge as the leading correction to independent fluctuators, and they leave a distinct signature in the CPMG response. Importantly, we find that whether a rate description suffices is set not by coupling strength alone but by whether a pair can exchange polarization coherently before detuning and damping suppress it.
one_liner: Kinetic cluster embedding models correlated spin-bath decoherence while propagating only the few clusters capable of coherent polarization exchange.
why_it_matters: The method preserves experimentally relevant pulse-sequence signatures and coherence times at far lower computational cost than high-order cluster expansions.
detailed_summary: KCE classifies bath-spin pairs using the ratio of flip-flop coupling to detuning and linewidth, treating exchange-capable pairs quantum mechanically and the remainder as kinetic random-telegraph fluctuators. For NV centers near surface electron spins, it propagates roughly seven four-spin clusters instead of more than 100,000 in ME-CCE4 while reproducing coherence times within 15%; agreement for a 3D P1 bath is within 16%. The model also predicts a distinct CPMG signature from coherent multispin clusters.
main_result: KCE reproduces high-order cluster-expansion coherence times within 15–16% using dramatically fewer propagated spin clusters.
application_angle: Efficient bath modeling can improve noise diagnosis, pulse-sequence design, and coherence optimization in diamond quantum sensors and processors.

title: From spectroscopy to quantum dynamics: assessing reduced models of a NaCs molecular gate
abstract: We investigate how spectroscopic calibration and basis selection affect predictions for a dipolar-exchange gate between two optically trapped $^{23}$Na$^{133}$Cs molecules. We construct a 128-state molecular Hamiltonian restricted to the $N=0,1$ rotational manifold, fit two effective optical parameters to three bright microwave transitions, and compare the resulting spectrum with four additional lines. In the coherent pair model, changing the optical polarization angle by $+0.1^\circ$ reduces the calculated gate fidelity from 94.64\% to 1.09\% at fixed carrier frequencies. Retuning the carriers and restoring the target Rabi frequencies recovers 89.31\%. The remaining sensitivity reflects changes in the multilevel pair dynamics that are not removed by target-frequency and target-Rabi recalibration. Enlarging the molecular basis produces nonmonotonic changes in fidelity, although the 11-state and 25-state calculations give closely agreeing logical maps after phase alignment. Two controls with isolated transfer probabilities near 98.45\% yield complete-gate fidelities differing by more than 11 percentage points. We relate these comparisons to a sufficient bound on the error of a projected propagator. The numerical tests quantify agreement among selected bases for a specified coherent Hamiltonian.
one_liner: A multilevel NaCs gate study shows that spectroscopic agreement and high isolated-transfer probability do not guarantee accurate two-molecule gate fidelity.
why_it_matters: It quantifies how calibration errors and basis truncation can undermine neutral-molecule gate predictions even after carrier and Rabi-frequency retuning.
detailed_summary: The authors construct a 128-state Hamiltonian for optically trapped NaCs molecules in the N=0,1 rotational manifolds and calibrate two optical parameters against three microwave lines. A +0.1° polarization-angle shift lowers predicted gate fidelity from 94.64% to 1.09% at fixed carriers; retuning the carriers and target Rabi frequencies restores only 89.31%. Basis enlargement gives nonmonotonic fidelity changes, although 11- and 25-state logical maps closely agree after phase alignment.
main_result: The calculations expose extreme polarization sensitivity and show that conventional spectroscopic recalibration does not remove multilevel gate errors.
application_angle: The results guide calibration tolerances and reduced-model validation for high-fidelity molecular quantum processors.

title: Self-injection-locked dark-soliton Kerr optical frequency combs with high even-order normal dispersion
abstract: We numerically investigate dissipative dark-soliton (DDS) microcombs under the action of pure high even-order normal (HEON) dispersion in a microresonator with the self-injection locking (SIL). Pure 4th, 6th, 10th, and 14th-order normal dispersion can support DDSs formed by interlocked switching waves, directly excited through a SIL-based turnkey scheme without detuning sweeps. Compared to the pure 4th-order case, the switching-wave tail oscillation period increases and its decay rate decreases with the increase of the dispersion order. Although the overall comb bandwidth narrows, the number of non-pump comb lines above a common absolute power threshold increases. Furthermore, the feedback phase controls the DDS duty cycle and intracavity comb-line power distribution, while the increase of the pump power improves the estimated pump-to-comb output conversion efficiency.
one_liner: Simulations predict turnkey self-injection-locked dark-soliton microcombs supported solely by fourth- through fourteenth-order normal dispersion.
why_it_matters: The scheme could simplify reliable microcomb startup while providing phase and pump controls over duty cycle, line powers, and conversion efficiency.
detailed_summary: Numerical Lugiato–Lefever-type modeling shows that pure fourth-, sixth-, tenth-, and fourteenth-order even normal dispersion can sustain dissipative dark solitons formed by interlocked switching waves. Self-injection locking enables direct excitation without a detuning sweep. Increasing dispersion order narrows the total bandwidth but raises the number of non-pump lines above a fixed power threshold, while feedback phase and pump power tune the spectrum and estimated conversion efficiency.
main_result: Pure high even-order normal dispersion supports directly excited dark-soliton combs across dispersion orders 4 through 14.
application_angle: Turnkey dark-soliton microcombs may benefit compact spectroscopy, communications, metrology, and frequency-synthesis systems.

title: Quantum Fluctuations in Noether's Theorem
abstract: When deriving the expression for the Noether's current one obtains a term that is an integral over the Euler-Lagrange equation. This term vanishes along the classical path and so does not contribute to the current. However, quantum particles do not necessarily follow the classical path; this concept is the basis of Feynman's path integral quantization formalism. Thus, for a quantum system, the Euler-Lagrange term does not vanish and, hence, corresponds to a quantum fluctuation of the Noether's current owing to the system deviating from the classical path. Here, we compute this quantum fluctuation from Noether's theorem and the path integral formalism. We find that, for a time invariant system, the expression for the quantum fluctuations is give by minus the functional expression for the Hamiltonian, $ΔE = -H(y)$, evaluated at the distance from the classical path, $y$. As an example we evaluate quantum energy fluctuations of a single Harmonic oscillator. In the short time limit we recover the energy-time uncertainty relation and in the long time limit we recover the zero point energy of the quantum harmonic oscillator.
one_liner: A path-integral treatment interprets the normally vanishing Euler–Lagrange term in Noether currents as a source of quantum fluctuations.
why_it_matters: The framework proposes a direct connection among off-classical paths, conserved-current fluctuations, energy–time uncertainty, and zero-point energy.
detailed_summary: The paper retains the Euler–Lagrange contribution to the Noether current because quantum paths need not satisfy the classical equations of motion. For time-translation symmetry, it identifies the energy fluctuation as ΔE = −H(y), with the Hamiltonian functional evaluated at displacement y from the classical path. Applied to a harmonic oscillator, the expression is reported to recover energy–time uncertainty at short times and zero-point energy at long times.
main_result: The proposed Noether-current fluctuation formula reproduces familiar short- and long-time energy scales for a harmonic oscillator.
application_angle: If validated more broadly, the formalism could offer a new analytical tool for fluctuation calculations in quantum optical and oscillator systems.

title: Shared Lookups and Lazy Residues: Fewer Toffoli Gates for Factoring RSA-2048
abstract: Gidney's 2025 construction for factoring RSA-2048 with few logical qubits spends most of its Toffoli gates on discrete-log table lookups and residue uncomputation. We reduce both costs. Shared lookups return entries for several primes of a residue number system at once because they have the same address. Retained intermediate residues remove recomputation during cleanup and enable lazy arithmetic with a single final modular reduction. We prove output preservation and estimate resources with an open benchmark built on the reference simulator. Against the best reference setting within the same logical-qubit budget, using the published model for the reference and benchmark counts for our circuits, we obtain $15\%$ fewer Toffolis at $1{,}461$ qubits ($5.08 \times 10^{9}$ per factoring) and $46\%$ fewer at $1{,}806$ qubits ($2.55 \times 10^{9}$). A matched ablation finds $28.8\%$ fewer Toffolis from three-prime sharing at fixed window and checkpoint settings. Architecture-specific timing determines how much becomes a runtime saving.
one_liner: Shared table lookups and retained residues reduce the logical Toffoli cost projected for factoring RSA-2048 under a fixed qubit budget.
why_it_matters: The circuit optimizations substantially lower a dominant fault-tolerant resource cost without changing the algorithm’s output.
detailed_summary: The construction shares discrete-log lookups across several residue-number-system primes with a common address and retains intermediate residues to avoid cleanup recomputation. Lazy arithmetic postpones modular reduction to a single final operation, with output preservation proved and circuits evaluated using an open benchmark. Relative to the best reference settings at matched logical-qubit budgets, projected Toffoli counts fall by 15% at 1,461 qubits and 46% at 1,806 qubits.
main_result: The optimized design projects 5.08×10^9 Toffolis at 1,461 logical qubits and 2.55×10^9 at 1,806 qubits.
application_angle: Lower Toffoli counts reduce the fault-tolerant hardware and runtime burden of large-scale cryptanalytic quantum computing, subject to architecture-specific timing.

title: Time- and phase-resolved emulation of sign-selective counterdiabatic dynamics in a superconducting qutrit
abstract: In cyclic three-level systems, phase-sensitive interference can convert a coupling-sign reversal into a population contrast, providing a controllable analogue of handedness. We emulate this mechanism in a superconducting transmon qutrit using two resonant single-photon drives and a phase-controlled effective two-photon drive. Effective loop phases \(Φ_L=+π/2\) and \(Φ_R=-π/2\), separated by \(π\), reverse the auxiliary contribution to the dark--bright coupling, canceling the intrinsic nonadiabatic term for \(L\) and reinforcing it for \(R\). Time-resolved trajectories reveal dark-pathway transfer for \(L\) and bright-manifold participation for \(R\). Measured late-time averages give a target-state population contrast of 0.929. Loop-phase measurements establish phase selectivity, while pulse-area and common-mode amplitude scans characterize the operating regime and control sensitivity. These results provide direct time- and phase-domain access to sign-selective counterdiabatic interference in a programmable cyclic qutrit.
one_liner: A superconducting transmon qutrit emulates sign-selective counterdiabatic interference with time- and loop-phase-resolved control.
why_it_matters: The experiment demonstrates programmable discrimination between opposite coupling signs through coherent interference, reaching 0.929 population contrast.
detailed_summary: Two resonant single-photon drives and a phase-controlled effective two-photon drive form a cyclic three-level loop in a transmon qutrit. Loop phases of +π/2 and −π/2 cancel or reinforce the intrinsic nonadiabatic dark–bright coupling, producing distinct dark-path and bright-manifold trajectories. Late-time measurements yield a target-state population contrast of 0.929, and amplitude and pulse-area scans map control sensitivity.
main_result: Phase-reversed cyclic driving produces sign-selective counterdiabatic dynamics with a measured target-state population contrast of 0.929.
application_angle: Programmable phase-sensitive interference can support robust control studies, synthetic chirality, and analogue simulations on superconducting quantum hardware.

title: Perfect Wave Transfer in Nonconformal Tomonaga-Luttinger Liquids
abstract: Perfect wave transfer (PWT) reproduces spatial reflection at a common finite time under a fixed Hamiltonian. We classify this process for open compact bosons and inhomogeneous Tomonaga--Luttinger liquids, distinguishing transfer of oscillator and neutral observables from transfer on the charged field algebra. In the single-charge model, the first two notions coincide. Global transfer additionally requires rephasing of the compact zero mode. For regular reflection-symmetric channels, exact oscillator transfer forces an odd multiple of the optical crossing time and a strictly ordered, parity-compatible spectrum differing from the conformal ladder at only finitely many levels. This spectral condition is also sufficient when the Robin boundary data induced by the physical profile are included. Requiring Neumann conditions after the Liouville transformation instead forces conformality. We construct an explicit, regular one-defect family for every $r>1/2$. Its transfer parameters are precisely the reduced fractions $r=p/q$ with odd numerator and denominator, with shortest transfer time $pL/v_0$. At the delay $3L/v_0$, the $r=3/5$ profile has numerical contrast $K_{\max}/K_{\min}\simeq 12.913$, compared with $81$ for $r=3$. Two independent conservative discretizations show second-order convergence on fixed mode bands. Occupation- and charge-constrained error estimates quantify robustness, while an exact homogeneous-chain calculation explains the $J^{2/3}$ resolved-band scale also observed in the engineered channels. These results provide a spectral design method and finite-device benchmarks for quadratic quantum channels. An interacting microscopic realization remains open.
one_liner: A spectral design framework enables perfect wave transfer in regular, nonconformal Tomonaga–Luttinger liquid channels.
why_it_matters: It supplies finite-device benchmarks and robustness bounds for engineering quadratic quantum channels with exact state-transfer dynamics.
detailed_summary: The authors classify perfect transfer of oscillator, neutral, and charged observables in open compact bosons and inhomogeneous Tomonaga–Luttinger liquids. For regular reflection-symmetric channels, oscillator transfer requires a parity-compatible spectrum and occurs at odd multiples of the optical crossing time. An explicit one-defect family supports exact transfer for rational parameters with odd numerator and denominator, while numerical discretizations show second-order convergence and quantify finite-band robustness.
main_result: Regular nonconformal channels are constructed that achieve exact oscillator transfer at analytically specified times and with quantified finite-device errors.
application_angle: The spectral conditions offer a design route for low-dimensional quantum channels, although an interacting microscopic implementation remains unresolved.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Classical Communications for DPMZM-based NG-PON2 Systems
abstract: This paper presents a framework for integrating quantum detection techniques into a Dual-Parallel Mach-Zehnder Modulator (DPMZM)-based Next Generation Passive Optical Network 2 (NG-PON2) communication system. We present a system model for the DPMZM-based NG-PON2 quantum communication system and characterize its signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), demonstrating its superiority over conventional MZM-based systems. We analyze the performance of various quantum modulation techniques, including binary phase-shift keying, quadrature phase-shift keying, and M-ary quadrature amplitude modulation. A comprehensive analytical framework is developed to evaluate the SNR, BER, and mutual information for both classical and quantum detection schemes within the DPMZM-based NG-PON2 quantum communication system. Our simulation results show that quantum detection significantly outperforms classical detection, and the DPMZM architecture further enhances the performance over the baseline MZM architecture by improving the effective modulation efficiency and receiver sensitivity.
one_liner: Quantum detection improves simulated NG-PON2 links using dual-parallel Mach–Zehnder modulation across several modulation formats.
why_it_matters: The framework suggests a path to higher receiver sensitivity and modulation efficiency in future passive optical access networks.
detailed_summary: The paper models an NG-PON2 link built around a dual-parallel Mach–Zehnder modulator and compares classical and quantum detection. It derives analytical metrics for SNR, bit-error rate, and mutual information under BPSK, QPSK, and M-ary QAM. Simulations indicate that quantum detection outperforms classical reception and that DPMZM improves performance relative to a conventional MZM baseline.
main_result: Simulations predict superior SNR, BER, mutual information, and receiver sensitivity from combining DPMZM modulation with quantum detection.
application_angle: The proposed architecture targets capacity and sensitivity upgrades for next-generation passive optical access networks.

title: Parametric $\mathrm{CZ}$ Gates in a Tunable Tripod Architecture with Fixed-Frequency Superconducting Qubits
abstract: Efficient implementation of the operations required for quantum error correction in superconducting quantum computers requires high gate fidelity, adequate qubit connectivity, and selective control of interactions. Sharing a single coupler among multiple qubits can improve connectivity, but also requires accounting for its effects on qubits outside the target pair. In this work, we numerically investigate the feasibility of implementing parametric-resonance $\mathrm{CZ}$ gates in a tunable tripod structure consisting of three fixed-frequency transmon qubits connected to a single tunable coupler. We modulate the external flux applied to the coupler and optimize the pulse parameters for each qubit pair to construct $\mathrm{CZ}_{01}$, $\mathrm{CZ}_{02}$, and $\mathrm{CZ}_{12}$ gates. We calculate the time evolution of a Hamiltonian that includes three energy levels for each circuit element and evaluate gate fidelity and leakage after virtual Z correction. The fidelities obtained for the target-pair computational blocks, whose input and output basis states have both the coupler and spectator qubit in their ground states, are 0.9943, 0.9834, and 0.9907, respectively. We also find that population preservation at the end of the gate depends on the initial state of the spectator qubit. These results demonstrate the possibility of constructing $\mathrm{CZ}$ operations for each qubit pair through flux modulation of a shared coupler while maintaining fixed data-qubit frequencies. They also highlight the need to evaluate performance and optimize control over the full computational space, including the spectator qubit.
one_liner: Flux-modulated parametric CZ gates connect every qubit pair in a three-transmon tripod sharing one tunable coupler.
why_it_matters: Shared couplers can raise superconducting-qubit connectivity, but spectator-state dependence exposes a key control challenge for error correction.
detailed_summary: A numerical three-level circuit model evaluates flux-modulated CZ gates between all pairs of three fixed-frequency transmons coupled through one tunable element. After pulse optimization and virtual-Z correction, target-block fidelities are 0.9943, 0.9834, and 0.9907. Population preservation varies with the spectator qubit's initial state, showing that target-subspace metrics alone do not capture full-system performance.
main_result: Parametric CZ operations are obtained for all three qubit pairs with target-block fidelities of 0.9834–0.9943 while data-qubit frequencies remain fixed.
application_angle: The topology could provide compact connectivity for superconducting error-correction circuits if spectator-dependent errors are controlled across the full computational space.

title: Interaction-enabled charging and thermal crossover of the spin-work deficit in a Hubbard double quantum dot
abstract: We study how conservation of total spin affects the extractable work of an interacting Hubbard double quantum dot charged in the presence of unresolved quasistatic detuning fluctuations. The full fermionic Fock space is used to model preparation through electronic reservoirs, whereas the additional work deficit associated with spin conservation arises entirely from the singlet and triplet states at half filling. At zero detuning, modulation of the symmetric tunnel barrier couples two singlets of even parity. The corresponding transition matrix element vanishes when U = V . An exact formula for the additional work deficit follows from passive spectral rearrangement under two extraction constraints: conservation of particle number alone and conservation of both particle number and total spin. At low temperature, an expansion in the detuning response gives a leading estimate of the noise amplitude at which this deficit first appears. Increasing the preparation temperature changes the triplet population and produces a crossover at s2 = q, where the additional spin constraint becomes nonbinding for the averaged state, even though both ergotropies may continue to decrease. We obtain a semi-analytic expression for this crossover by separating the thermal Gibbs weights from the singlet dynamics under a fixed charging pulse. Averaging over symmetric detuning disorder also restores parity in the density matrix and allows singlet eigenvalues of different parity to exchange order, changing the branch that determines the thermal boundary. The work values are optimal over specified classes of unitary operations and do not establish the yield of a finite discharge protocol.
one_liner: A Hubbard double quantum dot reveals how spin conservation, interactions, temperature, and detuning noise constrain extractable work.
why_it_matters: The analysis identifies operating boundaries for interaction-enabled quantum batteries under realistic symmetry and quasistatic-noise constraints.
detailed_summary: The study computes the extra work deficit caused by total-spin conservation in a charged Hubbard double quantum dot using the full fermionic Fock space. At half filling, singlet and triplet populations determine the difference between particle-number-constrained and spin-constrained ergotropy. Analytical and semi-analytical results locate low-temperature noise onset and a temperature-dependent crossover where the spin constraint becomes nonbinding for the disorder-averaged state.
main_result: Exact and semi-analytic expressions identify when spin conservation creates an additional ergotropy deficit and when thermal populations remove that constraint.
application_angle: The results guide charging conditions for quantum-dot energy-storage devices, though they do not demonstrate work extraction with a finite discharge protocol.

title: An acousto-optic colorimeter for color psychophysics
abstract: A complete model of human color perception requires the ability to present any color as a stimulus.Most existing measurements were collected with physical color samples, and current laboratory generators, such as displays and multi-primary LED systems, work with a small number of fixed primaries. Published color-difference data therefore cover about 40\% of the CIE~$xy$ chromaticity diagram, while commercial wide-gamut displays already reach two thirds of it and need difference metrics there. We describe an acousto-optic colorimeter that lets the experimenter choose the primaries. The device selects up to four narrow bands from a supercontinuum (white-light) laser, each with electronically set wavelength and intensity, and covers 95\% of the CIE~$xy$ chromaticity diagram. Threshold-scale color differences, presented in alternation as in a discrimination experiment, are reproduced with a mean error of 0.08--0.12 CIEDE2000 units ($ΔE_{00}$) at five CIE-recommended color centers. Because one color can be built from many combinations of narrow bands, the bands are chosen for the task: the finest adjustment for color matching, the least disagreement between observers for color-difference measurement. In simulations with 151~individual observers from a published dataset, with these bands observers see colors 0.6--1.9~$ΔE_{00}$ from the intended one on average, against 1.2--2.5~$ΔE_{00}$ on a calibrated wide-gamut LCD, lower at every center. The approach applies to any narrowband source and lets experimenters use saturated colors while limiting the effect of individual differences in color vision.
one_liner: A four-band acousto-optic source generates electronically tunable color stimuli spanning 95% of the CIE xy chromaticity diagram.
why_it_matters: It enables precise psychophysics with saturated, task-optimized stimuli beyond the fixed-primary gamut of displays and LED systems.
detailed_summary: The instrument selects up to four narrow spectral bands from a supercontinuum laser, with electronically controlled wavelength and intensity. It covers 95% of the CIE xy diagram and reproduces threshold-scale alternating stimuli with mean errors of 0.08–0.12 ΔE00 at five standard color centers. Simulations over 151 observers show lower average observer-dependent color error than a calibrated wide-gamut LCD at every tested center.
main_result: The device achieves 95% CIE xy coverage and reproduces threshold-scale color differences with 0.08–0.12 ΔE00 mean error.
application_angle: Selectable primaries support wide-gamut color-difference experiments while reducing errors caused by individual variation in color vision.

title: Single-photon scattering by a nanofiber-coupled atomic chain: beyond independent radiation
abstract: We study single-photon scattering by a nanofiber-coupled atomic chain, comparing a full microscopic model with an independent-radiation approximation. We show that nearly equal transmission probabilities can coexist with substantially different transmitted temporal modes, even after adjusting their relative delay. For a reference chain, a decomposition into collective atomic resonances relates this discrepancy mainly to spectral-phase changes caused by the omitted interatomic couplings. Parameter scans delimit this phase-dominated regime, and controlled comparisons separate the effects of coherent exchange and collective decay.
one_liner: Collective atomic couplings reshape transmitted single-photon temporal modes even when nanofiber-chain transmission probabilities barely change.
why_it_matters: It shows that transmission intensity alone can conceal phase and waveform errors critical to photonic quantum interfaces.
detailed_summary: The authors compare a microscopic model of a nanofiber-coupled atomic chain with an approximation in which atoms radiate independently. Similar transmission probabilities can mask substantial differences in the transmitted temporal mode that persist after compensating for delay. Collective-resonance decomposition and parameter scans attribute the discrepancy mainly to spectral-phase changes from coherent exchange and collective decay.
main_result: Interatomic couplings are shown to produce large temporal-mode changes in transmitted photons despite nearly unchanged transmission probability.
application_angle: Accurate collective modeling is essential for preserving photon waveforms in waveguide-QED memories, routers, and quantum-network interfaces.

title: A Tutorial on Practical QKD Post-Processing Algorithms Using a GUI-Based Simulation Framework
abstract: Recent experimental demonstrations of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) have attracted significant attention for their ability to establish information-theoretically secure encryption keys for next-generation communication systems. As practical deployment accelerates, the realization of compact, scalable, and high-throughput discrete-variable (DV) QKD systems has become increasingly important. While advances in photonic integration are enabling low-size, low-weight, and low-power QKD hardware, the security and performance of these systems rely heavily on efficient post-processing techniques to generate identical, secure keys. This tutorial presents a comprehensive algorithm-level review of practical post-processing techniques for DV-QKD, with particular emphasis on information reconciliation methods based on Cascade, Winnow, low-density parity-check (LDPC), and polar codes. We also analyze the theoretical asymptotic and finite-size secret key rates (SKRs) of DV-QKD and benchmark these bounds against the practical SKRs achieved using actual post-processing algorithms. Furthermore, we present a server-client model to implement the entire QKD post-processing pipeline. The performance is evaluated in terms of QBER and SKR across various system parameters, considering the complete post-processing pipeline, including sifting, information reconciliation, privacy amplification, and authentication. This tutorial also presents a graphical user interface (GUI) for the QKD post-processing methods, enabling researchers, industry practitioners, and academic users to visualize and analyze the impact of different post-processing techniques and system parameters, such as QBER, on the SKR performance of DV-QKD systems.
one_liner: A GUI-based simulator benchmarks complete DV-QKD post-processing pipelines and their practical secret-key rates.
why_it_matters: It connects finite-size security theory to implementable reconciliation, privacy amplification, authentication, and server-client workflows.
detailed_summary: The tutorial compares Cascade, Winnow, LDPC, and polar-code information reconciliation within a complete DV-QKD post-processing chain. It evaluates QBER and practical secret-key rate against asymptotic and finite-size bounds, while also covering sifting, privacy amplification, and authentication. A GUI and server-client model support algorithm selection and system-level exploration.
main_result: The work delivers an integrated framework for benchmarking practical DV-QKD post-processing algorithms against theoretical secret-key-rate bounds.
application_angle: The framework can guide selection and optimization of reconciliation methods for compact, scalable, high-throughput QKD deployments.

title: Tomography of approximately Gaussian mixed states
abstract: Moment-based tomography efficiently reconstructs Gaussian states, but stochastic phase noise generally produces mixed, non-Gaussian outputs. For approximately Gaussian outputs, we formulate reconstruction as a problem in quantum learning theory under model misspecification. Our trace-distance guarantee separates the intrinsic Gaussian approximation error from statistical errors in estimating the first moments and covariance matrix. Using recent Gaussian trace-distance bounds, we obtain linear dependence of the statistical contribution on moment errors when the covariance inverses remain bounded, improving on the square-root dependence on covariance error in earlier guarantees. A Fock-space truncation procedure provides certified, convergent lower and upper bounds on the intrinsic error. Under an explicit sub-Gaussian condition on the heterodyne outcomes, the sufficient sample count scales inversely with the square of the allowed statistical error remaining after accounting for the approximation error. We verify the statistical condition for stochastic phase rotations and heralded unitary-averaged states with bounded input squeezing. We apply the framework to probabilistic unitary averaging for phase noise reduction, quantifying reconstruction error and accounting for heralding overhead in the total number of estimation attempts.
one_liner: Moment-based tomography gains certified trace-distance guarantees for mixed states that are only approximately Gaussian.
why_it_matters: It makes efficient optical-state reconstruction more trustworthy under phase noise, model mismatch, and probabilistic heralding.
detailed_summary: The authors formulate approximate-Gaussian tomography as quantum learning under model misspecification, separating intrinsic model error from moment-estimation error. Their trace-distance bound depends linearly on moment errors when covariance inverses are bounded. Certified Fock-space truncation bounds the intrinsic error, and sub-Gaussian heterodyne statistics yield explicit sample-complexity guarantees.
platform_or_system: Heterodyne tomography of continuous-variable optical states
main_result: The method provides certified, convergent reconstruction-error bounds with improved linear sensitivity to covariance-estimation errors.
application_angle: It supports reliable characterization of noisy continuous-variable photonic states while accounting for phase noise and heralding overhead.

title: Motion-Induced Polaron Resonance beyond the Orthogonality Catastrophe
abstract: We investigate the spectroscopic response of a repulsively interacting, infinitely heavy impurity moving at constant velocity $v$ through a one-dimensional ideal Fermi gas. Using an exact functional-determinant approach, we calculate the Ramsey response and spectral function, fully accounting for many-body particle-hole excitations. We uncover a strongly nonmonotonic dependence on impurity velocity: decoherence is enhanced around the Fermi velocity, whereas sufficiently rapid motion restores a narrow, long-lived polaron resonance. A long-time wave-packet analysis yields analytical expressions for the polaron energy and decay rate over the full velocity range and quantitatively captures the numerical results. At high velocity, the polaron energy approaches the mean-field value, the decay rate vanishes as $1/v$, and the spectral weight approaches unity. Thus, rapid prescribed motion provides a dynamical route to suppressing the orthogonality catastrophe and restoring polaron coherence even for an infinitely heavy impurity, where recoil is entirely absent.
one_liner: Rapid impurity motion restores a narrow polaron resonance by dynamically suppressing the orthogonality catastrophe.
why_it_matters: The result identifies motion as a control knob for preserving impurity coherence and sharpening many-body spectroscopic signals.
detailed_summary: An exact functional-determinant calculation captures Ramsey response and spectral functions for an infinitely heavy repulsive impurity moving through a one-dimensional ideal Fermi gas. Decoherence peaks near the Fermi velocity, but at high velocity the resonance narrows, spectral weight approaches unity, and the decay rate falls as 1/v. A long-time wave-packet analysis reproduces the energy and decay behavior across the velocity range.
platform_or_system: Moving impurity in a one-dimensional ideal Fermi gas
main_result: Sufficiently fast prescribed motion restores a long-lived polaron resonance even without impurity recoil.
application_angle: Velocity-controlled coherence could improve impurity-based spectroscopy and dynamical probes of quantum many-body media.

title: Reconstructing intracell polarization with calibrated sapphire-window optics for collimated blue-light generation in a rubidium cell
abstract: We study the polarization dependence of collimated blue light (CBL) generated near 420~nm by resonant four-wave mixing in thermal rubidium vapor in a sapphire-window cell driven at 780 and 776~nm. Sapphire windows can transform the polarization of pump light before it reaches the vapor, complicating the interpretation of polarization-dependent nonlinear emission. We measured the 780-nm pump Stokes state at an external before-cell reference plane to calibrate the common HWP/QWP preparation optics and recorded 266 off-resonant external output Stokes states after the complete sapphire-window rubidium cell at 90, 100, and 110~$^\circ$C in two propagation orientations. Direct paired-wavelength measurements show a mean before-cell 780/776 separation of $4.29^\circ$ and temperature- and orientation-specific complete-cell rotations of $22.20^\circ$--$32.02^\circ$, with rms residuals of $4.83^\circ$--$12.87^\circ$. Using this calibrated co-prepared pump description, we analyzed 2574 measurements of total spectrally filtered 420-nm CBL intensity. Across the six temperature--orientation data sets, a complete nine-coefficient second-order response yielded cross-validated $R^2$ values of 0.636 to 0.828. These paired-wavelength measurements establish, for each temperature--orientation data set, a fixed relative Stokes-space map between the two co-prepared pump trajectories, with the residual of this mapping defining the experimental uncertainty of the correlated two-pump reduction used in the response model. Thus, the resulting framework combines a reconstructed vapor-entrance polarization coordinate with direct two-wavelength calibration of the assembled cell and provides a practical basis for polarization-controlled nonlinear-optical experiments in sapphire-window vapor cells.
one_liner: Calibrated Stokes-space maps reconstruct pump polarization inside a sapphire-window rubidium cell for blue-light generation.
why_it_matters: It resolves window-induced polarization distortions that otherwise obscure control and interpretation of vapor-cell nonlinear optics.
detailed_summary: The experiment calibrates 780- and 776-nm pump polarization through an assembled sapphire-window rubidium cell using 266 off-resonant Stokes measurements across temperatures and orientations. Complete-cell rotations span 22.20°–32.02°, with orientation- and temperature-dependent residuals. A nine-coefficient second-order model fitted to 2574 filtered 420-nm intensity measurements achieves cross-validated R² values of 0.636–0.828.
main_result: The study reconstructs vapor-entrance pump polarization and quantitatively predicts polarization-dependent 420-nm emission across six operating configurations.
application_angle: The calibration enables reproducible polarization control in compact atomic-vapor frequency converters and nonlinear-optical sources.

title: Interface-driven second harmonic generation in indium tin oxide/gold nanolayers: density and mass discontinuities matter
abstract: Second harmonic generation from transparent conductive oxides and metals is traditionally attributed to Coulomb, magnetic Lorentz, and convective sources. We show that this picture is incomplete in deeply subwavelength indium tin oxide/gold bilayers. Measurements reveal two robust spectral features, a broad maximum near 1000 nm and an epsilon-near-zero peak near 1350 nm, that persist across wide variations in material and excitation parameters. Hydrodynamic-Maxwell simulations identify an interface-specific convective mechanism activated by freeelectron density and effective-mass discontinuities at the oxide-metal boundary. As electronic homogenization develops across the bilayer, the response evolves toward one described by conventional Coulomb, Lorentz, and leading convective terms. These results establish second harmonic generation as a sensitive probe of interface-driven nonlinearities and suggest a broader role for electronic discontinuities in shaping nonlinear optical processes at surface and buried material interfaces.
one_liner: ITO/gold nanolayers exhibit interface-driven second-harmonic generation caused by carrier-density and effective-mass discontinuities.
why_it_matters: It reveals a missing nonlinear source in ultrathin heterostructures and turns SHG into a probe of buried electronic interfaces.
detailed_summary: Experiments on deeply subwavelength ITO/gold bilayers show a broad SHG maximum near 1000 nm and an epsilon-near-zero peak near 1350 nm. Hydrodynamic-Maxwell simulations attribute the response to an interface-specific convective term activated by discontinuities in free-electron density and effective mass. As electronic homogenization increases, conventional Coulomb, Lorentz, and leading convective sources regain dominance.
main_result: The work identifies electronic density and effective-mass discontinuities as a robust source of interface-driven second-harmonic generation.
application_angle: The mechanism offers new design freedom for nanoscale frequency converters and nondestructive optical characterization of buried interfaces.

title: Sharp error tolerance of the monogamy-of-entanglement game
abstract: The BB84 monogamy-of-entanglement (MoE) game has numerous applications in quantum cryptography, including quantum key distribution, position verification, and unclonable encryption. In this short note, we improve the error threshold for parallel repetition with identical answer strings from the approximately $3.7\%$ certified by the original bound to the sharp threshold $(1-1/\sqrt2)/2\approx14.64\%$. When the players need not give identical answers, we also obtain exponential decay whenever the sum of their error tolerances is below this threshold. These bounds strengthen existing security reductions to the BB84 MoE game, improving security bounds and certified noise tolerances for cryptographic protocols.
one_liner: The BB84 monogamy-of-entanglement game has a sharp parallel-repetition error threshold of about 14.64%.
why_it_matters: The stronger bound substantially raises certified noise tolerance in security reductions for several BB84-based cryptographic protocols.
detailed_summary: The note improves the certified error threshold for parallel repetition with identical answer strings from about 3.7% to the sharp value (1−1/√2)/2, approximately 14.64%. When players may return different strings, exponential decay still holds if the sum of their error tolerances remains below that threshold. The result directly strengthens security reductions based on the BB84 monogamy game.
main_result: A sharp 14.64% error threshold is established, with exponential security decay under corresponding identical- and unequal-answer conditions.
application_angle: The bound improves provable noise tolerance for QKD, position verification, unclonable encryption, and related protocols.

title: Direct-decision quantum sensing for classifying transient NMR signals
abstract: Task-oriented quantum sensing aims to extract decision-relevant information directly, without first reconstructing the full signal. We study this approach for mixture-threshold classification of transient NMR-like signals generated from molecular spin Hamiltonians, motivated by small-volume molecular sensing. Using analytical models and numerical simulations, we compare classical coil readout followed by matched-filter classification with quantum computational sensing (QCS), in which trainable controls interleaved with signal-driven sensor-qubit evolution map the transient directly to a decision score. We consider both the sensor-ensemble limit and strict single-sensor single-shot readout. Increasing QCS control depth can improve robustness and class-dependent output contrast. Ensemble accuracy can rise rapidly for some waveform pairs, whereas single-shot correctness improves more gradually because one projective outcome must distinguish the classes. Repeated acquisitions improve both routes by averaging independent fluctuations, while disorder-aware training mitigates quasistatic inhomogeneity in the modeled sensor ensemble. QCS can outperform inductive readout under the modeled conditions, for example when coil transfer is weak or receiver noise limits coil performance. However, the simulated QCS protocols at lower effective sensor coupling require long sensing intervals, whereas short-time protocols require a much stronger effective drive at the sensor. Practical advantage therefore depends on jointly attainable source-signal strength, signal-to-sensor transfer, qubit coherence, and readout resources.
one_liner: Trainable qubit controls classify transient NMR-like signals directly, potentially outperforming noisy or weakly coupled inductive readout.
why_it_matters: It quantifies when task-specific quantum sensing could benefit small-volume molecular detection without reconstructing the full NMR waveform.
detailed_summary: The study numerically compares matched-filter classification after classical coil readout with quantum computational sensing, where controlled sensor-qubit evolution maps transient molecular-spin signals directly to a decision score. Greater control depth improves robustness and class contrast, while disorder-aware training mitigates quasistatic ensemble inhomogeneity. The modeled quantum route can outperform inductive detection when coil transfer is weak or receiver noise dominates, but practical gains require a favorable balance of coupling strength, coherence time, acquisition count, and readout resources.
platform_or_system: Controlled sensor qubit for transient NMR signals
main_result: Simulations identify regimes where direct-decision quantum sensing exceeds inductive matched-filter classification and remains robust to modeled ensemble disorder.
application_angle: The method targets rapid classification of molecular mixtures in small-volume NMR sensing without full signal reconstruction.

title: Resonance-engineered single-photon routing in an asymmetric Jaynes-Cummings cavity-waveguide system
abstract: We investigate single-photon scattering and routing in an asymmetric cavity-waveguide quantum electrodynamics system consisting of a Jaynes-Cummings cavity-emitter subsystem coupled to two one-dimensional waveguides. Using a real-space scattering approach, we derive an exact three-channel scattering matrix and analytical expressions for the channel-resolved scattering amplitudes. The scattering response is governed by the interplay of asymmetric cavity-waveguide coupling, atom-cavity detuning, coherent preparation of a single-photon superposition across multiple input channels, and intrinsic dissipation. Coupling asymmetry controls the relative weights of the cavity-mediated scattering pathways, whereas atom-cavity detuning modifies their spectral response. Coherent multichannel input states provide an additional phase-sensitive control of the output probabilities through interference. In particular, we identify an analytical condition, $J_2=2J_1$ and $α_1=-α_2$, under which the probability in the second output channel becomes independent of photon energy; for an equal-weight normalized input, this probability is 1/2. We further show how cavity and atomic dissipation reduce the probability remaining in the guided channels. These results provide a framework for resonance-engineered single-photon routing in asymmetric Jaynes-Cummings cavity-waveguide systems.
one_liner: An exact scattering model shows how asymmetry, detuning, and coherent input phase control three-channel single-photon routing.
why_it_matters: The analytical design rules support phase-sensitive, resonance-engineered photon routing for integrated quantum photonic networks.
detailed_summary: A real-space scattering treatment yields an exact three-channel scattering matrix for a Jaynes-Cummings cavity-emitter subsystem coupled asymmetrically to two one-dimensional waveguides. Coupling asymmetry and atom-cavity detuning set the resonance pathways, while coherent multichannel inputs tune output probabilities through phase-sensitive interference. For J2=2J1 and opposite input amplitudes, the second-channel probability is energy independent and equals 1/2 for normalized equal-weight input; intrinsic cavity and atomic losses reduce guided-channel probability.
platform_or_system: Asymmetric cavity-emitter coupled to two 1D waveguides
main_result: The work derives exact routing amplitudes and an analytical condition producing an energy-independent 50% probability in one output channel.
application_angle: These rules could guide tunable single-photon routers and interference elements for chip-scale quantum networks.

title: Twisted Compactification, Quotient Quantum Codes and Logical Gates
abstract: Many quantum codes, including balanced-product, bivariate-bicycle and genon codes and the five-qubit code, are quotient codes: a larger code folded onto itself by identifying each check with its image under a deck transformation composed with a symmetry. We show that this is the lattice form of twisted compactification, in which a theory on $X\times F$ carries a symmetry background along $F$, and we use the correspondence in both directions. For monomial quotients of Pauli stabilizer codes, a transfer theorem gives the logical qudits, logical operators and distance bounds from those of the parent, with a Tate cohomology group counting the logical operators that are new. For higher-form and cup-product symmetries the twist is an entangling diagonal circuit; when a finite cover trivializes the background, the code is a dressed quotient, so abelian Pauli codes give non-abelian topological order such as $D(D_4)$. The dressings have Clifford level at most one less than the degree of the twist, and for cubic twists the code dimension is a count of solutions of quadratic equations in cup products, which certifies that the code is not a Pauli stabilizer code when it is not a power of two; on tori and slabs the distance is linear in the size. Twists also create logical gates: three toric codes on $S^3$ have no logical qubits, but on $\mathbb{RP}^3$ the same circuit is a logical $CCZ$. A quarter-turn twist of the 3D fermionic toric code gives codes of linear distance, from $[[768,2,9]]$ up, whose $p+ip$ pump is an explicit finite-time quasi-local evolution that preserves the code space exactly; using the spin-topological response formula of Barkeshli, Hsin and Kobayashi, we identify its logical action as $T$ up to Clifford factors. Finally, twisting abelian gauge theories reach only the quantum doubles $D(G)$ with $[G,G]$ central.
one_liner: Twisted compactification unifies quotient-code constructions and generates linear-distance codes with non-Clifford logical gates.
why_it_matters: It offers a general route from geometric symmetry twists to protected logical qudits, exotic topological order, and gates such as CCZ and T.
detailed_summary: The paper identifies quotient quantum codes as lattice realizations of twisted compactification and proves a transfer theorem connecting parent-code logical content and distance bounds to those of monomial quotients. Higher-form and cup-product twists can dress Abelian Pauli codes into non-Abelian topological phases, with Tate cohomology counting newly created logical operators. Examples include a logical CCZ on three toric codes over real projective three-space and linear-distance fermionic toric-code constructions whose finite-time p+ip pump implements T up to Clifford factors.
main_result: Symmetry twists are shown to produce quotient codes with linear distance and explicit protected CCZ or T logical actions in selected geometries.
application_angle: The framework provides code-design principles for fault-tolerant architectures requiring geometrically generated non-Clifford logical gates.

title: Scanning Probe Control, Quantum Dynamics, and Dispersive Readout of Suspended Carbon Nanotube Resonators
abstract: Suspended carbon nanotubes (CNTs) offer promising opportunities for quantum nanomechanics owing to their small effective mass, strong electrostatic tunability, and mechanical nonlinearity. We develop a unified theoretical framework for coherent control and readout of a suspended CNT driven by an atomic force microscope (AFM) tip and capacitively coupled to a Cooper-pair box (CPB). We first derive the linear and nonlinear Duffing response of the CNT and quantify the effects of AFM force gradients, tip-position fluctuations, and voltage noise on mechanical stability, dephasing, and heating. These results establish operating conditions for coherent actuation with limited backaction. We then quantize the Duffing oscillator, derive its Kerr anharmonicity, and identify the requirements for selective control of individual vibrational transitions. Estimates of thermal occupation and active cooling illustrate the constraints for CNT modes spanning frequencies from 54 MHz to 5.37 GHz. Finally, we derive the CNT--CPB interaction and its dispersive limit, showing how phonon number and parity can be mapped onto the CPB through Ramsey interferometry and detected using quantum-capacitance readout. The resulting framework identifies the conditions under which localized AFM actuation, nonlinear quantum dynamics, and superconducting state-resolved detection can operate within a single CNT device.
one_liner: A unified model combines AFM control, nonlinear phonon dynamics, and CPB-based dispersive readout in suspended carbon nanotubes.
why_it_matters: It specifies operating conditions for localized actuation and state-resolved detection in an exceptionally lightweight quantum nanomechanical platform.
detailed_summary: The theoretical framework derives linear and Duffing responses of a suspended CNT under AFM-tip driving, including force-gradient, tip-jitter, and voltage-noise contributions to instability, dephasing, and heating. Quantization yields Kerr anharmonicity and criteria for resolving individual vibrational transitions across modeled modes from 54 MHz to 5.37 GHz, with thermal occupation and cooling constraints evaluated. In the dispersive CNT-CPB regime, phonon number and parity are mapped onto the superconducting qubit using Ramsey interferometry and read out through quantum capacitance.
platform_or_system: AFM-driven suspended CNT coupled to a Cooper-pair box
main_result: The analysis identifies compatible regimes for coherent CNT actuation, nonlinear quantum control, and dispersive phonon-number or parity readout in one device.
application_angle: The architecture could enable ultrasensitive nanomechanical sensing and controlled studies of nonclassical vibrational states.

title: Quantum subsets discrimination and key sifting with success probability one
abstract: Non-distinguishability of non-orthogonal quantum states is the essential feature of quantum mechanics. In particular, one cannot deterministically orthogonalize the set of quantum states, while probabilistic orthogonalization is possible, including unambiguous state discrimination and discrimination between the subsets. Here, we propose a method for error-free subsets discrimination with significantly increased success probability, which may reach one even for non-orthogonal and linearly dependent input states. This method may be applied in quantum cryptography: An alternative basis reconciliation procedure is described, which may provide unit sifting probability even for a large number of bases and for non-orthogonal states within each basis.
one_liner: A proposed subset-discrimination method can identify nonorthogonal-state groups without error and, under stated conditions, with unit success probability.
why_it_matters: If its assumptions are physically realizable and secure, the method could eliminate basis-sifting loss even with many bases and nonorthogonal states.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes error-free discrimination between subsets of quantum states rather than deterministic identification of each state. It argues that the subset success probability can reach one even when the input states are nonorthogonal and linearly dependent. Applied to quantum cryptography, the construction is presented as an alternative basis-reconciliation procedure with potentially unit sifting probability for many bases, including bases containing nonorthogonal states.
main_result: The proposed protocol achieves error-free subset discrimination with a claimed success probability reaching unity and translates this into unit-probability key sifting.
application_angle: The approach could improve raw-key retention in multi-basis quantum communication, subject to implementation and security validation.

title: A Phase-Balanced Differential Rydberg-Atom Quantum Receiver for Weak GNSS Signal Detection
abstract: This paper proposes a phase-balanced differential Rydberg atomic quantum receiver (DRAQR) for weak-signal recovery, using local-oscillator phase control to reinforce differential signal responses and a shared squeezed-reservoir model to correlate inter-cell quantum projection noise (QPN) and photon shot noise (PSN). An analytical model incorporating QPN, PSN, intrinsic thermal noise (ITN), and inter-cell correlations quantifies signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) gain, outage-constrained minimum detectable power, and bit-error rate (BER) for square $M$-QAM. For the evaluated settings, SNR gain reaches approximately $10$~dB as PSN correlation approaches unity, with BER decreasing as correlation increases. Under Rician fading, at a $0$-dB threshold SNR and maximum outage probability of $0.1$, the minimum detectable power decreases from $-146.95$~dBm at $K=1.155$ to $-159.98$~dBm at $K=2.4$. Analytical results are validated against Monte-Carlo simulations over $150{,}000$ data runs per point for receiver-performance plots.
one_liner: A modeled differential Rydberg receiver uses phase balancing and correlated noise to improve weak GNSS recovery by about 10 dB.
why_it_matters: It connects atomic RF sensing with communication metrics relevant to satellite navigation, including detectable power, outage, and QAM error rate.
detailed_summary: The proposed differential receiver phase-aligns local oscillators across Rydberg-atom cells and models a shared squeezed reservoir that correlates quantum projection and photon shot noise. Its analytical treatment includes those noise sources plus intrinsic thermal noise, producing SNR, outage-constrained sensitivity, and square-QAM BER predictions. For the evaluated parameters, near-unity photon-shot-noise correlation gives about 10 dB SNR gain; Monte Carlo calculations with 150,000 runs per plotted point reproduce the analytical performance trends.
main_result: Modeling predicts roughly 10 dB SNR gain and minimum detectable powers down to -159.98 dBm under the reported Rician-fading conditions.
application_angle: The receiver concept targets weak GNSS and communication-signal recovery using atom-based RF front ends, pending experimental validation.

title: Vertically-coupled microring resonators for lithium niobate on insulator integrated photonics
abstract: We propose and demonstrate lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) microring resonators that are verticallycoupled to index-matched silicon-rich silicon nitride (SiN x ) access waveguides as an alternative to conventional lateral coupling schemes for integrated photonics applications. The wafer-scalable fabrication process involves a planarization step exploiting a single-step and reproducible spin-coating of a SU-8 epoxy spacer layer which allows a controlled separation to be established between the resonator and its access waveguide. The resulting multimode and single-mode microring resonators exhibit, for their fundamental TE 0 mode, intrinsic quality factors of 4.0 x 10 5 and 3.4 x 10 5 , respectively.
one_liner: Vertically coupled LNOI microrings achieve intrinsic quality factors up to 4.0×10^5 using wafer-scalable SU-8 spacer planarization.
why_it_matters: The vertical geometry relaxes lateral coupling constraints and offers a reproducible route to high-Q lithium-niobate photonic circuits.
detailed_summary: The authors vertically couple LNOI microring resonators to index-matched silicon-rich SiNx access waveguides through a controlled SU-8 spacer. A single spin-coating and planarization step supports a wafer-scalable alternative to conventional lateral coupling. Multimode and single-mode rings reach fundamental-TE intrinsic quality factors of 4.0×10^5 and 3.4×10^5, respectively.
